units.title: What is wine?
units.summary: From grape to glass: fermentation, the main styles and where color comes from.

cards.title: Wine is fermented grape juice
cards.body:
Ripe grapes are full of sugar. When **yeast** meets that sugar, it turns it into **alcohol** and **carbon dioxide**. This is **alcoholic fermentation**, and it is how every wine begins.

Yeast lives naturally on grape skins and in wineries, but most winemakers add selected yeast for a reliable result.

cards.title: Sugar decides strength and sweetness
cards.body:
- The more sugar in the grapes, the more alcohol the wine can have.
- If fermentation finishes, the wine is **dry**.
- If it stops early, some sugar remains and the wine tastes **sweet**.

cards.q: What does yeast convert into alcohol during fermentation?
cards.explain: Yeast feeds on the grape's natural sugars (glucose and fructose), producing alcohol and carbon dioxide. Acid, tannin and water are not fermented.

cards.q: Fermentation produces alcohol and ___ ___.
cards.explain: Carbon dioxide (CO₂) usually escapes as a gas. Trap it in a sealed bottle or tank and you get sparkling wine.

cards.q: A wine in which all the sugar has fermented is called dry.
cards.explain: Dry simply means there is little or no sugar left. It has nothing to do with the drying feeling of tannin.

cards.q: If fermentation is stopped while sugar remains, the wine will be…
cards.explain: Leftover sugar is called **residual sugar**. It can be kept by chilling and filtering out the yeast, or by adding alcohol, as with Port.

cards.q: Riper grapes with more sugar can produce wines with higher alcohol.
cards.explain: More sugar means more fuel for yeast. That is why wines from hot, sunny regions often reach 14–15% abv, while cool regions give 11–12.5%.

cards.title: Three families of wine
cards.body:
- **Still wine**: no bubbles. Most wine is still, at roughly 8–15% alcohol.
- **Sparkling wine**: carbon dioxide is trapped in the wine, so it fizzes. Champagne, Prosecco and Cava are examples.
- **Fortified wine**: grape spirit is added, raising alcohol to 15–22%. Port and Sherry are the classics.

cards.title: And three colors
cards.body: Still wines come in **white**, **rosé** and **red**. Sparkling and fortified wines can be any color too. There is red sparkling Lambrusco, pink Champagne and white Port.

cards.q: Which of these is a fortified wine?
cards.explain: Port has grape spirit added during fermentation, which stops it and leaves a sweet, strong wine (about 20% abv).

cards.q: Match each wine to its family
cards.explain: Champagne is sparkling, Sherry is fortified with grape spirit, and Rioja is a still red wine from Spain.

cards.q: Fortified wines usually have more alcohol than still wines.
cards.explain: Adding grape spirit lifts them to about 15–22% abv, compared with about 11–15% for most still wines.

cards.q: Wine with bubbles is called ___ wine.
cards.explain: The bubbles are carbon dioxide from fermentation, trapped in the wine under pressure.

cards.title: Color lives in the skin
cards.body:
Squeeze almost any grape, black or white, and the juice runs clear. Color, along with **tannin** and many aromas, sits in the **skins**.

- **White wine**: the juice is separated from the skins *before* fermentation.
- **Red wine**: black grapes ferment *with* their skins for days or weeks.
- **Rosé**: black grapes spend just a few hours to a couple of days on their skins.

cards.title: The color spectrum
cards.body: Young reds are purple or ruby and fade to garnet and tawny with age. Whites go the other way: they **deepen** from lemon to gold and amber.

cards.q: Where does red wine get its color?
cards.explain: The pulp of nearly all black grapes is colorless. Pigments called **anthocyanins** in the skins dissolve into the wine during fermentation.

cards.q: White wine can be made from black grapes.
cards.explain: Press black grapes gently and keep the juice away from the skins, and you get white wine. Much Champagne is made this way: Blanc de Noirs.

cards.q: How is most rosé made?
options: Black grapes with brief skin contact
cards.explain: A few hours on the skins gives a pink color. Blending red and white is banned for still rosé in the EU, with rosé Champagne the notable exception.

cards.q: Besides color, grape skins also give red wine ___.
cards.explain: Tannin is that drying, gripping sensation on your gums. It comes mainly from skins and seeds, and also from oak.

cards.q: As red wines age, their color tends to move toward…
cards.explain: Reds lose color with age: purple → ruby → garnet → tawny. Whites gain color: lemon → gold → amber.

cards.title: Where the flavor comes from
cards.body:
Three things shape every wine: the **grape** (its aromas and structure), the **place** (climate and soil, together called terroir) and the **winemaker** (choices like oak, temperature and timing).

The same grape can taste very different in Burgundy and California because two of those three things changed.

cards.title: Dry, off-dry, sweet
cards.body:
If yeast eats all the sugar, the wine is **dry**. Stop fermentation early, or start with very ripe or dried grapes, and some sugar remains: **off-dry**, **medium** or **sweet**.

Sweetness is about sugar, not fruitiness. A ripe, fruity wine can still be bone dry.

cards.q: Which three things shape the taste of a wine?
cards.explain: Variety, terroir and winemaking decisions explain most of the differences between wines.

cards.q: A fruity-smelling wine must contain sugar.
cards.explain: Fruitiness is aroma. Many very fruity wines, like New Zealand Sauvignon Blanc, are completely dry.

cards.q: The combined effect of climate, soil and slope on a wine is called ___.
cards.explain: Terroir is the French word for everything about a place that shows in the glass.

cards.q: What makes a wine sweet?
cards.explain: Residual sugar is what yeast didn't convert. Alcohol and oak can feel rich, but they are not sweetness.

cards.q: Match the wine to how it's made
cards.explain: Small changes in the process create completely different styles from the same grapes.

units.title: Tasting like a pro
units.summary: Look, smell, taste and describe: the systematic approach.

cards.title: Four steps, every time
cards.body: Professionals taste the same way every time: **look**, **smell**, **taste**, **conclude**. A routine makes your notes consistent, and it helps you remember wines.

cards.title: Reading the glass
cards.body:
Tilt the glass over something white.

- **Intensity**: pale, medium or deep. Look at the center (the core).
- **Color**: whites are lemon, gold or amber; rosés pink, salmon or orange; reds purple, ruby, garnet or tawny.
- **Clarity**: almost all wines should be clear.

cards.q: What is the first step when tasting wine?
cards.explain: Appearance comes first: clarity, intensity and color give early clues about grape, age and winemaking.

cards.q: Which color describes a young red wine?
cards.explain: Purple or ruby means youth. Tawny and garnet suggest age. Amber and gold are white wine colors.

cards.q: White wines get paler as they age.
cards.explain: The opposite: whites deepen, moving from lemon toward gold and amber as they age or spend time in oak.

cards.q: To judge color, tilt the glass against a ___ background.
cards.explain: A white tablecloth or sheet of paper shows the true color and lets you compare the core with the rim.

cards.title: Swirl, then sniff
cards.body:
Swirling releases aromas into the air above the wine. Take short sniffs and ask two questions:

- **How intense is it?** Light, medium or pronounced.
- **What does it smell of?** Start broad (fruit? flowers?), then get specific (lemon? raspberry? violet?).

cards.title: The aroma families
cards.body:
Most wine aromas fit into a few families: **fruit** (citrus, green, stone, tropical, red, black), **floral**, **herbal**, **spice**, **oak** (vanilla, toast) and **age** (honey, leather, earth).

You cannot be wrong: describe what *you* smell.

cards.q: Why do tasters swirl the wine in the glass?
cards.explain: Swirling coats the glass and helps aromatic compounds evaporate, concentrating the smell above the wine.

cards.q: Match the aroma to its family
cards.explain: Thinking in families first makes it much easier to find the exact word.

cards.q: Vanilla and toast aromas most often come from…
cards.explain: New oak, especially toasted barrels, gives vanilla, toast, smoke and sweet spice notes.

cards.q: Raspberry and strawberry are classed as black fruit aromas.
cards.explain: They are **red fruit** aromas, typical of lighter reds such as Pinot Noir and Grenache. Black fruit means blackcurrant, blackberry and black plum.

cards.title: What your mouth tells you
cards.body:
- **Sweetness**: tip of the tongue. Dry, off-dry, medium or sweet.
- **Acidity**: makes your mouth water.
- **Tannin**: dries and grips your gums (reds).
- **Body**: the weight of the wine, light to full.
- **Finish**: how long the flavor lasts after you swallow.

cards.title: Body is weight
cards.body: Think of milk: skimmed milk is **light**, whole milk **medium**, cream **full**. Alcohol, sugar and extract all add body.

cards.q: Which sensation makes your mouth water?
cards.explain: Acidity triggers saliva. High-acid wines like Sauvignon Blanc and Riesling taste fresh and crisp.

cards.q: A drying, gripping feeling on the gums is caused by…
cards.explain: Tannin binds to proteins in your saliva, leaving that drying sensation, like strong black tea.

cards.q: The length of time flavors linger after swallowing is called the ___.
cards.explain: A long finish is one of the clearest signs of a high-quality wine.

cards.q: A full-bodied wine feels heavier in the mouth than a light-bodied one.
cards.explain: Body is about weight and texture. Alcohol, sugar and dissolved solids all make a wine feel fuller.

cards.q: Match the sensation to where you feel it
cards.explain: Paying attention to *where* you feel something helps separate sensations, for example tannin from acidity.

cards.title: A simple tasting note
cards.body:
A useful note covers the essentials. For example:

*"Pale lemon. Pronounced aromas of grapefruit, gooseberry and grass. Dry, high acidity, light body, medium finish."*

That is all you need to recognize a classic Sauvignon Blanc.

cards.title: Quality in four letters
cards.body:
Professionals judge quality with **BLIC**:

- **Balance**: nothing sticks out.
- **Length**: a long finish.
- **Intensity**: pronounced flavors.
- **Complexity**: many layers.

cards.q: In BLIC, what does the L stand for?
cards.explain: Length (the finish) is a key marker of quality. Great wines linger for a long time.

cards.q: 'Legs' running down the glass show that a wine is high quality.
cards.explain: Legs (or tears) show alcohol and sugar levels, not quality.

cards.q: A wine whose fruit, acidity, tannin and alcohol are in harmony is said to be ___.
cards.explain: Balance is the first test of quality. No single element should dominate.

cards.q: Which description fits a light, crisp white?
cards.explain: Think Muscadet, Pinot Grigio or Chablis: fresh, zesty and light.

cards.title: Describing the finish
cards.body:
After you swallow (or spit), notice how long the flavor lingers. That is the **finish**.

A short finish fades in a few seconds; a long one stays for ten or more. Long, pleasant finishes are one of the clearest signs of quality.

cards.title: Balance and quality
cards.body:
Judge quality with **BLIC**: **Balance** (fruit, acid, tannin, alcohol in harmony), **Length** (the finish), **Intensity** (flavor concentration) and **Complexity** (many different aromas).

A wine that scores well on all four is very good or outstanding.

cards.q: What does the 'finish' of a wine describe?
options: How long the flavor lasts after swallowing
The last wine of a tasting
cards.explain: Finish, or length, is measured in seconds of pleasant flavor after the wine has gone.

cards.q: Match the letter of BLIC to its meaning
cards.explain: BLIC is a simple checklist for judging quality.

cards.q: A very long, pleasant finish is a sign of quality.
cards.explain: Length is one of the most reliable quality markers.

cards.q: Which sensation tells you a wine has high acidity?
options: A sweet taste on the tip of the tongue
cards.explain: Acidity makes you salivate. Drying gums mean tannin; warmth means alcohol.

cards.q: Warmth at the back of the throat is a sign of high ___.
cards.explain: Alcohol feels warm. Wines above about 14% can feel hot if fruit and acidity don't balance them.

units.title: The great white grapes
units.summary: Chardonnay, Sauvignon Blanc, Riesling and Pinot Grigio: the four whites everyone should know.

cards.title: The chameleon
cards.body:
**Chardonnay** takes on the character of where it grows and how it is made.

- **Cool climates** (Chablis, Champagne): green apple, lemon, high acidity.
- **Warm climates** (California, Australia): peach, pineapple, fuller body.
- **Oak and malolactic** add vanilla, toast and butter.

cards.title: Its home, Burgundy
cards.body: All white Burgundy is Chardonnay, from steely **Chablis** in the north to rich **Meursault** in the Côte de Beaune and the ripe wines of the **Mâconnais**.

cards.q: Which region makes crisp, unoaked Chardonnay with high acidity?
cards.explain: Chablis is Burgundy's coolest, northernmost corner. Its Chardonnay is lean and mineral with green apple and lemon, and often unoaked.

cards.q: Buttery aromas in Chardonnay usually come from…
cards.explain: During malolactic conversion, bacteria turn sharp malic acid into softer lactic acid, creating diacetyl, which smells of butter.

cards.q: Warm-climate Chardonnay shows riper flavors such as ___ and pineapple.
cards.explain: Warmth ripens the fruit toward stone and tropical flavors. Cool climates keep it in green apple and citrus.

cards.q: Chardonnay is one of the main grapes of Champagne.
cards.explain: Alongside Pinot Noir and Meunier. Champagne made only from Chardonnay is called **Blanc de Blancs**.

cards.title: Zesty and green
cards.body: **Sauvignon Blanc** is aromatic with high acidity: grapefruit, gooseberry, cut grass and green bell pepper. It is almost always unoaked and drunk young.

cards.title: Two classic homes
cards.body:
- **Loire Valley** (Sancerre, Pouilly-Fumé): restrained, flinty and mineral.
- **Marlborough, New Zealand**: pungent and exuberant, with passion fruit and fresh herbs.

cards.q: Which aroma is typical of Sauvignon Blanc?
cards.explain: Gooseberry, grapefruit, grass and green pepper are its signature notes. The green aromas come from compounds called methoxypyrazines.

cards.q: Sancerre is a wine from which grape?
cards.explain: Like most French wines, Sancerre is named after its place, not its grape. White Sancerre is 100% Sauvignon Blanc.

cards.q: Marlborough Sauvignon Blanc is famous for its intense passion fruit and herbaceous aromas.
cards.explain: Sunny days and cold nights in Marlborough create very intense aromas and crisp acidity.

cards.q: Sauvignon Blanc typically has ___ acidity.
cards.explain: Its crisp, mouthwatering acidity makes it a perfect match for goat cheese and seafood.

cards.title: The aristocrat
cards.body:
**Riesling** has very high acidity and intense aromas of lime, green apple, peach and blossom. It is never oaked for flavor.

It is made in every style from bone dry to very sweet, and great examples age for decades, developing honey and a famous **petrol** note.

cards.title: Germany and beyond
cards.body: Germany's **Mosel** makes delicate, low-alcohol Rieslings, often off-dry. **Alsace** and Australia's **Clare** and **Eden** valleys make dry, fuller styles.

cards.q: Which aroma is a classic sign of aged Riesling?
cards.explain: A compound called TDN develops with age and sunlight, giving the distinctive petrol (kerosene) note that Riesling lovers prize.

cards.q: Riesling is usually aged in new oak to add vanilla flavors.
cards.explain: Riesling is prized for pure fruit and acidity, so new oak is avoided. Large old casks or stainless steel are typical.

cards.q: Riesling is the most famous grape of which country?
cards.explain: Germany grows more Riesling than any other country, especially in the Mosel, Rheingau and Pfalz.

cards.q: Riesling can be made in every style from bone dry to very ___.
cards.explain: Its high acidity balances sugar beautifully, so sweet Rieslings never feel cloying.

cards.title: Two names, two styles
cards.body:
It is the same grape, with a greyish-pink skin, made in two styles:

- **Pinot Grigio** (northern Italy): light, crisp, neutral. Lemon, green apple and pear.
- **Pinot Gris** (Alsace): fuller, richer, with peach, honey and spice, sometimes off-dry.

cards.q: Italian Pinot Grigio is usually…
cards.explain: Picked early from high-yielding vineyards in the Veneto and Friuli, it is easy, refreshing and drunk young.

cards.q: Pinot Gris and Pinot Grigio are the same grape variety.
cards.explain: Gris (French) and Grigio (Italian) both mean grey. The style differs, not the grape.

cards.q: Match the grape to its classic aroma
cards.explain: Gooseberry and grass for Sauvignon, lime and petrol for Riesling, butter when Chardonnay goes through malolactic, and pear and lemon for Pinot Grigio.

cards.q: Alsace Pinot Gris compared to Italian Pinot Grigio is usually…
cards.explain: Alsace is one of France's sunniest, driest regions, and lower yields give riper, more textured wines.

cards.title: Aromatic whites
cards.body:
Some white grapes are naturally perfumed: **Muscat** smells of grapes and orange blossom, **Gewürztraminer** of lychee and rose, **Viognier** of apricot and honeysuckle, and **Riesling** of lime and white flowers.

They are usually made without new oak, so the grape's own aromas stay center stage.

cards.title: Neutral but versatile
cards.body:
**Chardonnay** is a blank canvas. Grown cool and made without oak, as in Chablis, it is crisp, with green apple and lemon. Grown warm and aged in new oak, it becomes rich, with peach, vanilla, butter and toast.

That flexibility is why it is planted almost everywhere.

cards.q: Which grape smells strongly of lychee and rose?
cards.explain: Lychee, rose and ginger are the classic Gewürztraminer signature, especially from Alsace.

cards.q: Chablis is made from Chardonnay.
cards.explain: Chablis, in northern Burgundy, is crisp, mineral, usually unoaked Chardonnay.

cards.q: Match the grape to its classic aroma
cards.explain: Knowing one signature aroma per grape is a great way to start identifying them.

cards.q: Buttery notes in Chardonnay usually come from…
cards.explain: Malolactic conversion softens acidity and creates diacetyl, the compound that smells of butter.

cards.q: Petrol notes in an older white wine are a famous sign of ___.
cards.explain: Aged Riesling often develops a petrol or kerosene note, prized by many fans.

units.title: The great black grapes
units.summary: Cabernet Sauvignon, Merlot, Pinot Noir and Syrah: the reds behind the world's most famous wines.

cards.title: The king of reds
cards.body: Small, thick-skinned berries give **deep color, high tannin and high acidity**. Expect blackcurrant, black cherry, green pepper and mint, plus cedar, vanilla and toast from oak.

cards.title: Bordeaux's Left Bank
cards.body: Cabernet ripens late, so it needs warmth. On the gravel soils of Bordeaux's **Left Bank** (Médoc, Pauillac, Margaux) it is blended with Merlot. **Napa Valley** and **Coonawarra** make riper single-varietal versions.

cards.q: Which aroma is most typical of Cabernet Sauvignon?
cards.explain: Blackcurrant (cassis) is the signature. Green bell pepper and mint can also appear, and cedar with age.

cards.q: Cabernet Sauvignon typically has…
cards.explain: Thick skins and a high ratio of seeds to pulp mean lots of tannin, which is why it ages so well, especially in oak.

cards.q: Cabernet Sauvignon is a key grape of Bordeaux's Left Bank.
cards.explain: Gravel soils drain well and store heat, helping late-ripening Cabernet to ripen fully.

cards.q: In cooler years, under-ripe Cabernet can smell of green bell ___.
cards.explain: These herbaceous notes come from methoxypyrazines, which fade as grapes ripen.

cards.title: Soft and plummy
cards.body: **Merlot** gives fuller body, softer tannins and riper fruit than Cabernet: red and black plum, black cherry and chocolate. It ripens earlier, so it suits cooler clay soils.

cards.title: Bordeaux's Right Bank
cards.body: Merlot is the most planted grape in Bordeaux and stars on the **Right Bank**: **Saint-Émilion** and **Pomerol** (home of Pétrus).

cards.q: Compared with Cabernet Sauvignon, Merlot usually has…
cards.explain: Merlot's thinner skins and plusher fruit make it rounder and more approachable young.

cards.q: Which Bordeaux area is dominated by Merlot?
cards.explain: Pomerol's clay soils suit Merlot. Pauillac and Margaux are Left Bank Cabernet country; Sauternes makes sweet whites.

cards.q: Merlot is the most widely planted grape in Bordeaux.
cards.explain: Merlot covers over half of Bordeaux's vineyards, far more than Cabernet Sauvignon.

cards.q: Merlot's typical fruit flavors are red and black ___.
cards.explain: Plum and black cherry, often with chocolate and vanilla from oak.

cards.title: Elegance in a glass
cards.body:
**Pinot Noir** is pale, light in tannin and high in acidity, with red cherry, raspberry and strawberry. With age it develops mushroom, forest floor and game.

It is thin-skinned and fussy, and does best in **cool climates**.

cards.title: From Burgundy to the world
cards.body: Red **Burgundy** is Pinot Noir. Other great sources include **Champagne** (for sparkling wine), **Oregon**, **Central Otago**, **Sonoma** and Germany (as Spätburgunder).

cards.q: Which statement fits Pinot Noir?
options: Pale color, high acidity, low tannin
cards.explain: Thin skins give less color and tannin; cool climates keep acidity high.

cards.q: Red Burgundy is made from…
cards.explain: Red Burgundy from the Côte d'Or is 100% Pinot Noir. Gamay is the grape of Beaujolais, just to the south.

cards.q: Pinot Noir prefers hot climates.
cards.explain: In heat it loses its delicacy and turns jammy. Cool to moderate climates suit it best.

cards.q: Match the aged Pinot Noir aroma to its family
cards.explain: Fruit comes from the grape; oak adds vanilla; bottle age brings earthy, savory notes like mushroom.

cards.title: One grape, two personalities
cards.body:
**Syrah** (France) and **Shiraz** (Australia) are the same grape.

- **Northern Rhône Syrah**: blackberry, black pepper, violet, savory and smoky.
- **Barossa Shiraz**: ripe blackberry, plum, chocolate and sweet spice, full and rich.

cards.title: Its homes
cards.body: In the Northern Rhône, **Hermitage** and **Côte-Rôtie** make some of the world's greatest Syrah. In Australia the **Barossa Valley** made Shiraz famous.

cards.q: Which aroma is classic in cool-climate Syrah?
cards.explain: A compound called rotundone gives the peppery note, strongest in cooler sites.

cards.q: Shiraz and Syrah are different grapes.
cards.explain: They are the same variety. The name often signals the style: 'Shiraz' for riper New World wines, 'Syrah' for more restrained ones.

cards.q: Which Australian region is most famous for rich Shiraz?
cards.explain: The warm Barossa has some of the world's oldest Shiraz vines, some planted in the 1840s.

cards.q: Match the grape to its classic region
cards.explain: Four classic pairings every wine lover should know.

cards.title: Thin skins, thick skins
cards.body:
Skin thickness explains a lot. Thin-skinned grapes like **Pinot Noir** and **Gamay** make pale, light, low-tannin reds. Thick-skinned grapes like **Cabernet Sauvignon**, **Syrah** and **Malbec** give deep color and firm tannin.

Color and tannin both come from the skins.

cards.title: Blends
cards.body:
Many great reds are **blends**. Bordeaux mixes Cabernet Sauvignon and Merlot (often with Cabernet Franc); the southern Rhône blends Grenache, Syrah and Mourvèdre (GSM).

Blending lets winemakers balance one grape's weak points with another's strengths.

cards.q: Which grape usually gives the palest red wine?
cards.explain: Pinot Noir has thin skins, so it gives less color and tannin than thick-skinned grapes.

cards.q: Match the grape to a classic home
cards.explain: Each of these places made its grape famous.

cards.q: GSM stands for Grenache, Syrah and Mourvèdre.
cards.explain: The classic southern Rhône blend, also popular in Australia.

cards.q: Which grape is known for black pepper aromas?
cards.explain: Cool-climate Syrah often shows black pepper, from a compound called rotundone.

cards.q: Color and tannin in red wine come from the grape ___.
cards.explain: Red wine gets its color by fermenting juice with the skins.

units.title: The wine world
units.summary: Where wine comes from: the wine belt, the classic countries and the names on bottles.

cards.title: Two bands around the globe
cards.body: Most of the world's vineyards sit in two bands, roughly **30° to 50° latitude** north and south of the equator. Closer to the poles, grapes struggle to ripen; closer to the equator, vines never get the winter rest they need.

cards.title: Old World and New World
cards.body:
- **Old World**: Europe and the Mediterranean, where winemaking goes back thousands of years: France, Italy, Spain, Portugal, Germany, Austria, Greece.
- **New World**: places where European vines arrived later: the USA, Chile, Argentina, Australia, New Zealand, South Africa.

cards.q: Between which latitudes are most vineyards found?
cards.explain: In both hemispheres. Altitude and ocean currents let some regions push beyond these limits.

cards.q: Old World or New World?
cards.explain: Italy has made wine for thousands of years; Chile's industry grew from Spanish missions in the 1500s.

cards.q: Australia is considered an Old World wine country.
cards.explain: Australia is New World. Vines arrived with European settlers in 1788.

cards.q: Which country makes the most wine by volume in a typical year?
cards.explain: Italy and France usually trade first place, with Spain third. Spain has the largest vineyard area.

cards.title: The classic regions
cards.body:
- **Bordeaux**: red blends of Cabernet Sauvignon and Merlot.
- **Burgundy**: Pinot Noir and Chardonnay.
- **Champagne**: sparkling wine.
- **Rhône**: Syrah in the north, Grenache blends in the south.
- **Loire**: Sauvignon Blanc, Chenin Blanc, Cabernet Franc.
- **Alsace**: aromatic whites.

cards.q: Which French region is famous for sparkling wine?
cards.explain: Only sparkling wine from the Champagne region in north-east France may be called Champagne.

cards.q: Highlighted on the map is…
cards.explain: Bordeaux lies on France's Atlantic coast, around the Gironde estuary.

cards.q: Provence is famous for pale, dry rosé.
cards.explain: Provence is the world's rosé capital, along the Mediterranean coast.

cards.q: Match the French region to its grape
cards.explain: French labels name places, so learning which grape grows where is essential.

cards.title: The big names
cards.body:
- **Italy**: Chianti and Brunello (Sangiovese), Barolo (Nebbiolo), Prosecco.
- **Spain**: Rioja (Tempranillo), Cava, Sherry.
- **Germany**: Riesling.
- **USA**: Napa Valley Cabernet.
- **Argentina**: Malbec. **New Zealand**: Sauvignon Blanc. **Australia**: Shiraz.

cards.q: Match the country to its signature grape
cards.explain: Each became famous worldwide for one star grape.

cards.q: Rioja comes from which country?
cards.explain: Rioja lies in northern Spain along the Ebro river, and is made mainly from Tempranillo.

cards.q: Napa Valley is in…
cards.explain: North of San Francisco, and famous for Cabernet Sauvignon.

cards.q: Prosecco is a sparkling wine from Italy.
cards.explain: From the Veneto and Friuli in north-east Italy, made from the Glera grape.

cards.title: Old World and New World
cards.body:
**Old World** means Europe's traditional wine countries: France, Italy, Spain, Germany, Portugal. Wines are usually named after the **place**.

**New World** means countries like the USA, Australia, Chile and New Zealand. Wines are often named after the **grape**, and styles tend to be riper and fruitier.

cards.title: Latitude and climate
cards.body:
Most vineyards lie between **30° and 50° latitude**. Closer to the poles, grapes struggle to ripen; closer to the equator, it is too hot for quality wine.

Altitude and cold ocean currents can cool a warm place: think of the high Andes or California's foggy coast.

cards.q: Old World wines are usually labeled by…
cards.explain: A Sancerre or a Chianti is named after where it comes from, not the grape.

cards.q: Most quality vineyards lie between 30° and 50° latitude.
cards.explain: This 'wine belt' gives enough warmth to ripen grapes and enough cool to keep freshness.

cards.q: Match the country to a famous grape
cards.explain: Each New World country has a signature grape.

cards.q: How can a region in a hot country still make fresh wines?
options: High altitude or cool ocean influence
cards.explain: Mountains and cold currents lower temperatures, keeping acidity in the grapes.

cards.q: Wine regions in Europe are often called the ___ World.
cards.explain: Old World vs New World is shorthand for tradition-led versus fruit-led winemaking.

units.title: Food & wine
units.summary: How food changes the taste of wine, and the few rules that make pairing easy.

cards.title: Food changes wine
cards.body:
A wine that tastes perfect alone can turn harsh with the wrong food, and vice versa. Some food components make wine taste **worse**, others **better**.

- **Tougher on wine**: sweetness and umami make wine taste more bitter, more acidic, less fruity.
- **Kinder to wine**: salt and acidity make wine taste softer, fruitier and less acidic.

cards.q: A sweet dessert makes a dry wine taste…
cards.explain: That is why dessert needs a wine at least as sweet as the dish, such as Sauternes or Moscato.

cards.q: Which food component makes wine taste softer and less bitter?
cards.explain: Salt is wine's friend: it reduces bitterness and acidity. Think salty Parmesan with Chianti, or oysters with Muscadet.

cards.q: Acidic foods make a wine taste less acidic.
cards.explain: Match acid with acid: a tomato sauce or a vinaigrette can make a crisp wine seem rounder and fruitier.

cards.q: Mushrooms, cured meats and soy sauce are rich in ___.
cards.explain: Umami makes wine taste more bitter and acidic. Choose fruity, low-tannin wines, or season with salt.

cards.q: Match the food to its effect on wine
cards.explain: These three interactions explain most pairing successes and disasters.

cards.title: Spice and protein
cards.body:
- **Chili heat** makes alcohol burn more and tannin taste bitter. Pick low-alcohol, off-dry, fruity whites such as Riesling or Gewürztraminer.
- **Fat and protein** soften tannin. That is why a big Cabernet loves a steak.

cards.q: Which wine best suits a spicy Thai curry?
cards.explain: A touch of sweetness and low alcohol calm the heat. High-alcohol, tannic wines make chili burn more.

cards.q: Why does a tannic red work well with steak?
options: Protein and fat soften the tannin
cards.explain: Tannin binds to protein, so the meat tames the wine's grip, and the wine cuts through the fat.

cards.q: Chili heat makes wines taste less alcoholic.
cards.explain: The reverse: chili heightens the burning sensation of alcohol.

cards.q: With chili dishes, choose wines low in alcohol and ___.
cards.explain: Tannin and alcohol both clash with spicy heat.

cards.title: Match weight, then flavor
cards.body:
Pair **light with light** and **rich with rich**. A delicate sole would be crushed by a Barossa Shiraz; a beef stew would make a Pinot Grigio vanish.

And remember regional pairing: **what grows together goes together**.

cards.q: Match the dish to the classic wine
cards.explain: Each is a textbook match: brine with crisp Muscadet, tangy goat cheese with high-acid Sauvignon Blanc, steak with tannic Cabernet, and rich duck with fresh, fruity Pinot Noir.

cards.q: Which wine suits a light seafood salad?
cards.explain: Light, fresh and saline, Albariño matches delicate seafood. The others are powerful and would overwhelm it.

cards.q: 'What grows together goes together' means local wines often suit local food.
cards.explain: Chianti with Tuscan steak, Sherry with tapas, Alsace Riesling with choucroute: centuries of trial and error.

cards.q: Which pairing follows the weight principle?
cards.explain: A hearty stew needs a full-bodied red with enough flavor to stand up to it.

cards.title: Sweetness and spice
cards.body:
**Sweet food** makes dry wine taste thin and sour, so pick a wine at least as sweet as the dish.

**Spicy heat** is made hotter by alcohol and tannin. Off-dry, low-alcohol whites like Riesling cool things down.

cards.title: Match the weight
cards.body:
Pair light with light and rich with rich. A delicate fish needs a light white; a braised beef stew wants a full-bodied red.

Then think of **acid**: acidic wines cut through fat and salt, and love tomato and lemon.

cards.q: What happens to a dry wine served with a sweet dessert?
cards.explain: Sweet food makes dry wine seem more acidic and bitter. The wine should be sweeter than the food.

cards.q: Which wine suits a spicy Thai curry best?
cards.explain: A touch of sweetness and low alcohol soothe chili heat; tannin and alcohol amplify it.

cards.q: High-acid wines go well with fatty and salty foods.
cards.explain: Acidity cuts through richness and is balanced by salt, like Champagne with fries.

cards.q: Match the dish to a classic wine
cards.explain: These classic pairings work through acid, tannin, or sweet and salty contrast.

cards.q: Tannic red wine can taste metallic with oily ___.
cards.explain: Fish oils and tannin clash; pick a white, a rosé or a light low-tannin red instead.

units.title: Serving & storing
units.summary: Temperatures, glasses, opening bottles, storing wine and spotting faults.

cards.title: Not too cold, not too warm
cards.body:
Temperature changes how wine tastes. Too cold mutes aromas and makes tannins harsh; too warm makes alcohol stand out.

- **Sparkling & sweet**: well chilled, 6–10 °C
- **Light whites & rosé**: chilled, 7–10 °C
- **Full whites**: lightly chilled, 10–13 °C
- **Light reds**: 13 °C
- **Fuller reds**: room temperature, 15–18 °C

cards.q: At what temperature should sparkling wine be served?
cards.explain: Well chilled keeps the bubbles fine and lively and the wine refreshing.

cards.q: Light reds like Beaujolais can be served slightly chilled.
cards.explain: Around 13 °C brings out their juicy fruit and freshness.

cards.q: Serving a full-bodied red too cold will…
cards.explain: Cold emphasizes tannin and bitterness and mutes the aromas. Serve fuller reds at 15–18 °C.

cards.q: Full-bodied whites such as oaked Chardonnay are best ___ chilled.
cards.explain: At 10–13 °C, their richer aromas and texture can show.

cards.title: The right glass
cards.body:
- **Reds**: a large bowl gives room to swirl and gather aromas.
- **Whites & rosé**: medium-sized, to keep them cool.
- **Sparkling**: a tall flute or tulip keeps the bubbles longer.

Fill only to the widest part of the bowl, or less, so there is room to swirl.

cards.title: Opening sparkling wine safely
cards.body:
The pressure in a Champagne bottle is about 5–6 atmospheres, roughly three times a car tire.

- Chill it well.
- Keep a thumb on the cork and point it away from people.
- Hold the cork and **turn the bottle**, easing it out with a gentle sigh, not a pop.

cards.q: Why do red wine glasses have a large bowl?
options: To allow swirling and gather aromas
cards.explain: Room to swirl releases aromas, and the wide bowl concentrates them toward your nose.

cards.q: When opening sparkling wine, you should twist the bottle, not the cork.
cards.explain: Holding the cork still and turning the bottle gives you control and a quiet, safe opening.

cards.q: Which glass is best for sparkling wine?
cards.explain: A narrow glass reduces the surface area, so bubbles last longer.

cards.title: Store wine like a cellar
cards.body:
- **Cool and steady**: about 10–15 °C, without big swings.
- **Dark**: light can damage wine.
- **On its side** for corked bottles, so the cork stays moist.
- Once open, re-seal and refrigerate. Most wines last 1–3 days; fortified wines last longer.

cards.title: Common faults
cards.body:
- **Cork taint (TCA)**: musty, damp cardboard, muted fruit.
- **Oxidation**: brownish color, bruised apple, flat.
- **Heat damage**: cooked, jammy flavors, sometimes a pushed-up cork.

cards.q: A wine smelling of damp cardboard is probably…
cards.explain: Cork taint is caused by TCA, a compound that can come from cork. It is not harmful, but it kills the fruit.

cards.q: Bottles with natural corks are best stored standing upright.
cards.explain: Lie them on their side so the cork stays in contact with the wine and does not dry out and let air in.

cards.q: Wine should be stored somewhere cool, dark and at a ___ temperature.
cards.explain: Fluctuating temperatures make the wine expand and contract, pushing air past the cork.

cards.q: A white wine that has turned brownish and smells of bruised apples is probably…
cards.explain: Too much oxygen dulls the fruit and browns the color. Some styles, like Oloroso Sherry, are deliberately oxidative.

cards.title: Opening and keeping
cards.body:
Once open, wine meets oxygen. Most still wines keep **2–5 days** with the cork back in, in the fridge. Sparkling wine keeps 1–3 days with a stopper.

Fortified wines like Tawny Port can keep for weeks.

cards.title: Decanting
cards.body:
**Decanting** means pouring wine into another vessel. It separates an old wine from its **sediment**, and lets young, tannic wines breathe so they taste softer.

Pour slowly and stop when you see sediment reach the neck.

cards.q: Why would you decant an old red wine?
cards.explain: Old reds throw a deposit of tannin and pigment; decanting leaves it behind.

cards.q: Sparkling wine should be served colder than full-bodied red wine.
cards.explain: Sparkling wine is best well chilled (6–10 °C); full reds around 15–18 °C.

cards.q: How long does an opened bottle of still wine usually keep in the fridge?
cards.explain: Oxygen slowly flattens the fruit. Fortified wines last much longer.

cards.q: Match the wine to its serving temperature
cards.explain: Too cold mutes aromas; too warm makes alcohol stand out.

cards.q: A wine that smells of wet cardboard is probably ___.
cards.explain: Cork taint (TCA) gives a musty, damp-cardboard smell and flattens the fruit.

units.title: Scores & critics
units.summary: What 92 points means, who gives the scores, and how to use them without being ruled by them.

cards.title: Why wine has scores
cards.body:
Shelf tags, apps and auction catalogs are full of numbers: **91 points**, **96 points**. They come from critics who taste thousands of wines a year and sum up each one in a single score.

The most common is the **100-point scale**, popularized in the 1980s by the American critic **Robert Parker** and his newsletter *The Wine Advocate*. It copies the grades of an American school report.

cards.title: Reading the numbers
cards.body:
Every wine starts at **50**. The rest rewards what is in the glass:

- **96–100 · Classic**: a great wine, complex and long. Rare.
- **90–95 · Outstanding**: real character and style.
- **85–89 · Very good**: well made, with something special.
- **80–84 · Good**: solid and pleasant.
- **Below 80**: plain, or with flaws.

In practice almost every score you see in a shop is between **85 and 100**: shops quote the good ones.

cards.title: What critics look at
cards.body:
A score is a judgment of **quality**, not of personal taste. Critics weigh the same things you learn in this course:

- **Balance**: fruit, acid, tannin and alcohol in harmony.
- **Length**: how long the flavor lasts after you swallow.
- **Intensity** and **complexity**: how much there is, and how many layers.
- **Typicity**: does it taste of its grape and place?

Many critics also give a **drinking window**, such as "2026–2040".

cards.q: On the 100-point scale, a wine scored 92 is…
cards.explain: 90–95 is 'outstanding': a wine with real character. 96–100 is 'classic', 85–89 'very good'.

cards.q: On the 100-point scale, the lowest score a wine can get is 0.
cards.explain: Every wine starts at 50; the 50 points above that reward quality. In practice published scores sit mostly between 80 and 100.

cards.q: Who made the 100-point scale famous?
cards.explain: Robert Parker's newsletter The Wine Advocate used it from 1978, and his praise of the 1982 Bordeaux vintage made him the world's most influential critic.

cards.title: The big names
cards.body:
- **Robert Parker / The Wine Advocate** (USA): the critic who made scores matter. Parker retired in 2019; the Advocate goes on with a team.
- **Wine Spectator** (USA): a magazine scoring about 15,000 wines a year, tasted blind. Its **Top 100** list each November moves markets.
- **James Suckling** (USA/Asia): former Spectator critic, generous scores, big on Italy and Bordeaux.
- **Vinous** (Antonio Galloni, USA): detailed reviews, strong on Italy and California.
- **Wine Enthusiast** (USA): magazine scores on the 100-point scale, broad coverage.

cards.title: The 20-point school
cards.body:
Many European critics prefer **20 points**:

- **Jancis Robinson MW** (UK): one of the most respected voices in wine, co-author of *The World Atlas of Wine*. A 17/20 is a very good wine; 18.5+ is exceptional.
- **Decanter** (UK): the magazine now gives 100-point scores, and runs the **Decanter World Wine Awards**, the biggest wine competition, with medals instead of points.
- **La Revue du Vin de France** and **Bettane+Desseauve** (France) also score out of 20.

cards.title: Crowds and medals
cards.body:
**Vivino** gathers ratings from millions of drinkers on a **1–5 star** scale. A 4.2 is very good; it tells you what people enjoy, which is not always what critics praise.

**Medals** on a bottle come from competitions: a gold medal means a panel liked it more than the other wines in that flight. Useful, but there are hundreds of competitions.

cards.q: Match the critic to the scale they are known for
cards.explain: Parker made the 100-point scale famous, Jancis Robinson scores out of 20, Vivino uses 1–5 stars, and competitions such as the DWWA award medals.

cards.q: Which magazine publishes a famous 'Top 100' list every November?
cards.explain: Wine Spectator's Top 100 of the year is one of the most watched lists in the trade.

cards.q: Jancis Robinson usually gives scores out of 20.
cards.explain: Like many European critics she uses the 20-point scale; 17 is very good, 18.5 and above exceptional.

cards.title: A number is not your taste
cards.body:
A 95-point Barolo is a great wine, but if you dislike firm tannin you may prefer an 89-point Pinot Noir. Use scores to **find well-made wines**, then trust your own palate.

Read the **note**, not just the number: "firm, needs time" tells you more than "94".

cards.title: Value hides below 90
cards.body:
Prices jump at **90 points**: shops love to quote them. Wines scored **87–89** are often the best value in the shop: very good wine without the score premium.

Also compare **like with like**: 90 points for a $12 Côtes du Rhône is a bigger achievement than 90 for a $200 Bordeaux.

cards.title: Scoring your own wines
cards.body: In the Journal, every tasting is scored on the **100-point scale**. Start at 50 and add points for balance, length, intensity and complexity. After a few tastings, your scores become a map of your own taste.

cards.q: Why are wines scored 87–89 often good value?
options: Prices jump once a wine reaches 90 points
They are made only in Europe
cards.explain: Shops and producers market 90+ scores heavily; a wine just below often costs less for very similar quality.

cards.q: A high score means you will personally enjoy the wine.
cards.explain: A score judges quality and typicity. Your own taste for, say, tannin or oak may differ; read the tasting note too.

units.title: Grape files
units.summary: Every Level 1 grape on one card: aromas, structure, origin and where it grows.

cards.title: Chardonnay
cards.body:
The world's most versatile white grape. A blank canvas that shows its place and its winemaker: steely in Chablis, creamy and oaky in California, toasty in Champagne.

- **Aromas:** green apple, lemon, peach, pineapple, butter, vanilla.
- **Structure:** medium body, medium acidity.
- **Origin:** Burgundy, France.
- **Where it grows:** Burgundy, Chablis, Côte de Beaune, Mâconnais, Champagne, Côte des Blancs.
- **Food:** roast chicken, lobster, creamy pasta, scallops.

cards.title: Sauvignon Blanc
cards.body:
Zesty, aromatic and instantly recognizable: high acidity with green, herbaceous aromas and citrus or tropical fruit.

- **Aromas:** grapefruit, gooseberry, grass, green bell pepper, asparagus, passion fruit.
- **Structure:** medium-low body, high acidity.
- **Origin:** Loire Valley & Bordeaux, France.
- **Where it grows:** Loire Valley, Sancerre, Pouilly-Fumé, Touraine, Bordeaux, Graves.
- **Food:** goat cheese, asparagus, oysters, green salads.

cards.title: Riesling
cards.body:
Thrillingly high acidity and intense aromas of citrus, stone fruit and flowers. Made bone dry to lusciously sweet, and one of the longest-lived whites.

- **Aromas:** lime, green apple, peach, apricot, blossom, wet stones.
- **Structure:** medium-low body, high acidity.
- **Origin:** Rhine Valley, Germany.
- **Where it grows:** Germany, Mosel, Rheingau, Pfalz, Nahe, Alsace.
- **Food:** spicy asian food, pork, duck, smoked fish.

cards.title: Pinot Grigio
cards.body:
Two styles from one grape: light, crisp and neutral as Italian Pinot Grigio, or rich, spicy and textured as Alsace Pinot Gris.

- **Aromas:** lemon, green apple, pear, peach, honey, almond.
- **Structure:** medium-low body, medium acidity.
- **Origin:** Burgundy, France (a color mutation of Pinot Noir).
- **Also called:** Pinot Gris, Grauburgunder.
- **Where it grows:** Veneto, Friuli, Trentino-Alto Adige, Alsace, Willamette Valley, Baden.
- **Food:** light pasta, seafood salad, mild curries, pâté (alsace style).

cards.q: Which grape shows **green apple, lemon, peach**?
cards.explain: The world's most versatile white grape. A blank canvas that shows its place and its winemaker: steely in Chablis, creamy and oaky in California, toasty in Champagne.

cards.q: Which grape shows **grapefruit, gooseberry, grass**?
cards.explain: Zesty, aromatic and instantly recognizable: high acidity with green, herbaceous aromas and citrus or tropical fruit.

cards.q: Which grape shows **lime, green apple, peach**?
cards.explain: Thrillingly high acidity and intense aromas of citrus, stone fruit and flowers. Made bone dry to lusciously sweet, and one of the longest-lived whites.

cards.q: Match each grape to a place where it grows
cards.explain: Each grape is matched with one of its key regions from the cards above.

cards.title: Cabernet Sauvignon
cards.body:
The king of red grapes: small, thick-skinned berries give deep color, high tannin and blackcurrant fruit. Built to age, especially with oak.

- **Aromas:** blackcurrant, black cherry, green bell pepper, mint, cedar, vanilla.
- **Structure:** high body, medium-high acidity, high tannin.
- **Origin:** Bordeaux, France.
- **Where it grows:** Bordeaux, Haut-Médoc, Pauillac, Margaux, Saint-Julien, Saint-Estèphe.
- **Food:** steak, lamb, hard cheeses, mushrooms.

cards.title: Merlot
cards.body:
Plush and approachable: red and black plum, softer tannins and fuller body than Cabernet. The main grape of Bordeaux's Right Bank.

- **Aromas:** black plum, red plum, black cherry, strawberry, chocolate, vanilla.
- **Structure:** medium-high body, medium acidity, medium tannin.
- **Origin:** Bordeaux, France.
- **Where it grows:** Bordeaux, Saint-Émilion, Pomerol, Fronsac, Castillon, Entre-Deux-Mers.
- **Food:** roast pork, duck, mushroom risotto, burgers.

cards.title: Pinot Noir
cards.body:
Light in color and tannin, high in acidity, haunting in aroma. Fragile and hard to grow, but sublime when it works.

- **Aromas:** red cherry, raspberry, strawberry, cranberry, violet, mushroom.
- **Structure:** medium-low body, medium-high acidity, medium-low tannin.
- **Origin:** Burgundy, France.
- **Where it grows:** Burgundy, Côte de Nuits, Côte de Beaune, Côte Chalonnaise, Champagne, Montagne de Reims.
- **Food:** duck, salmon, mushroom dishes, coq au vin.

cards.title: Syrah
cards.body:
Deep, spicy and dark-fruited. In the Rhône it is savory and peppery; as Australian Shiraz, ripe, rich and chocolatey.

- **Aromas:** blackberry, black plum, blueberry, black pepper, violet, liquorice.
- **Structure:** medium-high body, medium acidity, medium-high tannin.
- **Origin:** Northern Rhône, France.
- **Also called:** Shiraz.
- **Where it grows:** Rhône Valley, Hermitage, Côte-Rôtie, Crozes-Hermitage, Cornas, Saint-Joseph.
- **Food:** barbecue, lamb, game, pepper steak.

cards.q: Which grape shows **blackcurrant, black cherry, green bell pepper**?
cards.explain: The king of red grapes: small, thick-skinned berries give deep color, high tannin and blackcurrant fruit. Built to age, especially with oak.

cards.q: Which grape shows **black plum, red plum, black cherry**?
cards.explain: Plush and approachable: red and black plum, softer tannins and fuller body than Cabernet. The main grape of Bordeaux's Right Bank.

cards.q: Which grape shows **red cherry, raspberry, strawberry**?
cards.explain: Light in color and tannin, high in acidity, haunting in aroma. Fragile and hard to grow, but sublime when it works.

cards.q: Match each grape to a place where it grows
cards.explain: Each grape is matched with one of its key regions from the cards above.

units.title: Appellations to know
units.summary: Every Level 1 region on a card, with its map, grapes and climate.

cards.title: France
cards.body:
The benchmark for almost every classic style. France's regions gave the world its most imitated grapes, its appellation system and the very idea of terroir.

- **Grapes:** Cabernet Sauvignon, Merlot, Pinot Noir, Chardonnay, Syrah.
- **Climate:** Cool continental in the north and east, maritime on the Atlantic coast, Mediterranean in the south.
- **Quality system:** AOC/AOP (Appellation d'Origine Contrôlée/Protégée) rules control where grapes grow, which varieties are allowed, yields and winemaking. IGP (Vin de Pays) gives more freedom; Vin de France is the most basic category.
- Labels usually name the place, not the grape: Sancerre is Sauvignon Blanc, red Burgundy is Pinot Noir.
- Champagne, Bordeaux and Burgundy are among the most valuable wine regions on earth.

cards.title: Bordeaux
cards.body:
The world's most famous red wine region: blends of Cabernet Sauvignon and Merlot from châteaux on either side of the Gironde estuary, plus great sweet and dry whites.

- **Where:** France.
- **Grapes:** Merlot, Cabernet Sauvignon, Cabernet Franc, Petit Verdot, Sauvignon Blanc.
- **Climate:** Moderate maritime, moderated by the Atlantic and the Gironde estuary; vintages vary with autumn rain.
- **Quality system:** The 1855 Classification ranked Médoc (and one Graves) châteaux from First to Fifth Growth; Sauternes was ranked too. Saint-Émilion has its own classification, revised about every ten years. Pomerol has none.
- Blending spreads risk: Merlot ripens early, Cabernet Sauvignon late.
- The five First Growths are Lafite, Latour, Margaux, Haut-Brion and Mouton Rothschild (promoted in 1973).

cards.title: Burgundy
cards.body:
Terroir taken to its extreme: a narrow strip of slopes where Pinot Noir and Chardonnay change character from one vineyard to the next.

- **Where:** France.
- **Grapes:** Pinot Noir, Chardonnay, Gamay.
- **Climate:** Cool continental: cold winters, warm summers, risk of spring frost and hail. Vineyards face east and south-east for morning sun.
- **Quality system:** A pyramid: Regional (Bourgogne) → Village (e.g. Gevrey-Chambertin) → Premier Cru → Grand Cru (33 vineyards, about 1–2% of production).
- Vineyards are split between many owners, so a Grand Cru like Clos de Vougeot has more than 80 producers.
- A 'climat' is a precisely named vineyard plot; Burgundy's climats are a UNESCO World Heritage site.

cards.title: Rhône Valley
cards.body:
Two regions in one: the narrow, steep Northern Rhône devoted to Syrah, and the broad, sunny Southern Rhône of Grenache-based blends.

- **Where:** France.
- **Grapes:** Syrah, Grenache, Mourvèdre, Viognier, Marsanne & Roussanne.
- **Climate:** North: moderate continental, steep granite slopes. South: Mediterranean, hot and dry, swept by the cold Mistral wind.
- **Quality system:** Côtes du Rhône → Côtes du Rhône Villages → named villages → crus such as Gigondas and Châteauneuf-du-Pape.
- Châteauneuf-du-Pape allows 13 grape varieties.
- Côte-Rôtie means 'roasted slope', after its steep sun-baked terraces.

cards.title: Loire Valley
cards.body:
France's longest river and a paradise of fresh, high-acid wines: Muscadet, Chenin Blanc, Cabernet Franc and Sauvignon Blanc.

- **Where:** France.
- **Grapes:** Sauvignon Blanc, Chenin Blanc, Cabernet Franc, Melon de Bourgogne, Gamay.
- **Climate:** Cool: maritime near the Atlantic, becoming continental inland.

cards.q: Which grape is most associated with **Bordeaux**?
cards.explain: Bordeaux: The world's most famous red wine region: blends of Cabernet Sauvignon and Merlot from châteaux on either side of the Gironde estuary, plus great sweet and dry whites.

cards.q: Which grape is most associated with **Burgundy**?
cards.explain: Burgundy: Terroir taken to its extreme: a narrow strip of slopes where Pinot Noir and Chardonnay change character from one vineyard to the next.

cards.q: Match each region to its signature grape
cards.explain: Each region is matched with a grape it is known for, as in the cards above.

cards.title: Champagne
cards.body:
The home of the world's most celebrated sparkling wine, made by the traditional method from Chardonnay, Pinot Noir and Meunier.

- **Where:** France.
- **Grapes:** Chardonnay, Pinot Noir, Meunier.
- **Climate:** Cool continental at the northern limit of grape growing; chalk subsoil stores water and reflects light.
- **Quality system:** Villages are rated: 17 Grand Cru and 42 Premier Cru villages.
- Non-vintage Champagne must spend at least 15 months in bottle, 12 of them on lees; vintage at least 3 years.
- Most Champagne is a blend of many villages and years, assembled by large houses.

cards.title: Chablis
cards.body:
Steely, unoaked or lightly oaked Chardonnay: green apple, lemon and wet stones with high acidity. Petit Chablis, Chablis, Premier Cru and Grand Cru.

- **Where:** Burgundy, France.
- **Grapes:** Chardonnay.
- **Climate:** The northernmost part of Burgundy: cool, with frost risk. Kimmeridgian limestone full of fossil oyster shells.

cards.title: Côtes du Rhône
cards.body:
The big regional appellation, mostly in the south: juicy, spicy red blends with great value.

- **Where:** Rhône Valley, France.
- **Grapes:** Grenache, Syrah, Mourvèdre.

cards.title: Sancerre
cards.body:
The classic Sauvignon Blanc: citrus, gooseberry and flinty minerality, with high acidity. Also light Pinot Noir reds and rosés.

- **Where:** Loire Valley, France.
- **Grapes:** Sauvignon Blanc, Pinot Noir.
- **Climate:** Cool continental; chalk, flint (silex) and limestone soils.

cards.q: Which grape is most associated with **Champagne**?
cards.explain: Champagne: The home of the world's most celebrated sparkling wine, made by the traditional method from Chardonnay, Pinot Noir and Meunier.

cards.q: Which grape is most associated with **Chablis**?
cards.explain: Chablis: Steely, unoaked or lightly oaked Chardonnay: green apple, lemon and wet stones with high acidity. Petit Chablis, Chablis, Premier Cru and Grand Cru.

cards.q: Match each region to its signature grape
cards.explain: Each region is matched with a grape it is known for, as in the cards above.

cards.title: Italy
cards.body:
Wine is made in every one of Italy's 20 regions, with hundreds of native grapes. Its wines are made for the table: high acidity, savory and food-friendly.

- **Grapes:** Sangiovese, Nebbiolo, Pinot Grigio, Glera, Corvina.
- **Climate:** Alpine north, Mediterranean south; the Apennine mountains and the sea moderate the heat almost everywhere.
- **Quality system:** DOCG (strictest, guaranteed) → DOC → IGT (regional, more flexible, home of many Super Tuscans) → Vino. Classico marks a historic heartland; Riserva means longer ageing; Superiore, higher alcohol or stricter rules.

cards.title: Spain
cards.body:
The country with the most vineyard area in the world: Rioja and Ribera del Duero reds, Cava, Albariño and the unique fortified Sherry.

- **Grapes:** Tempranillo, Grenache, Albariño, Verdejo, Macabeo.
- **Climate:** Mostly hot and dry; the central plateau (Meseta) is high and continental; green, rainy Atlantic north-west.
- **Quality system:** DOCa/DOQ (Rioja, Priorat) → DO → Vino de la Tierra. Age terms: Joven, Crianza, Reserva, Gran Reserva (longer ageing in oak and bottle).

cards.title: United States
cards.body:
Wine is made in all 50 states, but the West Coast leads: Napa Cabernet, Sonoma Chardonnay and Pinot Noir, Oregon Pinot and Washington's Bordeaux varieties.

- **Grapes:** Cabernet Sauvignon, Chardonnay, Pinot Noir, Zinfandel, Merlot.
- **Climate:** California: Mediterranean, cooled by Pacific fog and breezes. Oregon: cool and wet. Eastern Washington: hot, dry desert irrigated by rivers.
- **Quality system:** Wines are labeled by grape. AVAs (American Viticultural Areas) define places; a varietal wine must contain at least 75% of the named grape.

cards.title: Australia
cards.body:
Bold, fruit-driven Shiraz made Australia famous, but its cool regions now shine for Chardonnay, Pinot Noir and Riesling.

- **Grapes:** Syrah, Cabernet Sauvignon, Chardonnay, Riesling, Sémillon.
- **Climate:** Mostly warm to hot; quality regions are in the cooler south, near the coast or at altitude.
- **Quality system:** Labeled by grape; Geographical Indications (GIs) define zones, regions and subregions.
- Some of the world's oldest vines, ungrafted Shiraz and Grenache from the 1840s, still grow in the Barossa.
- South Australia has never had phylloxera.

cards.title: New Zealand
cards.body:
Intense, pure-fruited wines. Marlborough Sauvignon Blanc became a global style; Central Otago and Martinborough make fine Pinot Noir.

- **Grapes:** Sauvignon Blanc, Pinot Noir, Chardonnay, Pinot Grigio, Syrah.
- **Climate:** Cool maritime: no vineyard is more than about 130 km from the sea. Long, sunny days with cool nights.

cards.title: Marlborough
cards.body:
New Zealand's largest region: pungent Sauvignon Blanc with passion fruit, gooseberry and grassy notes.

- **Where:** New Zealand.
- **Grapes:** Sauvignon Blanc, Pinot Noir, Chardonnay.
- **Climate:** Sunny and dry with cold nights, ideal for aromatic intensity and high acidity.

cards.q: Which grape is most associated with **Marlborough**?
cards.explain: Marlborough: New Zealand's largest region: pungent Sauvignon Blanc with passion fruit, gooseberry and grassy notes.

units.title: Words to know
units.summary: The vocabulary and styles the exams use, in short lists.

cards.title: Words to know
cards.body:
- **Acidity:** The tart, mouthwatering quality of wine. It keeps wine fresh and helps it age.
- **Alcohol by volume (abv):** The percentage of alcohol in a wine, usually 11–15% for table wines.
- **Aroma:** A smell from the grape or fermentation; often used for any smell in wine.
- **Body:** The sense of weight and richness in the mouth, from light to full.
- **Dry:** A wine with little or no perceptible sugar.
- **Finish:** How long the flavors linger after swallowing; a long finish is a sign of quality.
- **Fortified wine:** Wine with added grape spirit, such as Port or Sherry.

Solid deposits that form in some wines, especially older reds and Vintage Port.

cards.body:

- **Sparkling wine:** Wine with dissolved carbon dioxide bubbles.
- **Still wine:** Wine without bubbles.
- **Tannin:** Compounds from skins, seeds, stems and oak that dry and grip the gums.
- **Variety:** A type of grape, such as Merlot or Chardonnay.
- **Vintage:** The year the grapes were harvested.
- **Fermentation:** Yeast converting sugar into alcohol and carbon dioxide.

- **Off-dry:** Slightly sweet.
- **Varietal wine:** A wine named after (and made mainly from) one grape variety.

The traditional wine countries of Europe and the Mediterranean.

units.title: In the vineyard
units.summary: The vine's year, climate and weather, and what terroir really means.

cards.title: A year in the vineyard
cards.body:
A grapevine follows the same cycle every year:

- **Budburst**: green shoots emerge in spring.
- **Flowering & fruit set**: tiny flowers become berries.
- **Véraison**: berries soften and change color.
- **Harvest**: in autumn, when sugar, acid and flavor are in balance.
- **Dormancy**: the vine rests in winter and is pruned.

cards.title: What a grape needs
cards.body: Vines need **sunlight** (to make sugar), **warmth** (to ripen), **water** and **nutrients**. Most quality vineyards lie between **30° and 50°** latitude in both hemispheres.

cards.q: What is véraison?
options: When grapes change color and start to ripen
cards.explain: At véraison black grapes turn from green to purple, white grapes become translucent, and sugar starts to build fast.

cards.q: Most of the world's vineyards lie between which latitudes?
cards.explain: Closer to the equator it is too hot (no winter rest); closer to the poles it is too cold to ripen grapes.

cards.q: In the Northern Hemisphere, harvest usually happens in September and ___.
cards.explain: In the Southern Hemisphere, the seasons flip: harvest falls around February to April.

cards.q: Put each stage with its season (Northern Hemisphere)
cards.explain: Flowering also falls in late spring, and fruit set follows in early summer.

cards.title: Cool vs warm climates
cards.body:
**Climate** is a region's long-term average; **weather** is what happens in a given year.

- **Cool climates**: higher acidity, lower alcohol, lighter body, green and citrus fruit (or red fruit in reds).
- **Warm climates**: lower acidity, higher alcohol, fuller body, stone, tropical and black fruit.

cards.title: Natural air conditioning
cards.body:
Warm regions can still make fresh wines thanks to:

- **Altitude**: temperatures drop about 0.6 °C every 100 m.
- **Ocean currents and fog**: California's Pacific fog, Chile's Humboldt Current.
- **Large rivers and lakes**, which moderate temperatures.

cards.q: A cool-climate wine typically has…
cards.explain: Less heat means less sugar (so less alcohol) and more acid retained in the grapes.

cards.q: Weather explains why the same wine can vary from vintage to vintage.
cards.explain: A cold spring, a hot summer or autumn rain can change a vintage. That is why vintages matter most in marginal climates.

cards.q: How do high-altitude vineyards in hot countries keep wines fresh?
cards.explain: Argentina's Mendoza vineyards sit at 800–1,500 m, where cool nights preserve acidity.

cards.q: Warm-climate Chardonnay tastes of tropical fruit; cool-climate Chardonnay tastes of green ___ and citrus.
cards.explain: The same grape can taste very different depending on how much warmth it receives.

cards.title: A sense of place
cards.body: **Terroir** is everything about a site: soil, slope, aspect, altitude, climate and water. In Burgundy, neighboring vineyards a few meters apart can make very different wines.

cards.title: Slopes, soil and water
cards.body:
- **Slopes** facing the sun (south in the north, north in the south) get more heat.
- **Well-drained soils** (gravel, slate, chalk) stress vines gently, giving smaller, more concentrated berries.
- **Stony soils** store heat and release it at night.
- Too much water gives big, diluted grapes.

cards.q: In the Northern Hemisphere, which slope direction receives the most sun?
cards.explain: South-facing slopes catch more direct sunlight, which is vital in cool regions like the Mosel and Burgundy.

cards.q: Terroir includes soil, slope and local climate.
cards.explain: Terroir is the whole natural environment of a vineyard, and many add the human traditions of a place.

cards.q: Why are well-drained gravel soils prized in the Médoc?
options: They drain water and store heat
cards.explain: Gravel warms up and drains quickly, which helps late-ripening Cabernet Sauvignon.

cards.q: The Mosel's steep slate slopes absorb and reflect ___ onto the vines.
cards.explain: In such a northerly region, every bit of warmth counts.

lessons.title: Deep dive: a year in the vineyard

cards.title: Winter: pruning
cards.body:
While the vine sleeps, growers **prune** last year's canes. Pruning decides how many buds, and so how many bunches, the vine will carry.

- **Cane pruning** (Guyot): one or two long canes are kept and tied along a wire. Common in Bordeaux and Burgundy.
- **Spur pruning** (cordon, gobelet): many short two-bud spurs on a permanent arm or trunk.

Fewer buds usually means fewer but more concentrated grapes.

cards.title: Spring: budburst, frost and flowering
cards.body:
As soils warm past about **10 °C**, buds swell and burst. Young shoots are fragile: one clear, still night below freezing can kill them. Growers fight **spring frost** with candles, wind machines or sprinklers that coat buds in protective ice.

Around **June**, tiny flowers self-pollinate. Cold, wet or windy weather at flowering causes **coulure** (flowers fail) and **millerandage** (uneven small berries), cutting the crop.

cards.title: Summer: fruit set and véraison
cards.body:
After flowering, berries form and grow while hard and green. Mid-summer brings **véraison**: black grapes change color, all grapes soften and start piling up sugar while acid falls.

Growers trim shoots, remove leaves around bunches for sun and air, and sometimes **green harvest** (cut some bunches) so the rest ripen better.

cards.title: Autumn: harvest
cards.body:
Picking day is a balance of **sugar** (future alcohol), **acidity** (freshness) and **ripe tannins and flavors**.

- **Hand picking** allows selection of whole bunches; essential on steep slopes and for sparkling wine, sweet wine and whole-bunch ferments.
- **Machine harvesting** shakes berries off at night, quickly and cheaply, when grapes are cool.

cards.title: Phenolic ripeness
cards.body:
Sugar ripeness and **phenolic ripeness** are not the same thing. Phenolics are the skin and seed compounds that give color, tannin and flavor.

In hot places sugar races ahead; picking early keeps alcohol down but tannins taste green. In cool places the grapes may never get enough sugar. Great sites let both arrive together.

cards.q: What is véraison?
options: When grapes change color and start to ripen
cards.explain: At véraison black grapes turn purple, all grapes soften, sugar rises and acidity falls.

cards.q: Why do growers light candles or run wind machines in spring?
options: To protect young shoots from frost
cards.explain: Frost on a still night pools in low spots; wind machines mix in warmer air from above.

cards.q: Cold, wet weather at flowering can reduce the size of the crop.
cards.explain: Poor flowering (coulure) and uneven berry set (millerandage) both cut yields.

cards.q: Match the season to the vineyard job
cards.explain: The vineyard calendar runs from pruning in winter to picking in autumn (reversed in the Southern Hemisphere).

cards.q: Picking ___ of whole bunches is needed for traditional-method sparkling wine.
cards.explain: Whole, undamaged bunches are pressed gently so the juice stays pale.

lessons.title: Deep dive: soil, slope and water

cards.title: What soil really does
cards.body:
Soil matters less for "flavor" than for **water and heat**.

- **Free-draining** soils (gravel, sand, slate) keep roots searching deep and limit vigor: smaller berries, more concentration.
- **Water-holding** soils (clay) keep vines going in drought but can be cold and late in wet years.
- **Limestone** and chalk drain well yet hold water in their pores, keeping acidity fresh. Champagne, Chablis and Saint-Émilion sit on it.

cards.title: Stones that store heat
cards.body:
Dark **slate** in the Mosel and big rounded **galets** in Châteauneuf-du-Pape soak up the sun by day and give warmth back at night, helping grapes ripen in marginal places.

Light-colored chalk does the opposite: it reflects light up into the canopy.

cards.title: Slope, aspect and water
cards.body:
In cool regions, a **south-facing slope** (north-facing in the Southern Hemisphere) catches more sun at a better angle. Slopes also drain cold air and water away.

Nearby **rivers and lakes** reflect light and soften temperature swings: the Mosel, Rhine, Loire and Douro are lined with vineyards for a reason.

cards.title: Altitude and fog
cards.body:
Temperature falls about **0.6 °C every 100 m** you climb. Argentina's Mendoza and Salta grow fresh wines at 1,000–3,000 m in otherwise hot latitudes.

Cold ocean currents and **fog** do the same job near the coast: California's Sonoma Coast, Chile's Casablanca and South Africa's Elgin all rely on them.

cards.q: Why are south-facing slopes prized in cool Northern Hemisphere regions?
options: They get more and stronger sunlight
cards.explain: The sun hits a south-facing slope at a steeper angle, so more energy reaches each vine.

cards.q: Which soil drains well but still holds water for dry spells?
cards.explain: Porous chalk acts like a sponge, which is why Champagne vines rarely suffer drought.

cards.q: Vineyards at high altitude are cooler than low ones at the same latitude.
cards.explain: Roughly 0.6 °C cooler for every 100 m of altitude.

cards.q: Match the region to its signature soil
cards.explain: Each soil helps vines cope with that place's climate.

cards.title: Gravel
cards.body: Loose stones that drain fast and store the day's heat. The Left Bank of **Bordeaux** (the Médoc and Graves) is built on gravel banks left by ancient rivers, perfect for late-ripening **Cabernet Sauvignon**.

cards.title: Clay
cards.body: Cool and water-holding, so vines never go thirsty but ripen later. **Pomerol** and Saint-Émilion's clay suits early **Merlot**; clay often gives fuller, rounder wines.

cards.title: Limestone and chalk
cards.body: Porous white rock that holds water like a sponge yet drains well and keeps acidity bright. **Champagne**, **Chablis**, the Côte d'Or and Saint-Émilion's plateau all sit on it.

cards.title: Slate and schist
cards.body: Dark, flaky rock that soaks up sun and splits so roots can dive deep. The **Mosel** (slate) and the **Douro** (schist) grow some of the world's most striking wines on almost no soil at all.

cards.title: Volcanic
cards.body: Ash, pumice and basalt: poor, free-draining and rich in minerals. **Santorini**, **Etna**, the Canary Islands and parts of Campania make tense, smoky, saline wines.

cards.title: Granite
cards.body: Crumbly, acidic and warm. The crus of **Beaujolais** and the northern Rhône's **Côte-Rôtie** and **Hermitage** owe their perfumed, structured wines to granite.

cards.title: Special soils
cards.body:
- **Albariza** (Jerez): blinding white chalk that holds winter rain through the summer, the home of Sherry's Palomino.
- **Terra rossa** (Coonawarra): red iron-rich clay over limestone, famous for Cabernet.
- **Loess** (Austria's Wagram and Kremstal): fine wind-blown silt loved by Grüner Veltliner.

cards.q: Match the soil to its famous region
cards.explain: Each soil shaped a classic: drainage, heat and water are what matter most.

cards.q: Which soil holds water like a sponge yet still drains well?
cards.explain: Porous chalk stores water in its pores, so vines in Champagne rarely suffer drought.

cards.q: Clay soils tend to be cool and late-ripening.
cards.explain: They hold water and warm up slowly, which suits early grapes like Merlot.

cards.title: The growing season
cards.body:
In the Northern Hemisphere: **budburst** in spring (March–April), **flowering** in early summer, **véraison** (grapes soften and change color) in midsummer, and **harvest** from September to October.

Spring frost at budburst and rain at flowering are among the biggest risks to a crop.

cards.title: Sun, slope and water
cards.body:
South-facing slopes (north-facing in the Southern Hemisphere) catch more sun. Rivers and lakes reflect light and moderate temperature extremes.

Poor, well-drained soils make vines struggle a little, giving smaller crops with more concentrated flavor.

cards.q: What is 'véraison'?
options: When grapes soften and change color
cards.explain: At véraison black grapes turn from green to purple and sugar starts to build.

cards.q: Spring frost is a major risk around budburst.
cards.explain: Young shoots are easily killed by frost; growers use wind machines, sprinklers or candles to protect them.

cards.q: Match the stage to its season (Northern Hemisphere)
cards.explain: The vine's yearly cycle drives the whole calendar of a wine region.

cards.q: Why are poor, well-drained soils often prized for vines?
options: Lower yields with more concentrated grapes
They add sugar to the grapes
cards.explain: Vines that struggle a little put their energy into fewer, more flavorful grapes.

cards.q: In the Northern Hemisphere, the best vineyard slopes usually face ___.
cards.explain: South-facing slopes get the most sun, helping grapes ripen in cool climates.

units.title: In the winery
units.summary: How white, red and rosé wines are made, and what oak, lees and malolactic conversion add.

cards.title: Fresh and fruity
cards.body: For white wine, grapes are crushed and **pressed straight away**. Only the juice is fermented, usually **cool (12–22 °C)** in stainless steel, to keep delicate fruit aromas.

cards.q: When are white grapes pressed?
cards.explain: Separating juice from skins early keeps white wine pale and low in tannin.

cards.q: White wines are usually fermented at cooler temperatures than reds.
cards.explain: Cool fermentation preserves fresh, fruity and floral aromas.

cards.q: Most white wines are fermented in stainless ___ tanks.
cards.explain: Steel is neutral and easy to keep cool. Oak barrels or concrete add texture and flavor for richer styles.

cards.q: Why might a winemaker ferment Chardonnay in oak barrels?
options: To add richness, texture and toasty flavors
cards.explain: Barrel fermentation integrates oak flavors and adds weight. It is classic in Burgundy and California.

cards.title: Skins make the difference
cards.body:
For red wine, black grapes ferment **with their skins** at **20–32 °C**. Warmth and contact extract color and tannin. The floating cap of skins is punched down or pumped over to keep it in contact with the wine.

After fermentation, the wine is drained and the skins pressed.

cards.title: Rosé
cards.body: Rosé uses black grapes but only **brief skin contact**, a few hours to two days, then ferments cool like a white.

cards.q: Why are red wines fermented warmer than whites?
cards.explain: Higher temperatures help pull pigments and tannins out of the skins.

cards.q: The layer of skins floating on fermenting red wine is called the ___.
cards.explain: Winemakers punch it down or pump wine over it to extract color and keep it from drying out.

cards.q: Rosé is made by fermenting black grapes on their skins for several weeks.
cards.explain: That is red winemaking. Rosé gets only hours to a couple of days of skin contact.

cards.q: Match the process to the wine
cards.explain: Skin contact is what separates the three.

cards.title: Shaping the style
cards.body:
After fermentation, winemakers can add layers:

- **Oak**: new barrels add vanilla, toast, smoke and spice; any barrel lets in tiny amounts of oxygen that soften tannin.
- **Lees ageing**: contact with dead yeast adds texture and bready notes.
- **Malolactic conversion**: turns sharp malic acid into softer lactic acid and can add butter.

cards.q: Which flavor does new oak typically add?
cards.explain: Toasted oak adds vanilla, clove, coconut (especially American oak) and smoke.

cards.q: American oak typically gives stronger coconut and vanilla flavors than French oak.
cards.explain: That's why traditional Rioja, aged in American oak, often smells of coconut and vanilla.

cards.q: Ageing wine on dead yeast cells, called the ___, adds texture and bready flavors.
cards.explain: Muscadet sur lie and Champagne are classic examples of lees influence.

cards.q: Malolactic conversion makes a wine taste…
cards.explain: Malic acid (think green apple) is converted into milder lactic acid (think milk). Almost all reds and many Chardonnays go through it.

cards.q: What is the cheaper alternative to aging in oak barrels?
options: Oak chips or staves in a tank
cards.explain: They add oak flavor quickly, but without the slow oxygen exposure of a barrel.

lessons.title: Deep dive: from grape to red wine

cards.title: Sorting and crushing
cards.body:
At the winery, bunches go over a **sorting table** to remove leaves and bad berries. A **destemmer** pulls the berries off the stems; rollers then crack the skins.

Some winemakers keep **whole bunches** (stems and all) for a fresher, spicier, more aromatic red: common in Burgundy and northern Rhône.

cards.title: Fermentation on the skins
cards.body:
Red wine ferments **with the skins**, at about **20–32 °C**, warmer than whites. Heat and alcohol pull color, tannin and flavor out of the skins.

Carbon dioxide pushes the skins up into a thick **cap**. It must be kept wet:
- **Pump-over** (remontage): juice from the bottom is sprayed over the cap.
- **Punch-down** (pigeage): the cap is pushed down by hand or machine.

cards.title: Extraction and pressing
cards.body:
After fermentation the wine may sit on the skins for days or weeks (**post-fermentation maceration**) to soften and build tannin.

The free-run wine is drained off, then the skins are pressed. **Press wine** is darker and more tannic; the winemaker blends some back in for structure.

cards.title: Malolactic conversion
cards.body:
Almost all reds then go through **malolactic conversion** (MLC): bacteria turn sharp **malic acid** (green apple) into softer **lactic acid** (milk).

It makes wine rounder and more stable and can add a buttery note. For whites it is a choice: Burgundy Chardonnay often does it, Riesling and Sauvignon Blanc usually do not.

cards.title: Oak or not?
cards.body:
- **New oak** adds vanilla, toast, clove, coconut (American oak) and smooths tannins through slow oxygen exchange.
- **Old oak** gives gentle oxygen without much flavor.
- **Stainless steel** and concrete keep fruit pure.

Barrels are toasted over fire; the **toast level** (light, medium, heavy) changes the flavors.

cards.q: Why does red wine ferment with the grape skins?
options: To extract color, tannin and flavor
cards.explain: The juice of almost all black grapes is clear; the color is in the skins.

cards.q: What does malolactic conversion do?
options: Turns sharp malic acid into softer lactic acid
cards.explain: MLC softens acidity and can add buttery notes (diacetyl).

cards.q: Match the technique to what it means
cards.explain: These are the winemaker's main tools for managing extraction.

cards.q: American oak tends to give stronger coconut and vanilla notes than French oak.
cards.explain: It is wider-grained and richer in the compounds behind coconut aromas: think traditional Rioja.

cards.q: The layer of skins floating on fermenting red wine is called the ___.
