cards.explain: It is pushed up by carbon dioxide and must be kept moist to avoid spoilage.

lessons.title: Deep dive: whites, rosés and finishing touches

cards.title: White wine: cool and clean
cards.body:
For white wine, grapes are **pressed first** and the skins removed. The juice is cooled and allowed to settle so it ferments clean.

Fermentation is cool, about **12–22 °C**, to keep delicate fruit and floral aromas. Many aromatic whites stay in stainless steel; rich Chardonnay may ferment in barrel.

cards.title: Lees and bâtonnage
cards.body:
After fermentation, dead yeast cells, the **lees**, settle out. Leaving wine on fine lees adds texture and bready, nutty notes. Stirring them up is **bâtonnage**.

Muscadet *sur lie* and white Burgundy are classic examples.

cards.title: Rosé, three ways
cards.body:
- **Short maceration**: black grapes soak on their skins for a few hours, then the pink juice is fermented like a white.
- **Direct pressing**: whole black grapes pressed gently; very pale rosé (Provence style).
- **Saignée**: some juice is "bled" from a red ferment, concentrating the red and making a deeper rosé.

Blending red and white wine is only allowed in a few cases, such as rosé Champagne.

cards.title: Clarifying, stabilizing, bottling
cards.body:
Before bottling, wine is **fined** (proteins such as egg white or bentonite clay grab haze-causing particles) and often **filtered**.

**Cold stabilization** prevents harmless tartrate crystals ("wine diamonds"). A little **sulfur dioxide** protects against oxygen and microbes.

Closures: natural cork, technical cork, screw cap (keeps fruit fresh, no cork taint) or glass stopper.

cards.q: Why are most white wines fermented cooler than reds?
cards.explain: Low temperatures preserve volatile aromas; reds need warmth to extract from skins.

cards.q: Which rosé method bleeds juice from a red wine tank?
cards.explain: French for 'bleeding': the red left behind becomes more concentrated.

cards.q: Tartrate crystals in a bottle mean the wine has spoiled.
cards.explain: They are harmless potassium bitartrate, sometimes called wine diamonds.

cards.q: Match the term to its meaning
pairs: Removing haze with a binding agent
cards.explain: All about texture and clarity.

cards.title: Making red wine
cards.body:
Black grapes are crushed and fermented **with their skins**. The skins give color, tannin and flavor. Winemakers punch down or pump over the cap of skins to extract them.

After fermentation the wine is pressed off the skins, then usually aged before bottling.

cards.title: Oak or stainless steel?
cards.body:
**Stainless steel** keeps fruit pure and fresh. **Oak barrels** let in a little oxygen, soften tannins and, when new, add vanilla, toast and spice.

Small new barrels give the most flavor; large old casks give texture with little oak taste.

cards.q: Where does red wine get its color?
cards.explain: Juice of almost all black grapes is clear; color comes from contact with the skins.

cards.q: Small new oak barrels add more oak flavor than large old ones.
cards.explain: More wood surface per liter and fresh wood mean more vanilla, toast and spice.

cards.q: What does 'punching down' do?
options: Pushes the skins back into the fermenting wine
cards.explain: The skins float up as a cap; pushing them down extracts color and tannin.

cards.q: Match the choice to its effect
cards.explain: Each winemaking decision leaves a mark on the final wine.

cards.q: After fermentation, red wine is separated from the skins by ___.
cards.explain: The press squeezes out the wine trapped in the skins.

units.title: More white grapes
units.summary: Chenin Blanc, Sémillon, the aromatic grapes and Europe's crisp coastal whites.

cards.title: Chenin Blanc
cards.body: High acidity, apple, quince and honey. The **Loire** makes it in every style: dry, off-dry, sweet and sparkling (**Vouvray**, **Savennières**). **South Africa** grows more Chenin than anywhere else, with riper, often oaked styles.

cards.title: Sémillon
cards.body: Thin-skinned and prone to **noble rot**, Sémillon is the heart of **Sauternes**. In Australia's **Hunter Valley** it is picked early for a light, lemony dry wine that ages into toast and honey.

cards.q: Vouvray is made from which grape?
cards.explain: Vouvray, near Tours, makes Chenin Blanc from dry (sec) to sweet (moelleux), plus sparkling.

cards.q: Which country has the most Chenin Blanc vineyards?
cards.explain: Chenin Blanc (also called Steen) is South Africa's most planted grape.

cards.q: Sémillon is the main grape of sweet Sauternes.
cards.explain: Its thin skins make it susceptible to Botrytis cinerea, which concentrates the grapes.

cards.q: Hunter Valley Sémillon is light when young but ages to flavors of ___ and honey.
cards.explain: Despite seeing no oak, it develops toasty notes after years in bottle.

cards.title: Perfume in a glass
cards.body:
- **Gewürztraminer**: rose, lychee, ginger; low acidity, oily texture (Alsace).
- **Muscat**: smells of fresh grapes, orange blossom and peach (Moscato d'Asti, Alsace).
- **Viognier**: apricot, peach, honeysuckle; full and silky (Condrieu).

cards.q: Lychee and rose petal aromas are typical of…
cards.explain: Gewürztraminer is one of the most aromatic grapes in the world.

cards.q: Which grape smells most like fresh grapes?
cards.explain: Muscat is famous for actually tasting grapey, along with orange blossom and peach.

cards.q: Condrieu, in the Northern Rhône, is made from…
cards.explain: Condrieu is Viognier's spiritual home: apricot, peach and blossom with a rich, silky texture.

cards.q: Gewürztraminer typically has high acidity.
cards.explain: It is notably low in acidity, with a rich, almost oily texture.

cards.q: Match the aromatic grape to its classic note
cards.explain: Three perfumed grapes with very distinct signatures.

cards.title: Fresh and saline
cards.body:
- **Albariño** (Rías Baixas, Spain): peach, grapefruit and a salty, sea-breeze tang.
- **Grüner Veltliner** (Austria): green apple, citrus and white pepper.
- **Melon de Bourgogne** (Muscadet): light, lemony and briny, often aged sur lie.

cards.q: Which grape is famous in Spain's Rías Baixas?
cards.explain: On Galicia's cool, rainy Atlantic coast, Albariño makes fresh, saline whites perfect for seafood.

cards.q: White pepper is a signature aroma of…
cards.explain: Austria's signature grape combines green fruit with a peppery twist.

cards.q: Muscadet is often aged ___ lie, on its lees, for extra texture.
cards.explain: 'Sur lie' means on the lees. The wine is bottled straight off them, keeping freshness and a light yeasty note.

cards.q: Albariño is the same grape as Portugal's Alvarinho.
cards.explain: Across the border it makes the finest Vinho Verde in Monção and Melgaço.

cards.q: The Wachau, famous for Grüner Veltliner and Riesling, lies along which river?
cards.explain: Steep stone terraces line the Danube west of Krems.

cards.title: Grapes of the Atlantic
cards.body:
Cool, damp Atlantic coasts favor fresh, salty whites: **Albariño** in Rías Baixas (Spain), **Alvarinho** in Vinho Verde (Portugal) and **Melon de Bourgogne** in Muscadet (France).

All three are classic partners for seafood.

cards.title: Rhône and Mediterranean whites
cards.body: **Viognier**, **Marsanne** and **Roussanne** make rich, textured whites in the Rhône. Around the Mediterranean, **Vermentino** gives herbal, saline whites, and **Assyrtiko** from Santorini combines ripeness with striking acidity.

cards.q: Albariño and Alvarinho are…
options: The same grape in Spain and Portugal
cards.explain: It is called Albariño in Rías Baixas and Alvarinho in Vinho Verde.

cards.q: Match the grape to its homeland
cards.explain: Each of these whites is closely tied to one place.

cards.q: Grüner Veltliner often shows white pepper notes.
cards.explain: White pepper, green apple and lentil-like notes are typical of Austrian Grüner.

cards.q: Which white grape keeps high acidity even on hot, volcanic Santorini?
cards.explain: Assyrtiko is famous for keeping its fresh acidity in a hot climate.

cards.q: Muscadet is made from the ___ grape.
cards.explain: Muscadet, near the mouth of the Loire, is made from Melon de Bourgogne.

units.title: More black grapes
units.summary: Grenache, Tempranillo, Italy's great reds, and the New World stars Malbec, Zinfandel, Carmenère and Pinotage.

cards.title: Grenache
cards.body: Thin-skinned and heat-loving: **high alcohol, soft tannin**, strawberry, raspberry, white pepper and dried herbs. It is the backbone of **Châteauneuf-du-Pape** and Southern Rhône blends (GSM), and great for rosé.

cards.title: Tempranillo
cards.body: Spain's noble grape: red cherry, plum, leather and tobacco. In **Rioja** it is traditionally aged in **American oak**, adding vanilla and coconut. In **Ribera del Duero** it is darker and more powerful.

cards.q: What does GSM stand for?
cards.explain: The classic Southern Rhône blend, also popular in Australia's Barossa and McLaren Vale.

cards.q: Coconut and vanilla in traditional Rioja come from…
cards.explain: American oak has more of the compounds that smell of coconut (lactones) and vanilla.

cards.q: Grenache usually produces wines with high alcohol and soft tannins.
cards.explain: It accumulates sugar easily in hot climates, and its thin skins give gentle tannins.

cards.q: Which Spanish region is Tempranillo's most famous home?
cards.explain: Rioja, along the Ebro river, is Spain's classic red region.

cards.title: Sangiovese
cards.body: Italy's most planted grape: **sour cherry, tomato leaf and dried herbs**, with high acidity and firm tannin. The grape of **Chianti**, **Brunello di Montalcino** and **Vino Nobile di Montepulciano**.

cards.title: Nebbiolo
cards.body: "Tar and roses." **Pale** yet ferociously **tannic and acidic**, it makes Piedmont's **Barolo** and **Barbaresco**, among the longest-lived wines in the world.

cards.q: Chianti is made mainly from…
cards.explain: Chianti Classico must be at least 80% Sangiovese.

cards.q: Barolo is made from which grape?
cards.explain: 100% Nebbiolo, from hills south-west of Alba in Piedmont.

cards.q: Nebbiolo makes deeply colored, low-tannin wines.
cards.explain: Nebbiolo is relatively pale, fades to garnet early, and is very high in tannin and acidity.

cards.q: Nebbiolo's classic aromas are summed up as 'tar and ___'.
cards.explain: Rose petals and violets, with tar, liquorice and dried cherry.

cards.title: Signature grapes
cards.body:
- **Malbec** (Argentina): inky, plush, blackberry and violet. Altitude in Mendoza keeps it fresh.
- **Zinfandel** (California): jammy blackberry, high alcohol. Called Primitivo in Italy.
- **Carmenère** (Chile): red plum and green pepper; rediscovered in 1994.
- **Pinotage** (South Africa): a 1925 cross of Pinot Noir and Cinsault.

cards.q: Match the grape to its adopted home
cards.explain: Each of these became its country's signature red.

cards.q: Zinfandel is genetically identical to…
cards.explain: Both trace back to the Croatian grape Tribidrag (Crljenak Kaštelanski).

cards.q: Malbec originally came from Cahors in South West France.
cards.explain: It was once important in Bordeaux too, but Argentina made it world-famous.

cards.q: Pinotage is a cross of Pinot Noir and…
cards.explain: Created in 1925 at Stellenbosch University; Cinsault was known in South Africa as Hermitage, hence the name.

cards.title: Light and fragrant
cards.body:
- **Gamay**: the grape of **Beaujolais**. Juicy red cherry and raspberry, low tannin, high acidity; often made by carbonic maceration (banana, bubblegum).
- **Cabernet Franc**: raspberry, violet and a leafy note; the star of the Loire (**Chinon**) and a partner in Bordeaux blends.

cards.q: Beaujolais is made from…
cards.explain: Beaujolais lies just south of Burgundy and is almost entirely Gamay.

cards.q: Which technique gives Beaujolais Nouveau its banana and bubblegum notes?
cards.explain: Whole bunches ferment inside the berries in a CO₂ atmosphere, making soft, fruity, aromatic reds.

cards.q: Chinon in the Loire Valley is made mainly from Cabernet Franc.
cards.explain: Fragrant red fruit, violets and a leafy, pencil-shaving edge.

cards.q: Cabernet Franc is a parent of Cabernet ___.
cards.explain: Cabernet Franc × Sauvignon Blanc = Cabernet Sauvignon.

cards.title: Italy's great reds
cards.body:
**Sangiovese** is the grape of Chianti and Brunello di Montalcino: red cherry, herbs and high acidity. **Nebbiolo** makes Barolo and Barbaresco: pale color, rose and tar aromas, and big tannin.

Both love food thanks to their acidity.

cards.title: Iberia's great reds
cards.body: **Tempranillo** leads Rioja and Ribera del Duero, often aged in oak for vanilla and leather notes. **Touriga Nacional** is Portugal's star for Port and dry Douro reds, with violet and black fruit.

cards.q: Which grape makes Barolo?
cards.explain: Barolo and Barbaresco are 100% Nebbiolo, from Piedmont.

cards.q: Nebbiolo wines are usually deep, inky purple.
cards.explain: Nebbiolo is surprisingly pale, often garnet, despite huge tannin and acidity.

cards.q: Match the wine to its main grape
cards.explain: European wines are named after the place, so knowing the grape behind each is key.

cards.q: 'Tar and roses' is a classic description of…
cards.explain: Rose petal and tar (or liquorice) are Nebbiolo's signature aromas.

cards.q: Brunello di Montalcino is made from ___.
cards.explain: Brunello is the local name for the Sangiovese clone grown around Montalcino.

units.title: Sparkling wines
units.summary: How the bubbles get in, Champagne, Prosecco, Cava and sweetness levels.

cards.title: A second fermentation in bottle
cards.body: The finest sparkling wines are made by the **traditional method**: a still base wine gets yeast and sugar, then ferments **a second time inside its own bottle**. The trapped CO₂ makes the bubbles.

cards.title: The magic of lees
cards.body: The wine then rests on its dead yeast (**lees**) for months or years. As the yeast breaks down (**autolysis**), it gives **biscuit, bread and brioche** aromas and finer bubbles.

cards.q: In the traditional method, where does the second fermentation happen?
cards.explain: That's what makes Champagne, Cava and Crémant special, and labor-intensive.

cards.q: Brioche and biscuit aromas in Champagne come from…
cards.explain: Autolysis, the breakdown of dead yeast cells, releases these bready, toasty notes.

cards.q: Turning bottles so the yeast slides into the neck is called ___.
cards.explain: Riddling (remuage) used to be done by hand on wooden racks; today machines called gyropalettes do most of it.

cards.q: Dosage is the mix of wine and sugar added after disgorgement.
cards.explain: Dosage sets the final sweetness, from Brut Nature (no added sugar) to Doux.

cards.title: The original
cards.body:
A cold, northerly region with **chalk** soils. Three main grapes:

- **Chardonnay**: finesse and citrus.
- **Pinot Noir**: body and red fruit.
- **Meunier**: fruity roundness.

Most Champagne is a **non-vintage** blend of many villages and years, made in a consistent house style.

cards.q: Which three grapes dominate Champagne?
cards.explain: Macabeo, Xarel·lo and Parellada make Cava; Glera makes Prosecco.

cards.q: A Champagne labeled Blanc de Blancs is made from…
cards.explain: 'White from whites'. Blanc de Noirs is white wine from black grapes (Pinot Noir and Meunier).

cards.q: Non-vintage Champagne must age at least 15 months before release.
cards.explain: At least 12 months of that on lees. Vintage Champagne needs at least three years.

cards.q: Match the Champagne district to its main grape
cards.explain: Each district is known for the grape that best suits its soils and frost risk.

cards.title: The tank method
cards.body: **Prosecco** (from the **Glera** grape) gets its second fermentation in a large **pressure tank**. It's faster and cheaper, and keeps fresh **pear, apple and blossom** aromas without the bready notes.

cards.title: Other traditional-method wines
cards.body:
- **Cava** (Spain): Macabeo, Xarel·lo and Parellada; citrus and almond.
- **Crémant** (France): Loire, Alsace and Burgundy.
- **Franciacorta** (Italy), **English sparkling**, **Tasmania**, **Cap Classique** (South Africa).

cards.q: Prosecco is mostly made by…
cards.explain: Tank fermentation preserves Glera's fresh, fruity, floral character.

cards.q: Cava comes from which country?
cards.explain: Mostly from Penedès near Barcelona, made by the traditional method.

cards.q: Crémant is a French traditional-method sparkling wine made outside Champagne.
cards.explain: Same method, different places and often local grapes: often great value.

cards.q: Prosecco is made from the ___ grape.
cards.explain: Glera grows in the Veneto and Friuli. The best comes from the hills of Conegliano-Valdobbiadene.

cards.q: Which sparkling wine label term is drier: Brut or Extra Dry?
cards.explain: Confusingly, Extra Dry (12–17 g/L) is sweeter than Brut (under 12 g/L).

lessons.title: Deep dive: the traditional method step by step

cards.title: 1. The base wine
cards.body:
Grapes are picked early for high acidity and pressed gently as **whole bunches**. The first, purest juice is the *cuvée*; later pressings (*taille*) are fuller and less fine.

The juice ferments into a dry, sharp, low-alcohol **base wine**. Many base wines from different villages, grapes and years are blended into the house style: this is the **assemblage**.

cards.title: 2. Second fermentation in bottle
cards.body:
The blend is bottled with the **liqueur de tirage**: wine, sugar and yeast. A crown cap seals it.

Yeast eats the sugar, making about **1.5% more alcohol** and carbon dioxide that cannot escape: around **6 atmospheres** of pressure, three times a car tire.

cards.title: 3. Ageing on the lees
cards.body:
Dead yeast cells (lees) slowly break down (**autolysis**), giving bread, brioche, biscuit and toast notes and a finer, creamier mousse.

Champagne rules: at least **15 months** for non-vintage (12 on the lees) and **3 years** for vintage. Top houses go much longer, in cool chalk cellars under Reims and Épernay.

cards.title: 4. Riddling and disgorging
cards.body:
**Riddling** (*remuage*) turns and tilts bottles day by day until the sediment slides into the neck. Once done by hand on wooden *pupitres*, it is now mostly done by **gyropalettes**.

The neck is frozen, the cap removed, and pressure pops out the plug of ice and yeast: **disgorgement**.

cards.title: 5. Dosage and sweetness
cards.body:
The bottle is topped up with **liqueur d'expédition**, wine with a little sugar. This **dosage** sets the style:

- **Brut Nature**: 0–3 g/L
- **Extra Brut**: 0–6 g/L
- **Brut**: under 12 g/L (most Champagne)
- **Extra Dry**: 12–17 g/L (sweeter than Brut!)
- **Demi-Sec**: 32–50 g/L

cards.q: What creates the bubbles in traditional-method sparkling wine?
options: A second fermentation in the bottle
cards.explain: Sugar and yeast are added at bottling; the CO2 they make is trapped.

cards.q: Which is sweeter?
cards.explain: Confusingly, Extra Dry (12–17 g/L) is sweeter than Brut (under 12 g/L).

cards.q: Breakdown of dead yeast cells that gives brioche notes is called ___.
cards.explain: The longer on the lees, the more toasty and creamy the wine.

cards.q: Put the steps with their French names
cards.explain: These words appear on back labels and in every Champagne cellar tour.

cards.q: Non-vintage Champagne must age at least 15 months before release.
cards.explain: Vintage Champagne needs at least 3 years.

lessons.title: Deep dive: the world of bubbles

cards.title: Champagne's grapes and villages
cards.body:
Three main grapes: **Chardonnay** (finesse, citrus, the Côte des Blancs), **Pinot Noir** (body, red fruit, the Montagne de Reims) and **Meunier** (fruity, early-drinking, the Vallée de la Marne).

Villages are rated: 17 are **Grand Cru**, 42 **Premier Cru**.

cards.title: Who makes it
cards.body:
Labels carry a code:
- **NM** (négociant-manipulant): a house that buys grapes, like Moët or Bollinger.
- **RM** (récoltant-manipulant): a grower making wine only from their own vines, "grower Champagne".
- **CM**: a cooperative.

cards.title: Tank method: Prosecco and Asti
cards.body:
In the **tank method** (Charmat), the second fermentation happens in a big pressurized tank. It is fast and keeps the grape's fresh fruit and floral aromas.

**Prosecco** (Glera, Veneto and Friuli) is the best known; Conegliano Valdobbiadene is its hilly heartland. **Asti** and **Moscato d'Asti** use a single fermentation stopped early, so they stay sweet and low in alcohol.

cards.title: Other great sparklers
cards.body:
- **Cava** (Spain, mostly Penedès): traditional method with Macabeo, Xarel·lo, Parellada.
- **Crémant** (France: Loire, Alsace, Burgundy, Limoux…): traditional method, at least 9 months on lees.
- **Franciacorta** (Lombardy) and **Trentodoc**: Italy's traditional-method stars.
- **English sparkling wine**: chalk soils like Champagne's, booming since the 1990s.
- **Pét-nat** (*pétillant naturel*): bottled before the first fermentation finishes; cloudy and rustic.

cards.q: Which grape is the specialty of the Côte des Blancs?
cards.explain: Blanc de Blancs means 'white from whites': 100% white grapes, usually Chardonnay.

cards.q: What does 'RM' on a Champagne label tell you?
options: A grower made it from their own grapes
cards.explain: Récoltant-manipulant: grower Champagne.

cards.q: Match the sparkling wine to its method
cards.explain: Method shapes texture and flavor as much as the grape.

cards.q: Moscato d'Asti is fully sparkling and around 12% alcohol.
cards.explain: It is gently sparkling (frizzante), sweet and only about 5% alcohol.

cards.title: Bubble methods
cards.body:
**Traditional method**: second fermentation in the bottle, ageing on lees for toasty, fine-bubbled wines (Champagne, Cava, Crémant).

**Tank method**: second fermentation in a sealed tank for fresh, fruity wines (Prosecco).

cards.title: How sweet is Brut?
cards.body:
Sparkling sweetness runs from **Brut Nature** (no added sugar) through **Extra Brut** and **Brut** (the most common, dry) to **Extra Dry**, **Dry**, **Demi-Sec** and **Doux** (sweet).

Confusingly, Extra Dry is slightly sweeter than Brut.

cards.q: Which wine is usually made by the tank method?
cards.explain: Prosecco's second fermentation happens in pressurized tanks, keeping fresh pear and apple fruit.

cards.q: Extra Dry sparkling wine is drier than Brut.
cards.explain: A historical quirk: Extra Dry has a little more sugar than Brut.

cards.q: Match the sparkling wine to its country
cards.explain: Most wine countries have a sparkling tradition.

cards.q: Where does Champagne's toasty, bready character come from?
cards.explain: Dead yeast cells break down over months or years, giving brioche and biscuit notes.

cards.q: Removing the yeast plug from the neck of the bottle is called ___.
cards.explain: The neck is frozen, the cap removed, and pressure pushes out the yeast plug.

units.title: Sweet & fortified
units.summary: Noble rot, icewine, Port and Sherry.

cards.title: Concentrate the sugar
cards.body:
To make a sweet wine you need more sugar than yeast can ferment, or you stop fermentation early. Winemakers concentrate grapes by:

- **Late harvest**: leaving them to ripen and shrivel on the vine.
- **Noble rot**: Botrytis cinerea pierces the skins.
- **Freezing**: icewine.
- **Drying** after harvest: passito.

cards.q: What is Botrytis cinerea?
options: A type of yeast for Champagne
cards.explain: Under the right conditions (misty mornings, dry afternoons) it is 'noble rot', making wines like Sauternes and Tokaji.

cards.q: Icewine is made from grapes that are…
cards.explain: Pressed while frozen, only a little concentrated, sugary juice is released. Canada and Germany are famous for it.

cards.q: Sauternes is a sweet wine made with grapes affected by noble rot.
cards.explain: Sémillon and Sauvignon Blanc from Sauternes and Barsac, in southern Bordeaux.

cards.q: Hungary's famous noble rot wine is Tokaji ___.
cards.explain: Botrytized aszú berries are soaked in base wine or must, giving luscious, high-acid wines that live for decades.

cards.q: Match the sweet wine to its method
cards.explain: Three different routes to sweetness.

cards.title: Fortified mid-fermentation
cards.body: Port comes from Portugal's **Douro Valley**. Halfway through fermentation, **grape spirit** is added. This kills the yeast, leaving a **sweet, strong (about 20% abv)**, deeply colored wine.

cards.title: Ruby vs tawny
cards.body:
- **Ruby** styles (Ruby, Reserve, LBV, Vintage): aged to keep fresh black fruit.
- **Tawny** styles: aged for years in small casks, becoming brownish with nutty, caramel notes.

cards.q: When is grape spirit added to Port?
cards.explain: Adding spirit early stops fermentation and keeps the natural grape sugar.

cards.q: Port comes from which river valley?
cards.explain: Grapes grow on steep schist terraces; wines were traditionally shipped down to Porto's lodges in Vila Nova de Gaia.

cards.q: Tawny Port gets its nutty flavors from long ageing in small wooden casks.
cards.explain: Oxygen through the small casks turns the wine tawny and develops walnut, toffee and caramel notes.

cards.q: Port is typically about ___% alcohol.
cards.explain: Usually 19–22% abv.

cards.title: The world's most misunderstood wine
cards.body:
Sherry comes from the hot south of Spain around **Jerez**. Most is made from **Palomino** and is **dry**.

- **Fino & Manzanilla**: aged under **flor** (a layer of yeast); pale, bone dry, tangy, almond and bread.
- **Oloroso**: aged with oxygen; dark, nutty, dry.
- **Pedro Ximénez**: from sun-dried grapes; black, raisiny, very sweet.

cards.title: The solera
cards.body: Sherry ages in a **solera**, tiers of barrels where younger wine gradually refreshes older wine. The result is consistent year after year, so most Sherry has no vintage.

cards.q: What is flor?
options: A layer of yeast that protects Fino from oxygen
cards.explain: It grows on the wine's surface in partly filled barrels, keeping it pale and adding bready, salty notes.

cards.q: Most Sherry is sweet.
cards.explain: Fino, Manzanilla, Amontillado and Oloroso are naturally dry. Sweet styles are Pedro Ximénez, Moscatel and blended Cream Sherry.

cards.q: Which Sherry is darkest and sweetest?
cards.explain: PX is made from sun-dried grapes: syrupy, raisined and almost black.

cards.q: Manzanilla is a Fino-style Sherry aged in which seaside town?
cards.explain: Sea air helps flor grow thickly, giving an extra-salty tang.

cards.q: Sherry is aged in a fractional blending system called a ___.
cards.explain: Wine is drawn from the oldest tier and replaced from the next-oldest, and so on.

lessons.title: Deep dive: how sweetness is made

cards.title: Concentrate the sugar
cards.body:
Sweet wine needs grapes so sugary that yeast cannot (or is not allowed to) ferment it all. Four ways:

- **Noble rot** (*Botrytis cinerea*): misty mornings, sunny afternoons; the fungus pierces skins and water evaporates. Sauternes, Tokaji, Trockenbeerenauslese.
- **Drying**: grapes dry on mats or in lofts (*appassimento*, *passito*). Recioto, Vin Santo.
- **Freezing**: grapes freeze on the vine; water stays behind as ice when pressed. Icewine, Eiswein.
- **Late harvest**: simply leave grapes to shrivel on the vine.

cards.title: Icewine
cards.body:
Grapes must be picked frozen, at about **-8 °C** or colder, usually at night in December or January. Only a few drops of syrupy juice come from each bunch.

Canada (Ontario, often **Vidal** or Riesling) and Germany/Austria (Eiswein) are the leaders. The style is intensely sweet with piercing acidity.

cards.title: Stop the fermentation
cards.body:
Another route is to **stop** fermentation while sugar remains:
- Chilling and filtering out the yeast (Moscato d'Asti, many German Kabinett and Spätlese).
- Adding grape spirit, which kills the yeast: **fortification** (Port, Vins Doux Naturels).

cards.title: Tokaji Aszú
cards.body:
In Hungary's Tokaj, botrytized **aszú** berries (mainly **Furmint**) are picked one by one and soaked in fermenting wine. Sweetness used to be measured in **puttonyos**, the baskets of aszú added; today the minimum is 120 g/L of sugar.

**Eszencia** is the free-run syrup alone: so sweet it barely ferments, reaching just a few % alcohol.

cards.q: What does noble rot do to grapes?
options: Shrivels them and concentrates sugar and acid
cards.explain: Botrytis pierces the skin and water evaporates; it also adds honey, marmalade and saffron notes.

cards.q: How cold must grapes be for icewine?
cards.explain: At that temperature most of the water is frozen, leaving concentrated juice.

cards.q: Match the sweet wine to its method
cards.explain: Four different routes to sweetness.

cards.q: Furmint is the main grape of Tokaji.
cards.explain: Furmint's high acidity balances the huge sweetness; Hárslevelű is its partner.

lessons.title: Deep dive: Port, Sherry and Madeira

cards.title: Port: the Douro and Gaia
cards.body:
Port grapes (Touriga Nacional, Touriga Franca, Tinta Roriz and others) grow on steep **schist terraces** of the Douro. Fermentation lasts only two or three days before **grape spirit at 77%** is added, leaving a sweet wine of about **19–22%**.

Traditionally the young wine went downriver to the lodges of **Vila Nova de Gaia**, opposite Porto, to age.

cards.title: Ruby or tawny?
cards.body:
- **Ruby styles** age in big vats or bottle; fruit stays deep red and fresh. Ruby, Reserve, LBV (4–6 years in wood), and **Vintage Port**, made only in declared years and aged for decades in bottle.
- **Tawny styles** age in small casks; oxygen fades the color to amber and builds nutty, caramel notes. 10, 20, 30, 40 Year Old, and **Colheita** (single harvest).

cards.title: Sherry: flor or no flor
cards.body:
Sherry is made from **Palomino** in the chalky *albariza* soils around **Jerez**. The base wine is dry; it is fortified and aged in a **solera**, a stack of casks where young wine refreshes older wine.

- **Fino / Manzanilla**: fortified to about 15%, so a layer of yeast, **flor**, grows on top and protects it from air. Pale, salty, bone dry.
- **Oloroso**: fortified to about 17%, too strong for flor; ages with oxygen into a dark, nutty wine.
- **Amontillado** and **Palo Cortado** sit in between.
- **Pedro Ximénez**: sun-dried grapes, syrupy sweet.

cards.title: Madeira: cooked and immortal
cards.body:
On the Portuguese island of Madeira, wines are deliberately **heated**: in tanks (*estufagem*) or for years in warm attics (*canteiro*). The result tastes of caramel and walnut with soaring acidity, and can last for centuries once opened.

Styles follow the grapes, dry to sweet: **Sercial**, **Verdelho**, **Bual**, **Malmsey** (Malvasia).

cards.q: Why is fino sherry so pale?
options: A layer of flor yeast protects it from oxygen
It is made from white grapes only
cards.explain: Without air contact, it stays pale and fresh, with salty, bready notes.

cards.q: Where do the big Port houses traditionally age their wines?
cards.explain: Across the Douro from Porto; the lodges' signs line the riverfront.

cards.q: Match the Madeira style to its sweetness
cards.explain: The grape names on the label tell you the sweetness.

cards.q: Tawny Port gets its color from ageing in small casks.
cards.explain: Slow oxidation turns the red to amber-brown.

cards.q: A tiered system of casks where young sherry refreshes older sherry is a ___.
cards.explain: Wine is drawn from the oldest casks and topped up from the next oldest.

cards.title: Three roads to sweetness
cards.body:
1. **Noble rot** (botrytis) shrivels grapes and concentrates sugar: Sauternes, Tokaji.
2. **Freezing**: grapes picked frozen give Icewine/Eiswein.
3. **Drying**: grapes dried after picking make Recioto and Vin Santo.

Stopping fermentation early, as in Port, is a fourth route.

cards.title: Sherry styles
cards.body: **Fino** and **Manzanilla** age under a layer of yeast called **flor**: pale, dry, salty, almond. **Oloroso** ages without flor, in contact with air: dark, nutty, dry. **Pedro Ximénez** is a dark, raisin-sweet dessert sherry.

cards.q: What is 'flor' in sherry-making?
options: A layer of yeast on the wine
cards.explain: Flor protects Fino and Manzanilla from oxygen and gives a tangy, bready, almond character.

cards.q: Match the sweet wine to how it's made
cards.explain: Different routes to sugar create very different sweet wines.

cards.q: Oloroso sherry ages under flor.
cards.explain: Oloroso is fortified to a strength where flor can't survive, so it ages oxidatively and darkens.

cards.q: Which wine is fortified during fermentation, keeping natural sweetness?
cards.explain: Adding grape spirit stops fermentation, leaving sugar in the wine.

cards.q: Noble rot is caused by a fungus called ___.
cards.explain: Botrytis cinerea, in the right conditions, shrivels grapes and concentrates sugar and acid.

units.title: Reading labels
units.summary: Place versus grape, quality categories and the label terms that matter.

cards.title: Two ways to name a wine
cards.body:
- **Old World** labels often name the **place**: Chablis, Rioja, Barolo. You are expected to know the grape.
- **New World** labels usually name the **grape**: Napa Cabernet Sauvignon, Marlborough Sauvignon Blanc.

cards.q: Match the place-name wine to its grape
cards.explain: Learning these 'translations' unlocks most European wine lists.

cards.q: Red Burgundy is made from…
cards.explain: And white Burgundy is Chardonnay.

cards.q: In the USA, a wine labeled 'Merlot' must contain at least 75% Merlot.
cards.explain: US law requires at least 75% of the named variety (the EU usually requires 85%).

cards.q: Which country is considered New World?
cards.explain: New World countries include the USA, Australia, New Zealand, South Africa, Chile and Argentina.

cards.title: The EU system
cards.body:
European wine law has two main tiers:

- **PDO** (Protected Designation of Origin): strict rules on area, grapes, yields and methods. *AOC/AOP* in France, *DOC/DOCG* in Italy, *DO/DOCa* in Spain.
- **PGI** (Protected Geographical Indication): a wider area and more flexibility. *IGP / Vin de Pays*, *IGT*, *Vino de la Tierra*.

cards.q: Which is Italy's highest wine category?
cards.explain: Denominazione di Origine Controllata e Garantita, above DOC and IGT.

cards.q: PGI wines have stricter rules than PDO wines.
cards.explain: PDO is stricter. PGI allows more freedom, which is why some ambitious producers choose it (as with early Super Tuscans).

cards.q: Match the label term to its country
cards.explain: Each country has its own names for the EU PDO category.

cards.q: In Spain, Rioja and Priorat hold the top category, DOCa, also written ___ in Catalan.
cards.explain: Priorat uses the Catalan form, Denominació d'Origen Qualificada.

cards.title: Useful label terms
cards.body:
- **Vintage**: the harvest year.
- **Classico** (Italy): the historic heart of a region.
- **Riserva / Reserva**: aged longer before release.
- **Crianza, Reserva, Gran Reserva** (Spain): rising minimum ageing.
- **Grand Cru / Premier Cru**: top vineyard classifications (France).
- **Trocken**: dry (Germany). **Brut**: dry sparkling.

cards.q: On a Spanish label, which term means the longest ageing?
cards.explain: Red Rioja Gran Reserva: at least five years, two in oak.

cards.q: What does 'Classico' mean on an Italian label?
options: From the historic heart of the region
cards.explain: Chianti Classico is the original Chianti zone between Florence and Siena.

cards.q: The vintage on a label is the year the wine was bottled.
cards.explain: Vintage is the year the grapes were harvested.

cards.q: On a German label, ___ means dry.
cards.explain: Halbtrocken means off-dry. Spätlese is a ripeness level, not a sweetness term.

cards.title: Quality pyramids
cards.body: Most EU countries rank wines in a pyramid: **PDO** wines from tightly defined places with strict rules (AOC, DOC, DOCG, DO), **PGI** wines from wider areas with more freedom (IGP, IGT, Vino de la Tierra) and simple **wine** without a place.

cards.title: Ageing terms
cards.body: Spanish and Italian labels often show ageing: **Crianza**, **Reserva** and **Gran Reserva** in Spain; **Riserva** in Italy. Each means a longer minimum time in barrel and bottle before release.

cards.q: Which Spanish term means the longest minimum ageing?
cards.explain: For reds, Gran Reserva means at least five years of ageing, with time in oak.

cards.q: Match the label term to its country
cards.explain: Each country has its own words for top-quality, place-based wines.

cards.q: PGI wines have stricter rules than PDO wines.
cards.explain: PDO is the stricter, more specific category; PGI allows wider areas and more grapes.

cards.q: What does 'Riserva' on an Italian label tell you?
cards.explain: Riserva wines meet a longer minimum ageing period set by each DOC/DOCG.

cards.q: In Germany, a dry Prädikatswein is labeled ___.
cards.explain: Trocken means dry; Spätlese and Auslese describe ripeness at harvest, not sweetness.

units.title: Label decoder
units.summary: Read any bottle: how France, Germany, Italy, Spain, Portugal and the New World label their wines.

cards.title: Château first, place second
cards.body: A Bordeaux label names the **château** (the estate), the **appellation** and often a **classification** such as *Grand Cru Classé en 1855*. There's no grape on the front: it's a blend.

cards.title: In Burgundy, the vineyard is king
cards.body: Burgundy's hierarchy shows in the name: **Bourgogne** (regional) → **village** (Gevrey-Chambertin) → **Premier Cru** (village + vineyard) → **Grand Cru** (the vineyard alone, e.g. *Chambertin*).

cards.q: On a Bordeaux label, 'Mis en bouteille au château' means…
cards.explain: Estate bottling means the wine was made and bottled where the grapes were grown.

cards.q: Which Burgundy label shows a Grand Cru?
cards.explain: Grand Crus appear on their own name. The village name alone (Gevrey-Chambertin) is village level.

cards.q: Red Burgundy labels usually state 'Pinot Noir' on the front.
cards.explain: Place, not grape: red Burgundy is understood to be Pinot Noir, and white is Chardonnay.

cards.q: Match the Burgundy label to its level
cards.explain: The more precise the place, the higher the level.

cards.title: Champagne codes
cards.body: Look for the **house**, the **style** (Blanc de Blancs, Rosé), the **sweetness** (Brut, Extra Brut…) and the tiny **maker code**: **NM** (a house buying grapes), **RM** (a grower making their own), **CM** (a co-operative).

cards.title: Alsace names the grape
cards.body: Unusually for France, Alsace puts the **grape** first. *Grand Cru* plus a vineyard name marks the 51 best sites; *Vendanges Tardives* and *Sélection de Grains Nobles* signal sweet wines.

cards.q: What does 'RM' on a Champagne label tell you?
options: A grower made it from their own grapes
cards.explain: Récoltant-Manipulant: 'grower Champagne'.

cards.q: On a Champagne label, ___ ___ means it was made only from Chardonnay.
cards.explain: 'White from whites'. Blanc de Noirs is white wine from black grapes.

cards.q: Alsace wines are usually labeled with the grape variety.
cards.explain: Riesling, Gewurztraminer, Pinot Gris and Muscat are the classic four.

cards.title: German labels
cards.body: Expect a lot of information: **region**, **village + vineyard** (*Wehlener Sonnenuhr*), **grape** and the **Prädikat** ripeness level (Kabinett, Spätlese, Auslese…). **Trocken** means dry.

cards.title: Italy and Spain
cards.body:
- **Italy**: denomination (Chianti Classico, Barolo), category **DOCG/DOC/IGT**, and ageing terms (*Riserva*, *Gran Selezione*).
- **Spain**: region (Rioja) and the ageing ladder **Joven → Crianza → Reserva → Gran Reserva**. *Cosecha* = vintage.

cards.title: Port
cards.body: The style is everything: **Ruby**, **LBV**, **Vintage**, or **Tawny** with an age (10, 20, 30, 40 years).

cards.q: On 'Wehlener Sonnenuhr', what is Sonnenuhr?
cards.explain: Wehlen is the village (adding -er), Sonnenuhr ('sundial') the vineyard.

cards.q: Which Spanish term means the longest ageing?
cards.explain: Red Rioja Gran Reserva: at least five years, two in oak. Cosecha just means vintage.

cards.q: Match the label word to its meaning
cards.explain: A small vocabulary unlocks most European labels.

cards.q: A '20 Years Old Tawny' Port is made only from wine harvested exactly 20 years ago.
cards.explain: It's an indication of age: a blend whose character matches about 20 years in cask.

cards.title: Brand, grape, place
cards.body:
New World labels lead with the **brand** and the **grape**, then the region: an **AVA** in the USA, a **GI** in Australia, **WO** in South Africa.

In the USA, a named grape means ≥75% of it, a named AVA ≥85% of grapes from there, a vintage ≥95% from that year.

cards.title: Words without legal meaning
cards.body: "Reserve", "Old Vine" and "Special Selection" usually have **no legal definition** in the New World. They're the producer's own promise.

cards.q: On a US label, a named AVA means at least what share of grapes came from there?
cards.explain: For a named grape the US minimum is 75%; for an AVA, 85%.

cards.q: 'Reserve' on a Californian wine is a legally defined quality level.
cards.explain: It's a producer term. In Spain and Italy, Reserva/Riserva *are* legally defined.

cards.q: What does GI stand for on an Australian label?
cards.explain: Australia's system of zones, regions and subregions.

cards.title: Château, Domaine, Bodega
cards.body: The producer's name often starts with a word for estate: **Château** (Bordeaux), **Domaine** (Burgundy and elsewhere in France), **Bodega** (Spain), **Weingut** (Germany, Austria), **Quinta** (Portugal) and **Tenuta** (Italy).

cards.title: Burgundy's ladder
cards.body: Burgundy labels climb a ladder: **Bourgogne** (regional), **village** (e.g. Gevrey-Chambertin), **Premier Cru** (a named vineyard plus the village) and **Grand Cru** (the vineyard name alone, e.g. Chambertin).

cards.q: On a Burgundy label, which level shows only the vineyard name?
cards.explain: Grand Crus are so famous they stand alone: Montrachet, Chambertin, Romanée-Conti.

cards.q: Match the estate word to its country
cards.explain: Knowing these words helps you find the producer on any label.

cards.q: 'Mis en bouteille au château' means bottled at the estate.
cards.explain: Estate bottling shows the same property grew the grapes and bottled the wine.

cards.q: In Germany, which word tells you about ripeness at harvest?
cards.explain: Kabinett, Spätlese and Auslese are Prädikat levels based on grape ripeness.

cards.q: In Rioja, a wine aged at least two years, one in oak, is labeled ___.
cards.explain: Crianza red Rioja spends at least two years ageing, with at least one in oak.

units.title: Grape files
units.summary: Every Level 2 grape on one card: aromas, structure, origin and where it grows.

cards.title: Chenin Blanc
cards.body:
A chameleon with piercing acidity, made in every style: dry, off-dry, sweet and sparkling. Honeyed, apple-scented and capable of great age.

- **Aromas:** green apple, quince, pear, lemon, honey, wet wool.
- **Structure:** medium body, high acidity.
- **Origin:** Loire Valley, France.
- **Where it grows:** Loire Valley, Vouvray, Montlouis-sur-Loire, Savennières, Anjou, Saumur.
- **Food:** pork with apples, thai food, goat cheese, fruit tarts (sweet styles).

cards.title: Sémillon
cards.body:
Low in aroma when young but rich in texture. The heart of Sauternes, and in Australia's Hunter Valley a unique dry wine that ages into toast and honey.

- **Aromas:** lemon, green apple, grass, honey, toast, marmalade.
- **Structure:** medium body, medium acidity.
- **Origin:** Bordeaux, France.
- **Where it grows:** Bordeaux, Sauternes & Barsac, Graves, Pessac-Léognan, Hunter Valley, Margaret River.
- **Food:** foie gras (sweet), blue cheese (sweet), seafood (dry hunter).

cards.title: Gewürztraminer
cards.body:
The most perfumed grape of all: rose petals, lychee and ginger. Low acidity, deep color and an oily texture.

- **Aromas:** rose, lychee, peach, orange blossom, sweet spice, honey.
- **Structure:** medium-high body, medium-low acidity.
- **Origin:** Alto Adige, Italy (Tramin) & Alsace.
- **Where it grows:** Alsace, Trentino-Alto Adige, Germany, New Zealand.
- **Food:** munster cheese, spicy asian dishes, moroccan tagine, foie gras.

cards.title: Muscat
cards.body:
The one grape whose wine smells exactly of grapes. Floral, peachy and orange-scented, from feather-light Moscato d'Asti to syrupy Rutherglen Muscat.

- **Aromas:** green grape, orange blossom, rose, peach, apricot, lychee.
- **Structure:** medium-low body, medium-low acidity.
- **Origin:** Ancient Mediterranean; a family of related grapes.
- **Also called:** Moscato, Moscatel, Muskateller.
- **Where it grows:** Piedmont, Asti & Moscato d'Asti, Alsace, Rutherglen, Languedoc-Roussillon, Rhône Valley.
- **Food:** fruit desserts, panettone, blue cheese (fortified), aperitif (dry).

cards.title: Viognier
cards.body:
Full-bodied and heady with apricot, peach and honeysuckle. Low acidity, high alcohol and a silky texture.

- **Aromas:** apricot, peach, honeysuckle, violet, orange blossom, sweet spice.
- **Structure:** medium-high body, medium-low acidity.
- **Origin:** Northern Rhône, France.
- **Where it grows:** Rhône Valley, Condrieu, Languedoc-Roussillon, Eden Valley, Central Coast.
- **Food:** lobster, apricot chicken, mild curries, crab.

cards.title: Albariño
cards.body:
Fresh, saline and aromatic: peach, grapefruit and a sea-breeze tang. The seafood wine of the Atlantic coast.

- **Aromas:** peach, grapefruit, lemon, nectarine, blossom, saline.
- **Structure:** medium-low body, medium-high acidity.
- **Origin:** Galicia, Spain & northern Portugal.
- **Also called:** Alvarinho.
- **Where it grows:** Rías Baixas, Vinho Verde.
- **Food:** grilled sardines, octopus, ceviche, oysters.

cards.q: Which grape shows **green apple, quince, pear**?
cards.explain: A chameleon with piercing acidity, made in every style: dry, off-dry, sweet and sparkling. Honeyed, apple-scented and capable of great age.

cards.q: Which grape shows **lemon, green apple, grass**?
cards.explain: Low in aroma when young but rich in texture. The heart of Sauternes, and in Australia's Hunter Valley a unique dry wine that ages into toast and honey.

cards.q: Which grape shows **rose, lychee, peach**?
cards.explain: The most perfumed grape of all: rose petals, lychee and ginger. Low acidity, deep color and an oily texture.

cards.q: Match each grape to a place where it grows
cards.explain: Each grape is matched with one of its key regions from the cards above.

cards.title: Grüner Veltliner
cards.body:
Austria's signature white: crisp green fruit with a twist of white pepper.

- **Aromas:** green apple, lime, grapefruit, white pepper, grass.
- **Structure:** medium body, medium-high acidity.
- **Origin:** Austria.
- **Where it grows:** Austria, Wachau, Kremstal, Kamptal, Weinviertel, Wagram.
- **Food:** wiener schnitzel, asparagus, sushi, vegetable dishes.

cards.title: Grenache
cards.body:
Thin-skinned and generous: high alcohol, soft tannin, ripe strawberry and raspberry with white pepper and herbs. Loves heat and wind.

- **Aromas:** strawberry, raspberry, red cherry, white pepper, dried herbs, liquorice.
- **Structure:** medium-high body, medium-low acidity, medium-low tannin.
- **Origin:** Spain (Aragón).
- **Also called:** Garnacha, Cannonau.
- **Where it grows:** Rhône Valley, Châteauneuf-du-Pape, Gigondas, Vacqueyras, Côtes du Rhône, Tavel & Lirac.
- **Food:** roast lamb, stews, charcuterie, mediterranean vegetables.

cards.title: Tempranillo
cards.body:
Spain's noble grape: red cherry, plum and leather, with vanilla and coconut from traditional American oak.

- **Aromas:** red cherry, red plum, strawberry, leather, tobacco, vanilla.
- **Structure:** medium-high body, medium acidity, medium-high tannin.
- **Origin:** Rioja, Spain.
- **Also called:** Tinta Roriz, Tinto Fino, Aragonez.
- **Where it grows:** Rioja, Ribera del Duero, Toro, Navarra, La Mancha, Douro.
- **Food:** roast lamb, chorizo, manchego, paella.

cards.title: Sangiovese
cards.body:
Italy's most planted grape: sour cherry, tomato leaf and dried herbs, with high acidity and firm tannin. Made for food.

- **Aromas:** red cherry, red plum, dried herbs, tomato leaf, leather, earth.
- **Structure:** medium body, high acidity, medium-high tannin.
- **Origin:** Tuscany, Italy.
- **Also called:** Brunello, Prugnolo Gentile, Morellino.
- **Where it grows:** Tuscany, Chianti, Chianti Classico, Brunello di Montalcino, Vino Nobile di Montepulciano, Maremma.
- **Food:** tomato pasta, pizza, bistecca alla fiorentina, pecorino.

cards.title: Nebbiolo
cards.body:
Tar and roses: pale in color yet ferociously high in tannin and acidity. The grape of Barolo and Barbaresco.

- **Aromas:** red cherry, rose, violet, liquorice, tobacco, truffle.
- **Structure:** medium-high body, high acidity, high tannin.
- **Origin:** Piedmont, Italy.
- **Also called:** Spanna, Chiavennasca.
- **Where it grows:** Piedmont, Barolo, Barbaresco, Roero, Lombardy.
- **Food:** truffle pasta, braised beef, mushroom risotto, aged cheese.

cards.title: Malbec
cards.body:
Inky purple with ripe blackberry, plum and violet. Velvety tannins make Argentine Malbec one of the world's most loved reds.

- **Aromas:** blackberry, black plum, black cherry, violet, chocolate, vanilla.
- **Structure:** medium-high body, medium acidity, medium-high tannin.
- **Origin:** Cahors, South West France.
- **Also called:** Côt, Auxerrois.
- **Where it grows:** Mendoza, Uco Valley, Salta, Argentina, South West France.
- **Food:** grilled steak (asado), empanadas, barbecue.

cards.q: Which grape shows **green apple, lime, grapefruit**?
cards.explain: Austria's signature white: crisp green fruit with a twist of white pepper.

cards.q: Which grape shows **strawberry, raspberry, red cherry**?
cards.explain: Thin-skinned and generous: high alcohol, soft tannin, ripe strawberry and raspberry with white pepper and herbs. Loves heat and wind.

cards.q: Which grape shows **red cherry, red plum, strawberry**?
cards.explain: Spain's noble grape: red cherry, plum and leather, with vanilla and coconut from traditional American oak.

cards.q: Match each grape to a place where it grows
cards.explain: Each grape is matched with one of its key regions from the cards above.

cards.title: Zinfandel
cards.body:
Jammy and generous: blackberry, raspberry jam and sweet spice with high alcohol. California's heritage grape and Puglia's Primitivo.

- **Aromas:** blackberry, raspberry, jammy fruit, raisin, black pepper, sweet spice.
- **Structure:** medium-high body, medium acidity, medium tannin.
- **Origin:** Croatia.
- **Also called:** Primitivo, Crljenak Kaštelanski, Tribidrag.
- **Where it grows:** Lodi, Sierra Foothills, Napa Valley, Dry Creek Valley, Puglia.
- **Food:** barbecue ribs, pizza, burgers, chili.

cards.title: Cabernet Franc
cards.body:
Lighter and more fragrant than its offspring Cabernet Sauvignon: red fruit, violet and a leafy, green pepper note.

- **Aromas:** raspberry, red cherry, violet, green bell pepper, dried herbs.
- **Structure:** medium body, medium-high acidity, medium tannin.
- **Origin:** Basque Country / Bordeaux.
- **Also called:** Bouchet, Breton.
- **Where it grows:** Loire Valley, Chinon, Bourgueil, Saumur, Saint-Émilion, Pomerol.
- **Food:** roast pork, charcuterie, goat cheese, lentils.

cards.title: Gamay
cards.body:
The grape of Beaujolais: juicy, light and fragrant with red cherry, raspberry and banana. Best slightly chilled.

- **Aromas:** red cherry, raspberry, strawberry, banana, violet, kirsch.
- **Structure:** medium-low body, medium-high acidity, low tannin.
- **Origin:** Burgundy, France.
- **Where it grows:** Beaujolais, Loire Valley, Touraine.
- **Food:** charcuterie, roast chicken, picnic food, salmon.

cards.title: Pinotage
cards.body:
South Africa's own grape: dark fruit with smoky, earthy notes. Modern versions can be juicy or coffee-scented.

- **Aromas:** blackberry, black plum, smoke, coffee, earth, banana.
- **Structure:** medium-high body, medium acidity, medium tannin.
- **Origin:** South Africa (Pinot Noir × Cinsault, 1925).
- **Where it grows:** Stellenbosch, South Africa, Swartland.
- **Food:** braai (barbecue), game, smoky dishes.

cards.title: Carmenère
cards.body:
Chile's signature grape: red and black fruit with green pepper, paprika and herbs. Late ripening and soft.

- **Aromas:** red plum, blackberry, green bell pepper, dried herbs, black pepper, chocolate.
- **Structure:** medium-high body, medium acidity, medium tannin.
- **Origin:** Bordeaux, France.
- **Where it grows:** Chile, Colchagua, Maipo Valley, Maule.
- **Food:** grilled vegetables, chili con carne, lamb.

cards.q: Which grape shows **blackberry, raspberry, jammy fruit**?
cards.explain: Jammy and generous: blackberry, raspberry jam and sweet spice with high alcohol. California's heritage grape and Puglia's Primitivo.

cards.q: Which grape shows **raspberry, red cherry, violet**?
cards.explain: Lighter and more fragrant than its offspring Cabernet Sauvignon: red fruit, violet and a leafy, green pepper note.

cards.q: Which grape shows **red cherry, raspberry, strawberry**?
cards.explain: The grape of Beaujolais: juicy, light and fragrant with red cherry, raspberry and banana. Best slightly chilled.

cards.q: Match each grape to a place where it grows
cards.explain: Each grape is matched with one of its key regions from the cards above.

units.title: Appellations to know
units.summary: Every Level 2 region on a card, with its map, grapes and climate.

cards.title: Beaujolais
cards.body:
Gamay country: juicy, light reds from easy Beaujolais Nouveau to the serious granite-grown crus.

- **Where:** Burgundy, France.
- **Grapes:** Gamay.
- **Climate:** Semi-continental, warmer than Burgundy; granite hills in the north, clay and limestone in the south.
- Beaujolais Nouveau is released on the third Thursday of November, weeks after harvest.

cards.title: Alsace
cards.body:
German-influenced but French: aromatic, mostly dry varietal whites labeled by grape, in tall flute bottles.

- **Where:** France.
- **Grapes:** Riesling, Gewürztraminer, Pinot Grigio, Muscat, Pinot Blanc.
- **Climate:** One of France's driest regions: the Vosges mountains block rain from the west, giving long, sunny, dry autumns.
- **Quality system:** Alsace AOC, Alsace Grand Cru (51 vineyards) and Crémant d'Alsace.

cards.title: Provence
cards.body:
Rosé capital of the world: pale, dry, delicate pink wines. Bandol makes powerful Mourvèdre reds.

- **Where:** France.
- **Grapes:** Grenache, Cinsault, Mourvèdre, Syrah, Vermentino.
- **Climate:** Warm, sunny Mediterranean with the Mistral wind.

cards.title: Languedoc-Roussillon
cards.body:
France's largest vineyard area, from value varietal IGP Pays d'Oc wines to characterful blends from Minervois, Corbières and Faugères, and sweet Vins Doux Naturels in Roussillon.

- **Where:** France.
- **Grapes:** Grenache, Syrah, Carignan, Mourvèdre, Cinsault.
- **Climate:** Hot, dry Mediterranean.

cards.title: Sauternes & Barsac
cards.body:
The world's most famous noble-rot sweet wines: golden, honeyed, with apricot, marmalade and great ageing potential. Château d'Yquem is the icon.

- **Where:** Bordeaux, France.
- **Grapes:** Sémillon, Sauvignon Blanc.
- **Climate:** Autumn mists from the cold Ciron river meeting the warmer Garonne encourage noble rot; sunny afternoons dry the grapes.

cards.title: Saint-Émilion
cards.body:
A medieval hilltop town and UNESCO site on the Right Bank. Plush Merlot and Cabernet Franc blends from limestone and clay.

- **Where:** Bordeaux, France.
- **Grapes:** Merlot, Cabernet Franc.
- **Climate:** Limestone plateau and clay slopes; cooler soils suit early-ripening Merlot.
- **Quality system:** Saint-Émilion Grand Cru Classé, Premier Grand Cru Classé B and A, revised roughly every ten years.

cards.title: Pomerol
cards.body:
A tiny plateau of clay and gravel producing velvety, opulent Merlot, including Pétrus and Le Pin. No classification, yet some of the world's priciest reds.

- **Where:** Bordeaux, France.
- **Grapes:** Merlot, Cabernet Franc.

cards.q: Which grape is most associated with **Beaujolais**?
cards.explain: Beaujolais: Gamay country: juicy, light reds from easy Beaujolais Nouveau to the serious granite-grown crus.

cards.q: Which grape is most associated with **Alsace**?
cards.explain: Alsace: German-influenced but French: aromatic, mostly dry varietal whites labeled by grape, in tall flute bottles.

cards.q: Match each region to its signature grape
cards.explain: Each region is matched with a grape it is known for, as in the cards above.

lessons.title: France: Côte de Nuits, Côte de Beaune…

cards.title: Côte de Nuits
cards.body:
The northern half of the Côte d'Or and the home of great red Burgundy: Gevrey-Chambertin, Chambolle-Musigny, Vosne-Romanée (Romanée-Conti), Nuits-Saint-Georges.

- **Where:** Burgundy, France.
- **Grapes:** Pinot Noir.

cards.title: Côte de Beaune
cards.body:
The southern half of the Côte d'Or: the world's greatest Chardonnay in Meursault, Puligny- and Chassagne-Montrachet, plus fine reds from Pommard, Volnay and Corton.

- **Where:** Burgundy, France.
- **Grapes:** Chardonnay, Pinot Noir.

cards.title: Mâconnais
cards.body:
Ripe, rounded, mostly unoaked Chardonnay: Mâcon-Villages and the richer Pouilly-Fuissé and Saint-Véran.

- **Where:** Burgundy, France.
- **Grapes:** Chardonnay.
- **Climate:** Warmer and sunnier than the Côte d'Or.

cards.title: Côte-Rôtie
cards.body:
Perfumed, elegant Syrah from very steep terraces; up to 20% Viognier may be co-fermented for aroma and color.

- **Where:** Rhône Valley, France.
- **Grapes:** Syrah, Viognier.

cards.title: Condrieu
cards.body:
Viognier's spiritual home: heady apricot, peach and blossom, full-bodied and silky.

- **Where:** Rhône Valley, France.
- **Grapes:** Viognier.

cards.title: Hermitage
cards.body:
A single granite hill above Tain: powerful, long-lived Syrah and rich white Marsanne. One of France's greatest wines.

- **Where:** Rhône Valley, France.
- **Grapes:** Syrah, Marsanne & Roussanne.

cards.title: Crozes-Hermitage
cards.body:
The largest Northern Rhône appellation, around Hermitage: fruity, peppery, approachable Syrah.

- **Where:** Rhône Valley, France.
- **Grapes:** Syrah, Marsanne & Roussanne.

cards.q: Which grape is most associated with **Côte de Nuits**?
cards.explain: Côte de Nuits: The northern half of the Côte d'Or and the home of great red Burgundy: Gevrey-Chambertin, Chambolle-Musigny, Vosne-Romanée (Romanée-Conti), Nuits-Saint-Georges.

cards.q: Which grape is most associated with **Côte de Beaune**?
cards.explain: Côte de Beaune: The southern half of the Côte d'Or: the world's greatest Chardonnay in Meursault, Puligny- and Chassagne-Montrachet, plus fine reds from Pommard, Volnay and Corton.

cards.q: Match each region to its signature grape
cards.explain: Each region is matched with a grape it is known for, as in the cards above.

cards.title: Châteauneuf-du-Pape
cards.body:
The Southern Rhône's flagship: rich, warm, Grenache-led blends with red fruit, herbs (garrigue) and spice.

- **Where:** Rhône Valley, France.
- **Grapes:** Grenache, Syrah, Mourvèdre, Marsanne & Roussanne.
- **Climate:** Hot, dry and windy; famous large round stones (galets roulés) store the day's heat.

cards.title: Tavel & Lirac
cards.body:
Tavel is France's only all-rosé appellation: deeper, fuller, food-friendly rosé. Lirac makes all three colors.

- **Where:** Rhône Valley, France.
- **Grapes:** Grenache, Cinsault.

cards.title: Muscadet
cards.body:
Near the Atlantic, around Nantes: light, crisp, briny whites, often aged sur lie. The perfect oyster wine.

- **Where:** Loire Valley, France.
- **Grapes:** Melon de Bourgogne.

cards.title: Chinon
cards.body:
Fragrant Cabernet Franc with raspberry, violet and pencil-shaving notes.

- **Where:** Loire Valley, France.
- **Grapes:** Cabernet Franc.

cards.title: Vouvray
cards.body:
Chenin Blanc in every style: sec, demi-sec, moelleux and sparkling, from tuffeau limestone near Tours.

- **Where:** Loire Valley, France.
- **Grapes:** Chenin Blanc.

cards.title: Pouilly-Fumé
cards.body:
Across the river from Sancerre: Sauvignon Blanc with a smoky, flinty edge (fumé means smoked).

- **Where:** Loire Valley, France.
- **Grapes:** Sauvignon Blanc.

cards.q: Which grape is most associated with **Châteauneuf-du-Pape**?
cards.explain: Châteauneuf-du-Pape: The Southern Rhône's flagship: rich, warm, Grenache-led blends with red fruit, herbs (garrigue) and spice.

cards.q: Which grape is most associated with **Tavel & Lirac**?
cards.explain: Tavel & Lirac: Tavel is France's only all-rosé appellation: deeper, fuller, food-friendly rosé. Lirac makes all three colors.

cards.q: Match each region to its signature grape
cards.explain: Each region is matched with a grape it is known for, as in the cards above.

cards.title: Piedmont
cards.body:
Italy's most Burgundian region: hillside vineyards around Alba in the Langhe, home to Barolo and Barbaresco, plus everyday Barbera and Dolcetto and sweet Moscato d'Asti.

- **Where:** Italy.
- **Grapes:** Nebbiolo, Barbera, Dolcetto, Muscat, Cortese.
- **Climate:** Continental, at the foot of the Alps; fog in autumn; hillside vineyards for sun exposure.

cards.title: Tuscany
cards.body:
Sangiovese's heartland: Chianti, Brunello di Montalcino and Vino Nobile, plus the coastal Super Tuscans of Bolgheri.

- **Where:** Italy.
- **Grapes:** Sangiovese, Cabernet Sauvignon, Merlot, Trebbiano, Vermentino.
- **Climate:** Warm Mediterranean, cooled by altitude inland and sea breezes on the coast.
- Super Tuscans began in the 1970s when producers used Cabernet and Merlot outside DOC rules; Sassicaia now has its own DOC.

cards.title: Veneto
cards.body:
Italy's biggest-volume region: Prosecco, Soave, Valpolicella and Amarone, and oceans of Pinot Grigio.

- **Where:** Italy.
- **Grapes:** Corvina, Garganega, Glera, Pinot Grigio.

cards.title: Barolo
cards.body:
'King of wines': 100% Nebbiolo, aged at least 38 months (18 in wood). Tar and roses, high tannin and acidity, decades of life.

- **Where:** Piedmont, Italy.
- **Grapes:** Nebbiolo.
- Single vineyards (MGA) such as Cannubi and Brunate are now named on labels, like Burgundy crus.

cards.title: Barbaresco
cards.body:
Barolo's neighbor: Nebbiolo that is often slightly more elegant and approachable earlier; at least 26 months' ageing.

- **Where:** Piedmont, Italy.
- **Grapes:** Nebbiolo.

cards.q: Which grape is most associated with **Piedmont**?
cards.explain: Piedmont: Italy's most Burgundian region: hillside vineyards around Alba in the Langhe, home to Barolo and Barbaresco, plus everyday Barbera and Dolcetto and sweet Moscato d'Asti.

cards.q: Which grape is most associated with **Tuscany**?
cards.explain: Tuscany: Sangiovese's heartland: Chianti, Brunello di Montalcino and Vino Nobile, plus the coastal Super Tuscans of Bolgheri.

cards.q: Match each region to its signature grape
cards.explain: Each region is matched with a grape it is known for, as in the cards above.

cards.title: Asti & Moscato d'Asti
cards.body:
Sweet, low-alcohol, grapey sparklers from Moscato Bianco.

- **Where:** Piedmont, Italy.
- **Grapes:** Muscat.

cards.title: Chianti
cards.body:
A large DOCG around Florence and Siena: tart cherry, herbs and high acidity; at least 70% Sangiovese.

- **Where:** Tuscany, Italy.
- **Grapes:** Sangiovese.

cards.title: Chianti Classico
cards.body:
The historic heart of Chianti between Florence and Siena, marked by the black rooster. Min. 80% Sangiovese; Riserva and Gran Selezione above.

- **Where:** Tuscany, Italy.
- **Grapes:** Sangiovese.

cards.title: Brunello di Montalcino
cards.body:
100% Sangiovese from a warm hilltop town south of Siena; released five years after harvest. Powerful and age-worthy. Rosso di Montalcino is its younger sibling.

- **Where:** Tuscany, Italy.
- **Grapes:** Sangiovese.

cards.q: Which grape is most associated with **Asti & Moscato d'Asti**?
cards.explain: Asti & Moscato d'Asti: Sweet, low-alcohol, grapey sparklers from Moscato Bianco.

cards.q: Which grape is most associated with **Chianti**?
cards.explain: Chianti: A large DOCG around Florence and Siena: tart cherry, herbs and high acidity; at least 70% Sangiovese.

cards.title: Rioja
cards.body:
Spain's classic: Tempranillo-led blends, traditionally aged in American oak for vanilla and coconut notes.

- **Where:** Spain.
- **Grapes:** Tempranillo, Grenache, Carignan, Macabeo.
- **Climate:** Continental, protected by mountains from Atlantic weather; cooler in the west (Rioja Alta, Alavesa), warmer in the east (Rioja Oriental).
- **Quality system:** Crianza (2 years, 1 in oak), Reserva (3 years, 1 in oak), Gran Reserva (5 years, 2 in oak).

cards.title: Ribera del Duero
cards.body:
Powerful, dark Tempranillo (Tinto Fino) along the Duero river. Vega Sicilia is the legend.

- **Where:** Spain.
- **Grapes:** Tempranillo.
- **Climate:** High altitude (750–850 m) with hot days and very cold nights.

cards.title: Rías Baixas
cards.body:
Galicia's green coast: fresh, saline Albariño.

- **Where:** Spain.
- **Grapes:** Albariño.
- **Climate:** Cool, wet, Atlantic; vines trained high on pergolas for airflow.

cards.title: Penedès
cards.body:
Near Barcelona: the heart of Cava, Spain's traditional-method sparkling wine.

- **Where:** Spain.
- **Grapes:** Macabeo.

cards.title: Jerez (Sherry)
cards.body:
The Sherry Triangle of Jerez, El Puerto de Santa María and Sanlúcar de Barrameda: fortified wines aged in solera systems.

- **Where:** Spain.
- **Grapes:** Palomino, Pedro Ximénez.
- **Climate:** Hot, with cooling, humid Atlantic winds (poniente) that favor flor; white albariza chalk soils retain water.

cards.q: Which grape is most associated with **Rioja**?
cards.explain: Rioja: Spain's classic: Tempranillo-led blends, traditionally aged in American oak for vanilla and coconut notes.

cards.q: Which grape is most associated with **Ribera del Duero**?
cards.explain: Ribera del Duero: Powerful, dark Tempranillo (Tinto Fino) along the Duero river. Vega Sicilia is the legend.

cards.q: Match each region to its signature grape
cards.explain: Each region is matched with a grape it is known for, as in the cards above.

cards.title: Portugal
cards.body:
A treasure trove of native grapes: Port and Madeira, fresh Vinho Verde and increasingly world-class dry reds from the Douro, Dão and Alentejo.

- **Grapes:** Touriga Nacional, Tempranillo, Albariño, Baga.
- **Climate:** Atlantic-influenced and wet in the north-west, hot and dry inland and in the south.
- **Quality system:** DOC (Denominação de Origem Controlada) → Vinho Regional.

cards.title: Vinho Verde
cards.body:
Light, zesty, sometimes slightly spritzy whites; Alvarinho from Monção e Melgaço is the finest.

- **Where:** Portugal.
- **Grapes:** Albariño.
- **Climate:** Cool, rainy and green.

cards.title: Douro
cards.body:
The dramatic terraced valley of Port, now also famous for powerful dry reds. The world's first demarcated wine region (1756).

- **Where:** Portugal.
- **Grapes:** Touriga Nacional, Tempranillo.
- **Climate:** Hot, dry continental, sheltered by mountains; vineyards on steep schist terraces.

cards.q: Which grape is most associated with **Vinho Verde**?
cards.explain: Vinho Verde: Light, zesty, sometimes slightly spritzy whites; Alvarinho from Monção e Melgaço is the finest.

cards.q: Which grape is most associated with **Douro**?
cards.explain: Douro: The dramatic terraced valley of Port, now also famous for powerful dry reds. The world's first demarcated wine region (1756).

cards.title: Germany
cards.body:
Riesling's homeland: racy, aromatic whites from bone dry to lusciously sweet, along the Rhine, Mosel and their tributaries. Spätburgunder (Pinot Noir) is increasingly fine.

- **Grapes:** Riesling, Pinot Noir, Silvaner, Pinot Blanc, Pinot Grigio.
- **Climate:** Cool continental; the best vineyards are steep, south-facing river slopes that catch the sun and reflected heat.
- **Quality system:** Prädikatswein ripeness levels by sugar at harvest: Kabinett, Spätlese, Auslese, Beerenauslese, Eiswein, Trockenbeerenauslese. Trocken means dry. VDP estates use Grosse Lage/Grosses Gewächs for top dry wines.

cards.title: Mosel
cards.body:
The world's steepest vineyards: delicate, low-alcohol Riesling with high acidity, often off-dry or sweet.

- **Where:** Germany.
- **Grapes:** Riesling.
- **Climate:** Very cool; steep blue slate slopes above the winding river absorb and reflect heat.

cards.title: Rheingau
cards.body:
Where the Rhine flows west, giving a long south-facing slope: fuller, often drier Riesling. Schloss Johannisberg discovered late harvest in 1775.

- **Where:** Germany.
- **Grapes:** Riesling, Pinot Noir.

cards.q: Which grape is most associated with **Mosel**?
cards.explain: Mosel: The world's steepest vineyards: delicate, low-alcohol Riesling with high acidity, often off-dry or sweet.

cards.q: Which grape is most associated with **Rheingau**?
cards.explain: Rheingau: Where the Rhine flows west, giving a long south-facing slope: fuller, often drier Riesling. Schloss Johannisberg discovered late harvest in 1775.

cards.title: Austria
cards.body:
Precise, dry whites led by Grüner Veltliner and Riesling, serious reds from Burgenland and world-class sweet wines around Lake Neusiedl.

- **Grapes:** Grüner Veltliner, Riesling, Blaufränkisch, Zweigelt.
- **Climate:** Continental: warm days and cool nights; the Danube and Lake Neusiedl moderate temperatures.
- **Quality system:** DAC (Districtus Austriae Controllatus) marks typical regional styles. In the Wachau: Steinfeder, Federspiel and Smaragd by ripeness.

cards.title: Wachau
cards.body:
Steep stone terraces above the Danube: Austria's most famous dry Riesling and Grüner Veltliner (Smaragd is the ripest category).

- **Where:** Austria.
- **Grapes:** Grüner Veltliner, Riesling.
- **Climate:** Cool, but warm air from the Pannonian plain and the Danube help ripen grapes on steep terraces.

cards.q: Which grape is most associated with **Wachau**?
cards.explain: Wachau: Steep stone terraces above the Danube: Austria's most famous dry Riesling and Grüner Veltliner (Smaragd is the ripest category).

cards.title: Tokaj
cards.body:
Volcanic hills producing Tokaji Aszú, made by adding botrytized aszú berries to a base wine, plus dry Furmint and the rare Eszencia.

- **Where:** Hungary.
- **Grapes:** Furmint.
- **Climate:** Autumn mists from the Bodrog and Tisza rivers encourage noble rot.
- Tokaj's vineyards were classified in the 1730s, over a century before Bordeaux's 1855 classification.

cards.q: Which grape is most associated with **Tokaj**?
cards.explain: Tokaj: Volcanic hills producing Tokaji Aszú, made by adding botrytized aszú berries to a base wine, plus dry Furmint and the rare Eszencia.

lessons.title: United States: Napa & Sonoma, Napa Valley…

cards.title: Napa & Sonoma
cards.body:
California's North Coast: Napa Valley for world-famous Cabernet; larger, more varied Sonoma for Pinot Noir, Chardonnay and Zinfandel.

- **Where:** United States.
- **Grapes:** Cabernet Sauvignon, Chardonnay, Pinot Noir, Merlot, Zinfandel.
- **Climate:** Warm, sunny days; cool fog and wind from the Pacific and San Pablo Bay in the south and west.
- At the 1976 'Judgment of Paris', Napa wines beat top Bordeaux and Burgundy in a blind tasting.

cards.title: Napa Valley
cards.body:
America's most famous wine region: ripe, plush, oak-aged Cabernet Sauvignon and blends.

- **Where:** Napa & Sonoma, United States.
- **Grapes:** Cabernet Sauvignon, Merlot, Chardonnay, Petit Verdot, Zinfandel.
- **Climate:** Cooler in the south near the bay, hotter up-valley toward Calistoga.

cards.title: Willamette Valley
cards.body:
Oregon's heart: elegant, Burgundian Pinot Noir and Pinot Gris.

- **Where:** United States.
- **Grapes:** Pinot Noir, Pinot Grigio, Chardonnay.
- **Climate:** Cool and wet, sheltered by the Coast Range.

cards.title: Columbia Valley
cards.body:
Washington's vast region: ripe, fresh Cabernet, Merlot, Syrah and Riesling.

- **Where:** United States.
- **Grapes:** Cabernet Sauvignon, Merlot, Syrah, Riesling, Chardonnay.
- **Climate:** Semi-desert east of the Cascades: hot days, cold nights, irrigation from the Columbia river.

cards.q: Which grape is most associated with **Napa & Sonoma**?
cards.explain: Napa & Sonoma: California's North Coast: Napa Valley for world-famous Cabernet; larger, more varied Sonoma for Pinot Noir, Chardonnay and Zinfandel.

cards.q: Which grape is most associated with **Napa Valley**?
cards.explain: Napa Valley: America's most famous wine region: ripe, plush, oak-aged Cabernet Sauvignon and blends.

cards.q: Match each region to its signature grape
cards.explain: Each region is matched with a grape it is known for, as in the cards above.

cards.title: Chile
cards.body:
A long, thin country between the Andes and the Pacific. Reliable sunshine gives ripe, fruity Cabernet and Carmenère; cool coastal valleys make crisp whites and Pinot.

- **Grapes:** Cabernet Sauvignon, Carmenère, Merlot, Sauvignon Blanc, Chardonnay.
- **Climate:** Mediterranean. The cold Humboldt Current cools the coast; the Andes send cold air down at night.
- Chile has never been hit by phylloxera, thanks to natural barriers: desert, mountains, ocean and ice.
- Regions are now also labeled Costa (coastal), Entre Cordilleras (between the ranges) and Andes.

cards.title: Maipo Valley
cards.body:
Around Santiago: Chile's classic Cabernet Sauvignon, often with a minty edge in Alto Maipo.

- **Where:** Chile.
- **Grapes:** Cabernet Sauvignon, Carmenère, Merlot.

cards.title: Casablanca Valley
cards.body:
Chile's original cool-climate region, between Santiago and the coast: crisp whites and Pinot Noir.

- **Where:** Chile.
- **Grapes:** Sauvignon Blanc, Chardonnay, Pinot Noir.
- **Climate:** Cool, with morning fog from the Pacific.

cards.q: Which grape is most associated with **Maipo Valley**?
cards.explain: Maipo Valley: Around Santiago: Chile's classic Cabernet Sauvignon, often with a minty edge in Alto Maipo.

cards.q: Which grape is most associated with **Casablanca Valley**?
cards.explain: Casablanca Valley: Chile's original cool-climate region, between Santiago and the coast: crisp whites and Pinot Noir.

cards.title: Argentina
cards.body:
The world's Malbec capital. Altitude is everything: vineyards lie from about 600 m to over 3,000 m above sea level.

- **Grapes:** Malbec, Torrontés, Cabernet Sauvignon.
- **Climate:** High-altitude desert at the foot of the Andes: intense sun, big day–night temperature swings, irrigation from snowmelt.

cards.title: Mendoza
cards.body:
About 70% of Argentina's wine: ripe, velvety Malbec from Luján de Cuyo and Maipú.

- **Where:** Argentina.
- **Grapes:** Malbec, Cabernet Sauvignon.

cards.title: Uco Valley
cards.body:
Mendoza's high-altitude star: fresher, more floral Malbec and fine Chardonnay.

- **Where:** Argentina.
- **Grapes:** Malbec, Chardonnay.
- **Climate:** High (900–1,500 m) and cool at night.

cards.q: Which grape is most associated with **Mendoza**?
cards.explain: Mendoza: About 70% of Argentina's wine: ripe, velvety Malbec from Luján de Cuyo and Maipú.

cards.q: Which grape is most associated with **Uco Valley**?
cards.explain: Uco Valley: Mendoza's high-altitude star: fresher, more floral Malbec and fine Chardonnay.

cards.title: Barossa Valley
cards.body:
Australia's most famous region: rich, ripe Shiraz with chocolate and spice, from some of the world's oldest vines.

- **Where:** Australia.
- **Grapes:** Syrah, Grenache, Mourvèdre, Cabernet Sauvignon.
- **Climate:** Warm and dry.

cards.title: Clare Valley
cards.body:
Famous for bone-dry, lime-scented Riesling that ages to toast.

- **Where:** Australia.
- **Grapes:** Riesling, Syrah, Cabernet Sauvignon.
- **Climate:** Warm days and cool nights.

cards.title: Coonawarra
cards.body:
A strip of red 'terra rossa' soil over limestone: Australia's classic Cabernet, often with mint.

- **Where:** Australia.
- **Grapes:** Cabernet Sauvignon.
- **Climate:** Cool, with sea breezes.

cards.title: Margaret River
cards.body:
Western Australia's star: elegant Cabernet and Chardonnay, and crisp Sémillon–Sauvignon blends.

- **Where:** Australia.
- **Grapes:** Cabernet Sauvignon, Chardonnay, Sémillon, Sauvignon Blanc.
- **Climate:** Maritime, almost surrounded by ocean.

cards.title: Yarra Valley
cards.body:
Elegant Pinot Noir, Chardonnay and sparkling wine.

- **Where:** Australia.
- **Grapes:** Pinot Noir, Chardonnay.
- **Climate:** Cool, near Melbourne.

cards.title: Hunter Valley
cards.body:
Unique, long-lived Hunter Sémillon (low alcohol, ages to toast and honey) and medium-bodied Shiraz.

- **Where:** Australia.
- **Grapes:** Sémillon, Syrah.
- **Climate:** Hot, humid, with afternoon cloud and summer rain.

cards.title: Tasmania
cards.body:
Australia's coolest state: superb sparkling wine, Pinot Noir and Chardonnay.

- **Where:** Australia.
- **Grapes:** Pinot Noir, Chardonnay, Riesling.
- **Climate:** Cool maritime.

cards.q: Which grape is most associated with **Barossa Valley**?
cards.explain: Barossa Valley: Australia's most famous region: rich, ripe Shiraz with chocolate and spice, from some of the world's oldest vines.

cards.q: Which grape is most associated with **Clare Valley**?
cards.explain: Clare Valley: Famous for bone-dry, lime-scented Riesling that ages to toast.

cards.q: Match each region to its signature grape
cards.explain: Each region is matched with a grape it is known for, as in the cards above.

lessons.title: New Zealand: Central Otago, Hawke's Bay

cards.title: Central Otago
cards.body:
Dramatic mountain region making ripe, intense, dark-cherry Pinot Noir.

- **Where:** New Zealand.
- **Grapes:** Pinot Noir.
- **Climate:** The world's most southerly major region; continental, with hot days and cold nights.

cards.title: Hawke's Bay
cards.body:
Warmer North Island region: Bordeaux blends and peppery Syrah from the Gimblett Gravels.

- **Where:** New Zealand.

lessons.title: Styles: Light, crisp whites, Aromatic whites…

cards.title: Light, crisp whites
cards.body:
Pale, high in acidity, unoaked and refreshing.

- **How:** Cool climates or early picking keep acidity high and alcohol moderate. Fermented cool in stainless steel and released young.
- **Examples:** Muscadet, Pinot Grigio, Chablis, Albariño.

cards.title: Aromatic whites
cards.body:
Perfumed grapes that smell of flowers, spice and fruit.

- **How:** Usually unoaked, so the grape's own aromas (terpenes) take center stage.
- **Examples:** Riesling, Gewürztraminer, Muscat, Torrontés.

cards.title: Full-bodied whites
cards.body:
Rich, round whites, often with oak and malolactic conversion.

- **How:** Riper fruit from warmer sites, fermentation or ageing in oak, lees stirring (bâtonnage) and malolactic conversion add weight and texture.
- **Examples:** Oaked Chardonnay, Meursault, White Rioja, Marsanne-Roussanne.

cards.title: Rosé
cards.body:
Pink wines made from black grapes with brief skin contact.

- **How:** Skins soak in the juice for hours rather than days (or are pressed directly), then the juice is fermented cool like a white wine.
- **Examples:** Provence rosé, Tavel, Rosado from Navarra, White Zinfandel.

cards.title: Orange wine
cards.body:
White grapes fermented on their skins like a red.

- **How:** Skin contact for days or months gives amber color, texture and some tannin. An ancient method from Georgia, where wines are made in clay qvevri.
