cards.body: The VDP growers' association uses a Burgundy-style pyramid: **Gutswein**, **Ortswein** (village), **Erste Lage** (premier cru) and **Grosse Lage** (grand cru). A dry wine from a Grosse Lage is a **Grosses Gewächs** (GG), shown by "GG" on the bottle.

cards.title: Regions and bottles
cards.body:
- **Mosel**: steep slate, light, racy, low alcohol.
- **Rheingau**: south-facing slopes on the Rhine, fuller and drier.
- **Pfalz**: warmest, rich dry Riesling and Spätburgunder (Pinot Noir).
- **Nahe**, **Rheinhessen**, **Franken** (Silvaner in the flat *Bocksbeutel* bottle).

Most German wine comes in the tall **flûte** bottle: brown glass traditionally for the Rhine, green for the Mosel.

cards.q: What do German Prädikat levels measure?
cards.explain: A Spätlese can be dry or sweet; check for 'trocken'.

cards.q: What does 'GG' on a German bottle mean?
options: A dry wine from a top vineyard
cards.explain: Grosses Gewächs: dry wine from a VDP Grosse Lage.

cards.q: Put the Prädikat levels in order with their meaning
cards.explain: Each step up means riper, rarer grapes.

lessons.title: Deep dive: Austria, Hungary and Greece

cards.title: Austria
cards.body:
**Grüner Veltliner** (white pepper, citrus) and **Riesling** shine on the Danube terraces of the **Wachau**, **Kremstal** and **Kamptal**. The Wachau grades dry wines as **Steinfeder**, **Federspiel** and **Smaragd** (richest).

**Blaufränkisch** and **Zweigelt** make spicy reds in Burgenland; around Lake **Neusiedl**, mists bring noble-rot sweet wines.

cards.title: Hungary
cards.body: Beyond Tokaji: dry **Furmint** is now a serious white; **Eger** makes the red blend *Egri Bikavér* ("Bull's Blood"); **Villány** in the warm south grows Cabernet Franc and Bordeaux blends.

cards.title: Greece
cards.body:
- **Santorini**: **Assyrtiko** on volcanic ash; vines trained into low baskets (*kouloura*) to shelter grapes from wind. Sweet **Vinsanto** from sun-dried grapes.
- **Naoussa**: **Xinomavro**, tannic and tomato-scented, Greece's "Barolo".
- **Nemea**: soft, fruity **Agiorgitiko**.

cards.q: What is the richest dry wine category in the Wachau?
cards.explain: Named after the emerald lizard sunning itself on the terraces.

cards.q: Why are Santorini vines trained into baskets?
options: To protect grapes from strong winds and sun
cards.explain: The kouloura shelters bunches inside the coiled vine.

cards.q: Egri Bikavér is a sweet white wine.
cards.explain: It is a red blend from Eger, 'Bull's Blood'.

cards.title: Tokaji, wine of kings
cards.body:
In **Tokaj**, Hungary, noble rot was understood by the **1600s**; by legend a harvest delayed by Turkish raids led to the first Aszú. In **1730** the vineyards were classified, more than a century before Bordeaux's 1855 list.

Louis XIV called it "**the wine of kings, the king of wines**". Communism (1949–1989) turned Tokaj into a state farm; investment from France and Spain after 1990 revived it.

cards.title: Germany's late harvest
cards.body:
The Romans planted the **Mosel**, and monasteries such as **Kloster Eberbach** made the Rheingau famous. In **1775**, at **Schloss Johannisberg**, the messenger carrying permission to start the harvest was late; the grapes rotted, the wine was wonderful, and **Spätlese** ("late harvest") was born.

In the 1800s, top Rieslings cost more than First Growth Bordeaux. Wars, then cheap sweet exports such as Liebfraumilch, hurt its name; today's dry **Grosses Gewächs** wines have rebuilt it.

cards.title: Austria's clean start
cards.body:
In **1985** a few Austrian brokers were caught sweetening wine with **diethylene glycol**. Exports collapsed overnight. Austria responded with some of the strictest wine laws in the world.

A new generation focused on dry **Grüner Veltliner** and **Riesling** from the **Wachau** and Kamptal, and Austrian wine is now admired for its purity.

cards.q: What happened at Schloss Johannisberg in 1775?
options: A late messenger delayed the harvest and Spätlese was born
cards.explain: The overripe, partly botrytized grapes made exceptional wine: the start of Germany's late-harvest tradition.

cards.q: Tokaj's vineyards were classified in 1730, before Bordeaux's 1855 classification.
cards.explain: The Tokaj classification of 1730 is one of the oldest in the world.

cards.q: What did the 1985 scandal lead to in Austria?
options: Very strict wine laws and a focus on quality
The end of Austrian wine exports forever
cards.explain: After the glycol scandal Austria rebuilt its reputation on dry, pure, carefully controlled wines.

cards.title: German Riesling styles
cards.body: German Riesling ranges from bone-dry **Grosses Gewächs** to sweet **Beerenauslese** and **Trockenbeerenauslese**. The **Mosel** gives light, delicate, often off-dry wines on steep slate; the **Pfalz** and **Rheingau** give fuller, drier styles.

cards.title: Tokaji Aszú
cards.body: In Hungary's **Tokaj**, botrytized aszú berries are soaked in base wine or must. The result is one of the world's great sweet wines, with apricot, orange peel and honey, kept fresh by Furmint's acidity.

cards.q: Which German region is famous for steep slate slopes along a winding river?
cards.explain: The Mosel's slate slopes are among the steepest vineyards in the world.

cards.q: Match the wine to its main grape
cards.explain: Central Europe's classics rely on local stars.

cards.q: Trockenbeerenauslese is a dry wine.
cards.explain: Despite 'trocken' in the name, TBA is made from shriveled botrytized berries and is intensely sweet.

cards.q: In the Wachau, what is 'Smaragd'?
cards.explain: Steinfeder, Federspiel and Smaragd rank Wachau's dry whites by ripeness.

cards.q: Hungary's most famous sweet wine comes from ___.
cards.explain: Tokaj was the world's first classified wine region, in 1730.

units.title: The New World
units.summary: USA, Chile and Argentina, Australia, New Zealand and South Africa.

cards.title: The West Coast
cards.body:
- **California**: Mediterranean climate cooled by Pacific fog. Napa (Cabernet), Sonoma (Pinot, Chardonnay, Zinfandel), the Central Coast (Pinot in the Santa Rita Hills, Rhône varieties in Paso Robles), Lodi (old-vine Zinfandel).
- **Oregon**: cool, wet Willamette Valley; Pinot Noir and Pinot Gris.
- **Washington**: dry, irrigated Columbia Valley east of the Cascades; Cabernet, Merlot, Syrah, Riesling.

cards.title: Napa up close
cards.body: Napa is cooler in the south (Carneros, near San Pablo Bay) and hotter up-valley toward Calistoga. Famous AVAs include Oakville, Rutherford and Stags Leap District, plus mountain AVAs like Howell Mountain.

cards.q: Why does Washington's Columbia Valley need irrigation?
options: It lies in the rain shadow of the Cascades
The soils hold too much water
cards.explain: Eastern Washington is semi-desert. The Columbia river and its tributaries supply water.

cards.q: Which Oregon region is famous for Pinot Noir?
cards.explain: Its cool, cloudy climate echoes Burgundy.

cards.q: Carneros, in the south of Napa and Sonoma, is cooled by San Pablo Bay.
cards.explain: Wind and fog from the bay make it ideal for Pinot Noir, Chardonnay and sparkling wine.

cards.q: The 1976 Judgment of ___ put Napa Valley on the world map.
cards.explain: Stag's Leap Wine Cellars Cabernet and Chateau Montelena Chardonnay beat top French wines in a blind tasting.

cards.title: Chile: between ocean and Andes
cards.body: A narrow strip cooled by the **Humboldt Current** and Andean air. **Maipo** for Cabernet, **Colchagua** for Carmenère, **Casablanca** and Leyda for cool whites and Pinot Noir. Chile is phylloxera-free.

cards.title: Argentina: wine in the high desert
cards.body: High-altitude desert at the foot of the Andes. **Mendoza** and the **Uco Valley** for Malbec; **Salta** (Cafayate) for Torrontés at up to 3,000 m.

cards.q: Why can Argentina make fresh wines despite intense sun?
options: Very high altitude and cold nights
cards.explain: Altitude gives a big diurnal range. Strong UV also builds thick skins and deep color.

cards.q: Which Chilean valley is known for cool-climate Sauvignon Blanc?
cards.explain: Morning fog from the Pacific keeps it cool.

cards.q: Argentina's vineyards are irrigated with Andean snowmelt.
cards.explain: Rainfall in Mendoza is only about 200 mm a year.

cards.q: Match the region to its signature
cards.explain: Four classic South American pairings.

cards.title: Australia
cards.body:
- **Barossa** & **McLaren Vale**: rich Shiraz, Grenache.
- **Clare** & **Eden Valley**: dry, lime-scented Riesling.
- **Coonawarra**: Cabernet on terra rossa.
- **Margaret River**: Cabernet, Chardonnay.
- **Yarra Valley**, **Tasmania**: Pinot, Chardonnay, sparkling.
- **Hunter Valley**: Sémillon.

cards.title: New Zealand
cards.body: A cool maritime country. **Marlborough** Sauvignon Blanc (intense passion fruit and herbs); **Central Otago** and **Martinborough** Pinot Noir; **Hawke's Bay** Bordeaux blends and Syrah from the **Gimblett Gravels**.

cards.q: Coonawarra's famous red soil is called…
cards.explain: A thin strip of red clay over limestone, about 15 km long, ideal for Cabernet.

cards.q: Which New Zealand region is the world's most southerly major wine region?
cards.explain: Its continental climate, the only one in New Zealand, makes ripe, intense Pinot Noir.

cards.q: Clare Valley is known for sweet, oaky Riesling.
cards.explain: Clare and Eden Valley Rieslings are bone dry, lime-scented and unoaked, and age to toast.

cards.q: Hawke's Bay's Gimblett ___ are stony soils prized for Syrah and Bordeaux blends.
cards.explain: Former riverbed stones that drain well and store heat.

cards.title: The Cape
cards.body:
Mediterranean climate cooled by the **Benguela Current** and the south-easterly **Cape Doctor** wind.

- **Stellenbosch**: Cabernet, Bordeaux blends, Pinotage.
- **Swartland**: old-vine Chenin and Rhône blends.
- **Constantia**, **Elgin**, **Walker Bay**: cool-climate whites and Pinot.
- **Cap Classique**: traditional-method sparkling.

cards.q: What is the 'Cape Doctor'?
cards.explain: It cools vineyards and blows away disease.

cards.q: Which region led South Africa's old-vine Chenin revival?
cards.explain: Dry-farmed bush vines in a hot, dry region, championed by a new wave of winemakers.

cards.q: Vin de Constance is a historic sweet wine once loved by Napoleon.
cards.explain: Made from Muscat in Constantia since the 1700s and revived in the 1980s.

cards.q: South African traditional-method sparkling wine is called Cap ___.
cards.explain: Usually Chardonnay and Pinot Noir, with lees ageing like Champagne.

lessons.title: Deep dive: America and the Southern Hemisphere

cards.title: California and the Judgment of Paris
cards.body:
In **1976**, at a blind tasting in Paris, a Napa Cabernet (Stag's Leap Wine Cellars) and Chardonnay (Chateau Montelena) beat top Bordeaux and Burgundy. The New World arrived.

**Napa Valley** is Cabernet country, with sub-AVAs like Oakville, Rutherford and Stags Leap. Cool, foggy **Sonoma Coast**, **Russian River** and **Carneros** suit Pinot Noir and Chardonnay. Oregon's **Willamette Valley** rivals Burgundy for Pinot.

cards.title: Chile and Argentina
cards.body:
**Chile**: a long, thin country cooled by the Humboldt current and Andes winds. Phylloxera never arrived, so many vines grow on their own roots. Signature grape: **Carmenère**. Coastal valleys (Casablanca, Leyda) make crisp Sauvignon Blanc.

**Argentina**: **Malbec** from **Mendoza**, at 800–1,500 m, especially the cool **Uco Valley**. **Torrontés** in Salta, among the highest vineyards on Earth.

cards.title: Australia
cards.body:
- **Barossa** and **McLaren Vale**: rich Shiraz and GSM blends, some vines over 150 years old.
- **Coonawarra**: Cabernet on red *terra rossa*.
- **Clare** and **Eden Valley**: dry, limey Riesling.
- **Hunter Valley**: long-lived Sémillon.
- **Margaret River**: Bordeaux-style Cabernet and Chardonnay.
- **Yarra Valley** and **Tasmania**: cool-climate Pinot and sparkling.

Australia led the world in **screw caps**.

cards.title: New Zealand and South Africa
cards.body:
**New Zealand**: **Marlborough** Sauvignon Blanc (passion fruit, grass) made the country famous; **Central Otago** grows Pinot Noir in the world's southernmost vineyards.

**South Africa**: winemaking since **1659**. **Chenin Blanc** (locally Steen) is its most planted grape; **Pinotage** (Pinot Noir × Cinsault, 1925) its own crossing. Stellenbosch, Swartland and the cool Elgin and Hemel-en-Aarde valleys lead.

cards.q: What happened at the 1976 Judgment of Paris?
options: California wines beat top French wines blind
cards.explain: It put Napa on the world map.

cards.q: Which grape is Chile's signature, once confused with Merlot?
cards.explain: It was only identified in Chile in 1994.

cards.q: Match the region to its star grape
cards.explain: Each New World region found its specialty.

cards.q: Pinotage is a crossing of Pinot Noir and Cinsault.
cards.explain: Created at Stellenbosch University in 1925; Cinsault was then called Hermitage, hence the name.

cards.title: Missions and gold rush
cards.body:
**Spanish missionaries** planted vines in the Americas for sacramental wine: Peru and Mexico in the 1500s, **Chile** in the 1550s, **California**'s missions from **1769** with the humble **Mission** grape.

The **Gold Rush** brought thirsty miners and European immigrants. Then **Prohibition** (1920–1933) closed most wineries; only sacramental and "grape juice" producers survived.

cards.title: Napa's rise
cards.body:
**Robert Mondavi** opened his Oakville winery in **1966**, the first big new winery in Napa since Prohibition, and labeled wines by grape (Cabernet Sauvignon, Fumé Blanc) instead of borrowing French names.

The **1976 Judgment of Paris** put Napa on the map; **Opus One** (1979) joined Mondavi with Mouton Rothschild.

cards.title: South Africa, Australia, New Zealand
cards.body:
**South Africa**: the Dutch planted vines at the Cape in **1655**; **Constantia**'s sweet wine was drunk by Napoleon. Under apartheid, exports were boycotted; since **1994** the Cape has reinvented itself around old-vine Chenin and Swartland.

**Australia**: vines came with the First Fleet in **1788**; **German Lutherans** settled the **Barossa** in the 1840s, and their Shiraz vines survive. **Penfolds Grange** (1951) showed Australia could make icons.

**New Zealand**: Marlborough's first commercial vineyards were planted in **1973**; **Cloudy Bay** (1985) made it a world classic.

cards.title: Chile and Argentina
cards.body:
In the 1850s Chilean landowners imported French vines, including **Carmenère**, just before phylloxera devastated France. Chile stayed phylloxera-free and kept these old vines.

**Argentina** drank its own huge production until the 1990s, when exporters bet on **Malbec** from high **Mendoza** vineyards. Pioneers such as **Nicolás Catena** proved altitude could make world-class wine.

cards.q: When did Robert Mondavi open his Napa winery?
cards.explain: The first major new Napa winery since Prohibition; Mondavi championed labeling wines by grape.

cards.q: Who planted the Barossa's old Shiraz vines in the 1840s?
cards.explain: Silesian Lutherans settled the Barossa; vines from that era still produce wine today.

cards.q: Prohibition (1920–1933) closed most American wineries.
cards.explain: Only producers of sacramental wine and grape juice could legally continue; the industry took decades to recover.

cards.title: Cool spots in warm countries
cards.body: New World producers chase cool sites for elegance: **Adelaide Hills** and **Tasmania** in Australia, **Casablanca** and **San Antonio** in Chile, **Sonoma Coast** in California and **Central Otago** in New Zealand.

cards.title: Signature styles
cards.body: **Marlborough Sauvignon Blanc**: passion fruit and cut grass. **Barossa Shiraz**: rich black fruit and chocolate. **Mendoza Malbec**: plum and violet. **Napa Cabernet**: ripe cassis and polished tannin. **Stellenbosch Chenin**: ripe stone fruit and honey.

cards.q: Which region makes intense, passion-fruit Sauvignon Blanc?
cards.explain: Bright sun, cool nights and long seasons give Marlborough its pungent style.

cards.q: Match the region to its signature grape
cards.explain: Each region built its fame on one grape.

cards.q: Chile's Casablanca Valley is cooled by the Pacific Ocean.
cards.explain: Morning fog and sea breezes make Casablanca ideal for Sauvignon Blanc and Chardonnay.

cards.q: Why are Mendoza's vineyards good for Malbec despite the desert?
cards.explain: Vineyards up to 1,500 m give cool nights; Andes snowmelt provides water.

cards.q: Pinotage is a South African cross of Pinot Noir and ___.
cards.explain: Created in 1925; Cinsault was then called Hermitage in South Africa, hence the name.

units.title: Tasting in depth
units.summary: Structured assessment, quality, readiness and faults: thinking like a sommelier.

cards.title: Measuring precisely
cards.body:
At an advanced level, each structural element gets a precise scale:

- Acidity, tannin, body and finish: **low, medium−, medium, medium+, high**.
- Alcohol: low (under 11%), medium, high (14%+).
- Tannin also has a **nature**: ripe or unripe, fine-grained or coarse.

Precise structure narrows down grape and origin much faster than aromas alone.

cards.title: Development
cards.body:
- **Youthful**: only primary (and secondary) aromas.
- **Developing**: tertiary notes appear alongside fresh fruit.
- **Fully developed**: mostly tertiary aromas.
- **Tired**: fruit fading, drying out.

cards.q: A wine showing fresh fruit with some leather and earth is…
cards.explain: Tertiary notes alongside primary fruit mean the wine is on its way to maturity.

cards.q: High acidity, high tannin, pale garnet, tar and roses suggests…
cards.explain: Nebbiolo's unusual mix of pale color and fierce structure is a giveaway.

cards.q: Unripe tannins tend to feel green, coarse and astringent.
cards.explain: Ripe tannins feel fine-grained and silky. Tannin texture is a clue to grape ripeness and winemaking.

cards.q: Alcohol above about ___% is described as high.
cards.explain: Below 11% is low; 11–13.9% is medium.

cards.title: BLIC in practice
cards.body:
- **Balance**: fruit vs acid vs tannin vs alcohol vs sweetness.
- **Length**: medium+ or long for good wine.
- **Intensity**: pronounced aromas and flavors.
- **Complexity**: many layers: primary, secondary, tertiary.

Then decide readiness: **too young**, **can drink now but has potential**, **drink now**, or **too old**.

cards.q: A wine with intense fruit, high tannin and high acidity that is still very primary is probably…
cards.explain: Concentrated fruit plus structure is what allows a wine to improve with age.

cards.q: A short finish is a sign of outstanding quality.
cards.explain: Great wines have long, complex finishes.

cards.q: Match each BLIC element to its question
cards.explain: Four simple questions behind every professional quality call.

cards.q: Which wine is most likely to improve with bottle age?
cards.explain: Concentration, acidity and structure let it evolve for decades. The others are made to drink young.

cards.title: When wine goes wrong
cards.body:
- **TCA (cork taint)**: musty, damp cardboard, muted fruit.
- **Oxidation**: brownish, flat, bruised apple.
- **Reduction**: struck match, rotten egg, rubber; sometimes fixed by aeration.
- **Brettanomyces**: barnyard, sticking plaster, sweaty saddle.
- **Volatile acidity (VA)**: vinegar, nail-varnish remover.
- **Heat damage**: cooked, stewed fruit.

cards.q: A wine smelling of nail-varnish remover and vinegar has…
cards.explain: Caused by acetic acid and ethyl acetate, usually from bacteria and oxygen exposure.

cards.q: Struck-match or rotten-egg aromas indicate…
cards.explain: Sulfur compounds form when wine lacks oxygen during winemaking. Mild cases blow off with swirling or decanting.

cards.q: Brettanomyces can give barnyard and sticking-plaster aromas.
cards.explain: A little can add complexity for some drinkers; a lot strips the fruit.

cards.q: Match the fault to its smell
cards.explain: Recognizing faults is part of every sommelier's training.

cards.title: Assessing readiness
cards.body:
Ask: is the wine **too young** (tight, primary fruit, firm tannin), **ready** (fruit and developing notes in balance), or **past its best** (fading fruit, drying tannin)?

Long-lived wines need the structure to age: acidity, tannin or sugar, plus concentrated fruit.

cards.title: Deductive tasting
cards.body: Blind tasters reason from clues. High acid and light color suggest a cool climate. Deep color, ripe black fruit and high alcohol suggest warmth. Vanilla and toast suggest new oak; leather and earth suggest age.

cards.q: Which wine is most likely from a cool climate?
cards.explain: Cool climates keep acidity and give leaner, fresher fruit.

cards.q: Match the clue to what it suggests
cards.explain: Each clue narrows down the grape, place and winemaking.

cards.q: Wines with high acidity or tannin often age well.
cards.explain: Structure protects a wine while its fruit slowly evolves.

cards.q: A red tastes of dried fruit, leather and has drying tannin. It is probably…
cards.explain: Fading fruit and drying tannin are signs a wine has passed its peak.

cards.q: Concentration of flavor, balance, length and complexity together judge a wine's ___.
cards.explain: These BLIC factors let you judge quality objectively.

units.title: The story of wine
units.summary: From Georgian clay jars to phylloxera, the 1855 classification and the Judgment of Paris: how the wine world was made.

cards.title: Eight thousand years in clay
cards.body:
The oldest traces of grape wine, about **8,000 years** old, come from **Georgia** in the South Caucasus: residues inside clay jars. Georgians still ferment wine in buried clay vessels called **qvevri**, a method UNESCO lists as world heritage.

The oldest known winery, about **6,100 years** old, was found in the **Areni-1 cave** in Armenia, with a pressing floor and fermentation jars.

cards.title: Egypt, Phoenicia and Greece
cards.body:
In **ancient Egypt**, wine was for kings and priests; jars in Tutankhamun's tomb were labeled with the vintage, the estate and the chief winemaker, an early wine label.

**Phoenician** traders, from today's **Lebanon**, carried vines and wine across the Mediterranean. The **Greeks** planted vines in southern Italy, which they called **Oenotria**, "land of vines", and in Provence, at Marseille, around 600 BC.

cards.title: Rome builds Europe's vineyards
cards.body:
The **Romans** spread the vine wherever their legions went: up the **Rhône**, into **Bordeaux** (Burdigala), **Burgundy**, the **Mosel** and the **Rhine**. Many of Europe's great regions began as Roman vineyards along rivers, which carried both water for the vines and barrels to market.

Roman wine was often sweetened with honey or flavored with herbs and resin, and drunk mixed with water.

cards.q: Where do the oldest traces of grape wine (about 8,000 years old) come from?
cards.explain: Residues in clay jars in Georgia, in the South Caucasus, are the oldest evidence of grape wine. Georgians still use buried clay qvevri.

cards.q: What did the Greeks call southern Italy?
cards.explain: Oenotria means 'land of vines'. Burdigala was the Roman name for Bordeaux.

cards.q: The Romans spread vineyards along rivers such as the Rhône, Mosel and Rhine.
cards.explain: Rivers gave vines water, warmth from reflected sun, and a road for barrels to market. Many great regions began as Roman vineyards.

cards.title: The monks of Burgundy
cards.body:
After Rome fell, **monasteries** kept winemaking alive. In Burgundy, **Benedictine** monks of Cluny and **Cistercian** monks of Cîteaux (founded 1098) spent centuries tasting the wines of each plot, building walls around the best ones.

The **Clos de Vougeot**, walled by the Cistercians in the 14th century, is the most famous. Their idea that each **climat** (named plot) tastes different is the root of **terroir** and of Burgundy's Grands Crus.

cards.title: Bordeaux becomes English
cards.body:
In **1152** Eleanor of Aquitaine married **Henry Plantagenet**, soon King Henry II of England. Bordeaux became English for **three centuries**, until 1453.

English merchants shipped huge volumes of light red **clairet**, the origin of the British word **claret** for red Bordeaux. Trade, not monks, shaped Bordeaux: a merchant's city facing the sea.

cards.title: The Dutch drain the Médoc
cards.body:
In the **1600s**, **Dutch** engineers drained the marshy Médoc, revealing the **gravel ridges** where Cabernet Sauvignon would thrive. Dutch traders also wanted sweet whites and brandy, boosting Sauternes and Cognac.

By the 1700s, estates such as **Haut-Brion**, Lafite and Latour were selling their wine **by name** in London: the birth of the "château" brand.

cards.q: Which monks walled the Clos de Vougeot in Burgundy?
cards.explain: The Cistercians of Cîteaux, founded in 1098, studied Burgundy's plots for centuries and walled the Clos de Vougeot.

cards.q: Bordeaux belonged to England for three centuries after Eleanor of Aquitaine married Henry Plantagenet in ___.
cards.explain: The marriage in 1152 made Bordeaux English until 1453; the British still call red Bordeaux 'claret'.

cards.q: Dutch engineers drained the Médoc's marshes in the 1600s.
cards.explain: Draining revealed the gravel ridges of the Left Bank, where Cabernet Sauvignon ripens on warm stones.

cards.title: The plague from America
cards.body:
In the **1860s**, vines in the southern Rhône began to wither and die. The culprit, identified in **1868** by the botanist **Jules-Émile Planchon**, was **phylloxera**: a tiny yellow aphid-like insect that feeds on vine **roots**.

It had crossed the Atlantic on American vines brought to Europe as botanical curiosities. Faster steamships meant the bugs survived the trip.

cards.title: A continent's vineyards destroyed
cards.body:
Over the next **thirty years**, phylloxera spread through almost every European vineyard: France, Spain, Italy, Portugal, Germany, then Australia, South Africa and California.

France lost around **40% of its vines**. Growers tried everything: flooding vineyards, injecting carbon disulfide into the soil, even burying live toads under vines. Millions emigrated; some French winemakers moved to **Rioja**, raising its quality.

cards.title: The cure: grafting
cards.body:
American vines had evolved with phylloxera and their roots resist it. The solution, championed by Planchon and the American entomologist **Charles Valentine Riley**, was to **graft** European *Vitis vinifera* onto **American rootstocks**. **Thomas Munson** in Texas bred many of the rootstocks used.

Today almost every vine in the world grows on American roots. The fruit, and the wine, still come from the European vine on top.

cards.title: The survivors
cards.body:
A few places never had phylloxera, or it couldn't survive there:

- **Chile**, protected by the Andes, the Pacific and the Atacama desert.
- **Sandy soils** such as Colares in Portugal and parts of the Mosel; the insect can't move through sand.
- **Santorini**'s volcanic ash, and parts of **South Australia**, kept free by strict quarantine. Barossa has Shiraz vines from the **1840s**.

After phylloxera, fraud and fake wine were common; the **AOC** system (1935) was partly France's answer.

cards.q: What does phylloxera attack?
cards.explain: The insect feeds on roots; the vine slowly starves. American vines' roots can resist it, European vines' cannot.

cards.q: How did growers finally beat phylloxera?
options: Grafting European vines onto American rootstocks
cards.explain: Grafting keeps the European vine's fruit on resistant American roots. Almost every vineyard in the world is grafted today.

cards.q: Chile's vineyards were never hit by phylloxera.
cards.explain: Mountains, ocean and desert isolate Chile, so many of its vines still grow on their own roots.

cards.q: Which French botanist identified phylloxera in 1868?
cards.explain: Planchon found the insect on dying vines in the southern Rhône and helped promote grafting as the cure.

cards.title: A list for a world fair
cards.body:
For the **1855 Exposition Universelle** in Paris, Emperor **Napoleon III** wanted Bordeaux's best wines shown. The merchants of Bordeaux ranked the châteaux by **price**, the market's long verdict on quality.

The result: **61 red wines** in five tiers, from First to Fifth Growth, almost all from the **Médoc**, plus **Haut-Brion** from Graves; and a list of **Sauternes and Barsac**, with **Château d'Yquem** alone at the top as *Premier Cru Supérieur*.

cards.title: Almost unchanged since
cards.body:
The list has barely moved. **Cantemerle** was added in 1856, and in **1973** **Mouton Rothschild** was promoted to First Growth after Baron Philippe de Rothschild's fifty-year campaign. Its motto changed from "First I cannot be, second I do not deign to be, Mouton I am" to "**First I am, second I was, Mouton does not change**."

The five First Growths: **Lafite**, **Latour**, **Margaux**, **Haut-Brion** and **Mouton**.

cards.q: How did the merchants decide the 1855 ranking?
options: By the price the wines fetched
By the size of the estate
By the age of the château
cards.explain: Price over many years was taken as the market's verdict on quality.

cards.q: Which château was promoted to First Growth in 1973?
cards.explain: The only promotion of a First Growth in the list's history. Pétrus and Cheval Blanc are on the Right Bank and not in the 1855 list.

cards.title: A tasting nobody expected to matter
cards.body:
On **24 May 1976**, the English wine merchant **Steven Spurrier** held a blind tasting in Paris. Nine French experts (top chefs, sommeliers and the head of the Appellation authority) tasted top **Bordeaux** and **Burgundy** against unknown wines from **California**.

Only one journalist came: **George Taber** of *Time* magazine.

cards.title: California wins
cards.body:
The winners were both Californian:

- **Reds**: **Stag's Leap Wine Cellars 1973** Cabernet Sauvignon, ahead of Mouton Rothschild and Haut-Brion.
- **Whites**: **Chateau Montelena 1973** Chardonnay, ahead of top white Burgundies such as Meursault-Charmes.

Taber's story, "Judgment of Paris", went around the world. One judge asked for her scorecard back.

cards.title: Why it changed everything
cards.body:
The result proved that great wine could be made **outside France**. Investment poured into **Napa**, then Oregon, Australia, Chile and beyond. French producers began investing abroad: Mouton Rothschild partnered with Robert Mondavi to create **Opus One** (1979).

French critics said red Bordeaux needs time. A **rematch in 2006**, thirty years on, again put California reds on top, led by **Ridge Monte Bello 1971**.

cards.q: Which red won the 1976 Judgment of Paris?
cards.explain: A Napa Cabernet from Stags Leap District beat the best of Bordeaux, judged blind by French experts.

cards.q: Which wine won the white flight?
cards.explain: Chateau Montelena, from Calistoga in northern Napa, beat top white Burgundies.

cards.q: The 1976 tasting was judged by Californian experts.
cards.explain: All nine judges were French, which is what made the result so shocking. The wines were tasted blind.

cards.q: The English merchant who organized the 1976 tasting was Steven ___.
cards.explain: Steven Spurrier ran a wine shop and school in Paris; George Taber was the Time journalist who reported it.

cards.title: Scientists in the cellar
cards.body:
After the war, **Émile Peynaud** in Bordeaux and others brought science to winemaking: clean cellars, control of **malolactic** conversion and **temperature-controlled** fermentation in steel. Wine became more reliable everywhere.

**Stainless steel** tanks with cooling jackets made fresh, fruity whites possible in warm places like Australia and Spain.

cards.title: Critics and the globe
cards.body:
**Robert Parker**'s praise of the **1982 Bordeaux** vintage, when others doubted it, made him the world's most powerful critic, and made ripe, rich styles fashionable in the 1990s.

**Flying winemakers** from Australia and Bordeaux consulted around the world; **Malbec** turned Argentina into a star; New Zealand's **Sauvignon Blanc** (Cloudy Bay, 1985) created a new classic.

cards.title: Today and tomorrow
cards.body:
The pendulum has swung back toward **freshness**, less new oak, organic and biodynamic farming, natural wines, and old local grapes rescued from extinction.

**Climate change** is moving the map: English sparkling wine now wins blind tastings, harvests in Champagne are weeks earlier than 30 years ago, and growers plant higher and cooler.

cards.q: Which vintage made Robert Parker famous?
cards.explain: Parker called 1982 a great vintage when others were cautious; he was right, and his influence soared.

cards.q: Climate change is making harvests earlier in regions such as Champagne.
cards.explain: Warmer seasons ripen grapes sooner; Champagne now picks weeks earlier than a generation ago, and cooler places such as England are rising.

units.title: Grape files
units.summary: Every Level 3 grape on one card: aromas, structure, origin and where it grows.

cards.title: Torrontés
cards.body:
Argentina's aromatic white: exuberantly floral like Muscat, but dry, with a bitter-citrus finish.

- **Aromas:** rose, orange blossom, peach, lemon zest, lychee.
- **Structure:** medium body, medium acidity.
- **Origin:** Argentina (a cross of Muscat of Alexandria and Criolla Chica).
- **Where it grows:** Salta, Argentina.
- **Food:** empanadas, spicy asian dishes, ceviche.

cards.title: Furmint
cards.body:
The great grape of Tokaj: searing acidity, smoky minerality and a strong affinity for noble rot.

- **Aromas:** lime, pear, quince, smoke, apricot, marmalade.
- **Structure:** medium body, high acidity.
- **Origin:** Hungary.
- **Where it grows:** Tokaj, Hungary, Somló.
- **Food:** foie gras, blue cheese, roast pork.

cards.title: Assyrtiko
cards.body:
Bone-dry, mineral and saline, keeping high acidity even in hot sun. Grown on Santorini in basket-shaped vines (kouloura).

- **Aromas:** lemon, grapefruit, saline, flint, wet stones, smoke.
- **Structure:** medium body, high acidity.
- **Origin:** Santorini, Greece.
- **Where it grows:** Santorini, Greece, Crete.
- **Food:** grilled fish, octopus, feta, fava dip.

cards.title: Melon de Bourgogne
cards.body:
The neutral grape behind Muscadet: light, lemony and briny, often given texture by ageing on its lees (sur lie).

- **Aromas:** lemon, green apple, saline, bread dough, wet stones.
- **Structure:** low body, medium-high acidity.
- **Origin:** Burgundy, France.
- **Also called:** Muscadet.
- **Where it grows:** Muscadet, Loire Valley.
- **Food:** oysters, moules marinière, fish and chips.

cards.title: Garganega
cards.body:
The grape of Soave: almond, lemon and white flowers, with a gentle, textured finish.

- **Aromas:** lemon, pear, almond, blossom, peach.
- **Structure:** medium-low body, medium acidity.
- **Origin:** Veneto, Italy.
- **Where it grows:** Veneto.
- **Food:** risotto, seafood pasta, mild cheeses.

cards.title: Glera
cards.body:
The grape of Prosecco: light, fresh, with pear, apple and white flowers.

- **Aromas:** pear, green apple, melon, blossom, acacia.
- **Structure:** low body, medium acidity.
- **Origin:** Veneto & Friuli, Italy.
- **Where it grows:** Veneto, Friuli.
- **Food:** aperitivo, prosciutto e melone, fried snacks.

cards.q: Which grape shows **rose, orange blossom, peach**?
cards.explain: Argentina's aromatic white: exuberantly floral like Muscat, but dry, with a bitter-citrus finish.

cards.q: Which grape shows **lime, pear, quince**?
cards.explain: The great grape of Tokaj: searing acidity, smoky minerality and a strong affinity for noble rot.

cards.q: Which grape shows **lemon, grapefruit, saline**?
cards.explain: Bone-dry, mineral and saline, keeping high acidity even in hot sun. Grown on Santorini in basket-shaped vines (kouloura).

cards.q: Match each grape to a place where it grows
cards.explain: Each grape is matched with one of its key regions from the cards above.

cards.title: Verdejo
cards.body:
Rueda's grape: herbaceous and citrusy with a slightly bitter almond finish.

- **Aromas:** lime, grapefruit, fennel, grass, almond, peach.
- **Structure:** medium-low body, medium-high acidity.
- **Origin:** Rueda, Spain.
- **Where it grows:** Rueda.
- **Food:** tapas, salads, white fish.

cards.title: Cortese
cards.body:
The grape of Gavi: delicate, crisp and lemony with a hint of almond.

- **Aromas:** lemon, green apple, almond, blossom.
- **Structure:** medium-low body, medium-high acidity.
- **Origin:** Piedmont, Italy.
- **Where it grows:** Gavi, Piedmont.
- **Food:** pesto, seafood, vitello tonnato.

cards.title: Verdicchio
cards.body:
Central Italy's finest white: high acidity, lemon, green almond and a gently bitter finish; ages surprisingly well.

- **Aromas:** lemon, green apple, almond, fennel, wet stones.
- **Structure:** medium body, medium-high acidity.
- **Origin:** Marche, Italy.
- **Where it grows:** Marche.
- **Food:** fish soup, fried seafood, pasta with clams.

cards.title: Fiano
cards.body:
Waxy, nutty and honeyed southern Italian white with good acidity. Best from Fiano di Avellino.

- **Aromas:** pear, peach, hazelnut, honey, acacia, smoke.
- **Structure:** medium body, medium acidity.
- **Origin:** Campania, Italy.
- **Where it grows:** Campania, Sicily.
- **Food:** seafood risotto, buffalo mozzarella, roast chicken.

cards.title: Greco
cards.body:
Greco di Tufo: firm, mineral and peachy with bright acidity and a light phenolic grip.

- **Aromas:** peach, lemon, almond, wet stones.
- **Structure:** medium body, medium-high acidity.
- **Origin:** Campania, Italy.
- **Where it grows:** Campania.
- **Food:** grilled fish, pizza bianca, seafood.

cards.title: Palomino
cards.body:
A neutral, low-acid grape that is the perfect base for Sherry, where flor and oxygen create the flavors.

- **Aromas:** almond, bread dough, saline, walnut.
- **Structure:** medium-low body, medium-low acidity.
- **Origin:** Andalucía, Spain.
- **Also called:** Palomino Fino, Listán.
- **Where it grows:** Jerez (Sherry).
- **Food:** jamón, olives, almonds, fried fish.

cards.q: Which grape shows **lime, grapefruit, fennel**?
cards.explain: Rueda's grape: herbaceous and citrusy with a slightly bitter almond finish.

cards.q: Which grape shows **lemon, green apple, almond**?
cards.explain: The grape of Gavi: delicate, crisp and lemony with a hint of almond.

cards.q: Which grape shows **lemon, green apple, almond**?
cards.explain: Central Italy's finest white: high acidity, lemon, green almond and a gently bitter finish; ages surprisingly well.

cards.q: Match each grape to a place where it grows
cards.explain: Each grape is matched with one of its key regions from the cards above.

lessons.title: Grape files: Pedro Ximénez, Marsanne & Roussanne…

cards.title: Pedro Ximénez
cards.body:
Sun-dried in Jerez and Montilla to make PX: black, syrupy and intensely raisined.

- **Aromas:** raisin, fig, prune, coffee, toffee, chocolate.
- **Structure:** high body, medium-low acidity.
- **Origin:** Andalucía, Spain.
- **Also called:** PX.
- **Where it grows:** Jerez (Sherry).
- **Food:** vanilla ice cream, blue cheese, chocolate desserts.

cards.title: Marsanne & Roussanne
cards.body:
Rhône partners: Marsanne brings body and nutty richness, Roussanne aroma and acidity. White Hermitage is their peak.

- **Aromas:** pear, peach, almond, honey, acacia, sweet spice.
- **Structure:** medium-high body, medium-low acidity.
- **Origin:** Northern Rhône, France.
- **Where it grows:** Hermitage, Crozes-Hermitage, Saint-Joseph, Châteauneuf-du-Pape, Rhône Valley.
- **Food:** roast poultry, lobster, rich fish dishes.

cards.title: Trebbiano
cards.body:
High-yielding and neutral with high acidity. Across Italy it makes simple whites; in France, as Ugni Blanc, it is distilled into Cognac and Armagnac.

- **Aromas:** lemon, green apple, pear, almond.
- **Structure:** medium-low body, medium-high acidity.
- **Origin:** Italy.
- **Also called:** Ugni Blanc.
- **Where it grows:** Abruzzo, Tuscany, Emilia-Romagna.
- **Food:** light pasta, salads.

cards.title: Vermentino
cards.body:
Herbal, citrusy and saline: the Mediterranean seaside white of Sardinia, Liguria, coastal Tuscany and Provence (as Rolle).

- **Aromas:** lime, grapefruit, green apple, fennel, saline, almond.
- **Structure:** medium-low body, medium acidity.
- **Origin:** Mediterranean coast.
- **Also called:** Rolle.
- **Where it grows:** Sardinia, Tuscany, Provence.
- **Food:** grilled fish, pesto, bouillabaisse.

cards.title: Pinot Blanc
cards.body:
Gentle, round and apple-scented, a softer cousin of Chardonnay. Widely used for Crémant d'Alsace.

- **Aromas:** red apple, pear, almond, blossom.
- **Structure:** medium-low body, medium acidity.
- **Origin:** Burgundy, France (a mutation of Pinot Noir).
- **Also called:** Pinot Bianco, Weissburgunder.
- **Where it grows:** Alsace, Trentino-Alto Adige, Baden, Pfalz.
- **Food:** quiche, light fish, tarte flambée.

cards.title: Macabeo
cards.body:
The main white grape of Rioja (as Viura) and a key Cava grape. Neutral and fresh, or nutty when aged in old oak.

- **Aromas:** lemon, green apple, blossom, almond, hazelnut.
- **Structure:** medium-low body, medium acidity.
- **Origin:** Spain.
- **Also called:** Viura.
- **Where it grows:** Rioja, Penedès.
- **Food:** tapas, seafood paella, croquetas.

cards.q: Which grape shows **raisin, fig, prune**?
cards.explain: Sun-dried in Jerez and Montilla to make PX: black, syrupy and intensely raisined.

cards.q: Which grape shows **pear, peach, almond**?
cards.explain: Rhône partners: Marsanne brings body and nutty richness, Roussanne aroma and acidity. White Hermitage is their peak.

cards.q: Which grape shows **lemon, green apple, pear**?
cards.explain: High-yielding and neutral with high acidity. Across Italy it makes simple whites; in France, as Ugni Blanc, it is distilled into Cognac and Armagnac.

cards.q: Match each grape to a place where it grows
cards.explain: Each grape is matched with one of its key regions from the cards above.

cards.title: Silvaner
cards.body:
Earthy, herbal and quietly mineral; at its best in Franken, bottled in the squat Bocksbeutel flask.

- **Aromas:** green apple, pear, grass, wet stones.
- **Structure:** medium-low body, medium acidity.
- **Origin:** Central Europe.
- **Where it grows:** Franken, Rheinhessen.
- **Food:** asparagus, freshwater fish, salads.

cards.title: Barbera
cards.body:
Deep in color but low in tannin, with mouthwatering acidity and juicy black cherry: Piedmont's everyday red.

- **Aromas:** black cherry, red plum, blackberry, dried herbs, vanilla.
- **Structure:** medium body, high acidity, medium-low tannin.
- **Origin:** Piedmont, Italy.
- **Where it grows:** Barbera d'Asti, Piedmont.
- **Food:** pizza, pasta with ragù, salami.

cards.title: Dolcetto
cards.body:
'Little sweet one', yet dry: soft acidity, grippy tannin, black cherry and bitter almond. Drunk young in Piedmont.

- **Aromas:** black cherry, black plum, liquorice, almond.
- **Structure:** medium body, medium-low acidity, medium tannin.
- **Origin:** Piedmont, Italy.
- **Where it grows:** Dogliani, Piedmont.
- **Food:** antipasti, salumi, pasta.

cards.title: Montepulciano
cards.body:
Deeply colored, plummy and soft: Montepulciano d'Abruzzo. Not to be confused with the Tuscan town of Montepulciano.

- **Aromas:** black cherry, black plum, dried herbs, liquorice.
- **Structure:** medium-high body, medium acidity, medium tannin.
- **Origin:** Abruzzo, Italy.
- **Where it grows:** Abruzzo, Marche.
- **Food:** lamb skewers, pizza, pasta with meat sauce.

cards.title: Aglianico
cards.body:
'The Barolo of the South': very high tannin and acidity, black fruit, smoke and leather. From volcanic soils in Taurasi and Vulture.

- **Aromas:** black cherry, black plum, smoke, leather, black pepper, earth.
- **Structure:** high body, high acidity, high tannin.
- **Origin:** Southern Italy (Campania, Basilicata).
- **Where it grows:** Campania, Basilicata.
- **Food:** braised meats, game, aged cheeses.

cards.title: Nero d'Avola
cards.body:
Sicily's star red: ripe black cherry and plum, medium acidity and soft-to-firm tannins.

- **Aromas:** black cherry, black plum, liquorice, sweet spice.
- **Structure:** medium-high body, medium acidity, medium tannin.
- **Origin:** Sicily, Italy.
- **Where it grows:** Sicily.
- **Food:** caponata, grilled meats, pasta alla norma.

cards.q: Which grape shows **green apple, pear, grass**?
cards.explain: Earthy, herbal and quietly mineral; at its best in Franken, bottled in the squat Bocksbeutel flask.

cards.q: Which grape shows **black cherry, red plum, blackberry**?
cards.explain: Deep in color but low in tannin, with mouthwatering acidity and juicy black cherry: Piedmont's everyday red.

cards.q: Which grape shows **black cherry, black plum, liquorice**?
cards.explain: 'Little sweet one', yet dry: soft acidity, grippy tannin, black cherry and bitter almond. Drunk young in Piedmont.

cards.q: Match each grape to a place where it grows
cards.explain: Each grape is matched with one of its key regions from the cards above.

cards.title: Corvina
cards.body:
The main grape of Valpolicella and Amarone: sour cherry and almond when fresh, dried cherry and chocolate when dried (appassimento).

- **Aromas:** red cherry, almond, dried herbs, kirsch, raisin, chocolate.
- **Structure:** medium body, medium-high acidity, medium-low tannin.
- **Origin:** Veneto, Italy.
- **Where it grows:** Veneto.
- **Food:** risotto all'amarone, polenta, aged parmigiano.

cards.title: Mourvèdre
cards.body:
Thick-skinned and sun-loving: blackberry, game, leather and herbs, with high tannin. The 'M' in GSM.

- **Aromas:** blackberry, black plum, game, leather, black pepper, garrigue.
- **Structure:** high body, medium acidity, high tannin.
- **Origin:** Spain.
- **Also called:** Monastrell, Mataro.
- **Where it grows:** Provence, Châteauneuf-du-Pape, Jumilla, Barossa Valley, McLaren Vale.
- **Food:** game, braised lamb, barbecue.

cards.title: Carignan
cards.body:
High in acidity, tannin and color. Once a bulk grape; old bush vines in Priorat, Languedoc and Chile now make serious wines.

- **Aromas:** red cherry, blackberry, dried herbs, liquorice, earth.
- **Structure:** medium-high body, medium-high acidity, medium-high tannin.
- **Origin:** Aragón, Spain.
- **Also called:** Cariñena, Mazuelo, Samsó.
- **Where it grows:** Languedoc-Roussillon, Priorat, Rioja, Maule, Baalbek.
- **Food:** cassoulet, sausages, stews.

cards.title: Cinsault
cards.body:
Light, fragrant and low in tannin: strawberry and flowers. Important in rosé and as a parent of Pinotage.

- **Aromas:** strawberry, raspberry, red cherry, blossom.
- **Structure:** medium-low body, medium acidity, low tannin.
- **Origin:** Southern France.
- **Where it grows:** Provence, Languedoc-Roussillon, Itata & Bío Bío, Swartland, Bekaa Valley, Baalbek.
- **Food:** mezze, grilled fish, rosé-friendly salads.

cards.title: Touriga Nacional
cards.body:
Portugal's finest black grape: deep, floral and concentrated, with violet, blackberry and firm tannin. A key Port grape.

- **Aromas:** blackberry, black plum, violet, liquorice, dried herbs.
- **Structure:** high body, medium-high acidity, high tannin.
- **Origin:** Portugal (Dão & Douro).
- **Where it grows:** Douro, Dão, Alentejo.
- **Food:** roast kid, hard cheese, chocolate (port).

cards.title: Petit Verdot
cards.body:
A late-ripening Bordeaux blending grape: inky color, violet and spice, firm tannins. Used in small amounts for structure.

- **Aromas:** blackberry, violet, sweet spice, dried herbs.
- **Structure:** high body, medium-high acidity, high tannin.
- **Origin:** Bordeaux, France.
- **Where it grows:** Bordeaux, Napa Valley.
- **Food:** grilled red meat, hard cheeses.

cards.q: Which grape shows **red cherry, almond, dried herbs**?
cards.explain: The main grape of Valpolicella and Amarone: sour cherry and almond when fresh, dried cherry and chocolate when dried (appassimento).

cards.q: Which grape shows **blackberry, black plum, game**?
cards.explain: Thick-skinned and sun-loving: blackberry, game, leather and herbs, with high tannin. The 'M' in GSM.

cards.q: Which grape shows **red cherry, blackberry, dried herbs**?
cards.explain: High in acidity, tannin and color. Once a bulk grape; old bush vines in Priorat, Languedoc and Chile now make serious wines.

cards.q: Match each grape to a place where it grows
cards.explain: Each grape is matched with one of its key regions from the cards above.

cards.title: Mencía
cards.body:
Fragrant, fresh and medium-bodied: red cherry, blackberry and herbs from steep slate slopes in Bierzo.

- **Aromas:** red cherry, blackberry, violet, dried herbs, black pepper.
- **Structure:** medium body, medium-high acidity, medium tannin.
- **Origin:** North-west Spain.
- **Also called:** Jaen.
- **Where it grows:** Bierzo, Dão.
- **Food:** roast pork, grilled vegetables, octopus.

cards.title: Blaufränkisch
cards.body:
Austria's serious red: dark cherry, pepper and mineral, with bright acidity and firm tannin.

- **Aromas:** black cherry, blackberry, black pepper, wet stones, dried herbs.
- **Structure:** medium body, medium-high acidity, medium-high tannin.
- **Origin:** Central Europe.
- **Also called:** Lemberger, Kékfrankos.
- **Where it grows:** Mittelburgenland, Leithaberg, Neusiedlersee, Eger, Württemberg.
- **Food:** roast duck, goulash, game.

cards.title: Zweigelt
cards.body:
Austria's most planted red: juicy red cherry, soft tannins and fresh acidity.

- **Aromas:** red cherry, raspberry, black pepper.
- **Structure:** medium-low body, medium acidity, medium-low tannin.
- **Origin:** Austria (St. Laurent × Blaufränkisch, 1922).
- **Where it grows:** Neusiedlersee, Carnuntum, Austria.
- **Food:** schnitzel, charcuterie, pizza.

cards.title: Xinomavro
cards.body:
'Acid-black': pale, high in acidity and tannin, with tomato, olive and red fruit. Often compared to Nebbiolo.

- **Aromas:** red cherry, tomato leaf, dried herbs, earth, leather.
- **Structure:** medium body, high acidity, high tannin.
- **Origin:** Northern Greece.
- **Where it grows:** Naoussa, Amyndeo.
- **Food:** moussaka, lamb, stuffed tomatoes.

cards.title: Agiorgitiko
cards.body:
'St George's grape': soft, plummy and spicy, from medium to full bodied depending on altitude.

- **Aromas:** red plum, red cherry, sweet spice, nutmeg.
- **Structure:** medium body, medium acidity, medium tannin.
- **Origin:** Nemea, Greece.
- **Where it grows:** Nemea.
- **Food:** souvlaki, tomato-based dishes, lamb.

cards.title: Tannat
cards.body:
As its name suggests, fiercely tannic: black fruit, spice and smoke. Madiran's grape and Uruguay's flagship.

- **Aromas:** blackberry, black plum, liquorice, smoke, sweet spice.
- **Structure:** high body, medium-high acidity, high tannin.
- **Origin:** South West France (Madiran).
- **Where it grows:** South West France.
- **Food:** cassoulet, duck confit, grilled steak.

cards.q: Which grape shows **red cherry, blackberry, violet**?
cards.explain: Fragrant, fresh and medium-bodied: red cherry, blackberry and herbs from steep slate slopes in Bierzo.

cards.q: Which grape shows **black cherry, blackberry, black pepper**?
cards.explain: Austria's serious red: dark cherry, pepper and mineral, with bright acidity and firm tannin.

cards.q: Which grape shows **red cherry, raspberry, black pepper**?
cards.explain: Austria's most planted red: juicy red cherry, soft tannins and fresh acidity.

cards.q: Match each grape to a place where it grows
cards.explain: Each grape is matched with one of its key regions from the cards above.

cards.title: Negroamaro
cards.body:
'Black-bitter': dark plum, earth and a bitter twist, from the heel of Italy (Salice Salentino).

- **Aromas:** black plum, black cherry, earth, dried herbs, liquorice.
- **Structure:** medium-high body, medium acidity, medium tannin.
- **Origin:** Puglia, Italy.
- **Where it grows:** Puglia.
- **Food:** orecchiette with sausage, grilled meats.

cards.title: Baga
cards.body:
High-acid, high-tannin grape of Bairrada, for age-worthy reds and fine traditional-method sparkling wines.

- **Aromas:** red cherry, cranberry, tobacco, smoke, earth.
- **Structure:** medium body, high acidity, high tannin.
- **Origin:** Bairrada, Portugal.
- **Where it grows:** Bairrada.
- **Food:** roast suckling pig (leitão).

cards.title: Meunier
cards.body:
Champagne's third grape: buds late and ripens early, avoiding frost. Adds fruity roundness to young Champagne.

- **Aromas:** red apple, red cherry, strawberry, bread.
- **Structure:** medium-low body, medium-high acidity, low tannin.
- **Origin:** France (a mutation of Pinot Noir).
- **Also called:** Pinot Meunier, Schwarzriesling.
- **Where it grows:** Champagne, Vallée de la Marne.
- **Food:** aperitif, charcuterie, fried chicken.

cards.title: Obaideh
cards.body:
Lebanon's best-known native white grape: soft, round and gently aromatic, often compared to Chardonnay. Used in dry whites and to distil arak.

- **Aromas:** lemon, pear, melon, almond, honeysuckle.
- **Structure:** medium body, medium-low acidity.
- **Origin:** Lebanon.
- **Where it grows:** Mount Lebanon, Bekaa Valley.
- **Food:** fattoush, grilled halloumi, fish with tahini.

cards.title: Merwah
cards.body:
Ancient mountain grape from Mount Lebanon, often linked to Sémillon. Waxy texture, citrus and a light nutty finish; a key white in Château Musar's white.

- **Aromas:** lemon, green apple, honey, hazelnut.
- **Structure:** medium body, medium acidity.
- **Origin:** Lebanon.
- **Where it grows:** Mount Lebanon.
- **Food:** mezze, roast chicken, kibbeh.

cards.q: Which grape shows **black plum, black cherry, earth**?
cards.explain: 'Black-bitter': dark plum, earth and a bitter twist, from the heel of Italy (Salice Salentino).

cards.q: Which grape shows **red cherry, cranberry, tobacco**?
cards.explain: High-acid, high-tannin grape of Bairrada, for age-worthy reds and fine traditional-method sparkling wines.

cards.q: Which grape shows **red apple, red cherry, strawberry**?
cards.explain: Champagne's third grape: buds late and ripens early, avoiding frost. Adds fruity roundness to young Champagne.

cards.q: Match each grape to a place where it grows
cards.explain: Each grape is matched with one of its key regions from the cards above.

units.title: Appellations: France
units.summary: Every French appellation in Level 3, on its map.

cards.title: Jura
cards.body:
Quirky mountain region known for Vin Jaune, a Savagnin wine aged under a flor-like yeast for over six years, plus Vin de Paille and Crémant du Jura.

- **Where:** France.
- **Grapes:** Chardonnay, Pinot Noir.

cards.title: Savoie
cards.body:
Alpine vineyards making crisp, light whites (Jacquère, Altesse) and reds (Mondeuse) perfect with fondue.

- **Where:** France.
- **Grapes:** Gamay, Chardonnay.

cards.title: South West France
cards.body:
A patchwork of local grapes and styles: Cahors (Malbec), Madiran (Tannat), Bergerac (Bordeaux varieties) and Jurançon (sweet and dry whites).

- **Where:** France.
- **Grapes:** Malbec, Tannat, Merlot, Sémillon.

cards.title: Médoc
cards.body:
The northern, lower-lying part of the Left Bank peninsula. More clay and Merlot than the Haut-Médoc; good-value reds and many Crus Bourgeois.

- **Where:** Bordeaux, France.
- **Grapes:** Cabernet Sauvignon, Merlot.

cards.title: Haut-Médoc
cards.body:
The heart of the Left Bank, home to four famous communes and most of the 1855 classified growths.

- **Where:** Bordeaux, France.
- **Grapes:** Cabernet Sauvignon, Merlot, Cabernet Franc, Petit Verdot.
- **Climate:** Gravel ridges near the estuary drain well and store heat, helping late-ripening Cabernet.

cards.title: Saint-Estèphe
cards.body:
The northernmost famous commune: more clay, firmer and more rustic wines with high acidity and tannin. Cos d'Estournel and Montrose are leaders.

- **Where:** Bordeaux, France.
- **Grapes:** Cabernet Sauvignon, Merlot.

cards.title: Pauillac
cards.body:
Home of three First Growths (Lafite, Latour, Mouton). Powerful, long-lived Cabernet with blackcurrant, cedar and pencil shavings.

- **Where:** Bordeaux, France.
- **Grapes:** Cabernet Sauvignon, Merlot.

cards.title: Saint-Julien
cards.body:
Small and consistent: balanced, elegant, classic claret between Pauillac and Margaux. Léoville Las Cases, Ducru-Beaucaillou.

- **Where:** Bordeaux, France.
- **Grapes:** Cabernet Sauvignon, Merlot.

cards.q: Which grape is most associated with **Jura**?
cards.explain: Jura: Quirky mountain region known for Vin Jaune, a Savagnin wine aged under a flor-like yeast for over six years, plus Vin de Paille and Crémant du Jura.

cards.q: Which grape is most associated with **Savoie**?
cards.explain: Savoie: Alpine vineyards making crisp, light whites (Jacquère, Altesse) and reds (Mondeuse) perfect with fondue.

cards.q: Match each region to its signature grape
cards.explain: Each region is matched with a grape it is known for, as in the cards above.

cards.title: Margaux
cards.body:
Thin gravel soils give the most perfumed, silky wines of the Médoc. Château Margaux is its First Growth.

- **Where:** Bordeaux, France.
- **Grapes:** Cabernet Sauvignon, Merlot.

cards.title: Pessac-Léognan
cards.body:
The northern Graves, on Bordeaux's doorstep. Smoky, earthy reds and the best oaked dry whites. Home of First Growth Haut-Brion.

- **Where:** Bordeaux, France.
- **Grapes:** Cabernet Sauvignon, Merlot, Sauvignon Blanc, Sémillon.

cards.title: Graves
cards.body:
Named after its gravel soils, south of the city along the Garonne. Red and dry white wines.

- **Where:** Bordeaux, France.
- **Grapes:** Cabernet Sauvignon, Merlot, Sauvignon Blanc, Sémillon.

cards.title: Entre-Deux-Mers
cards.body:
'Between two seas': the land between the Garonne and Dordogne rivers. Fresh dry whites and plenty of Bordeaux AOC red.

- **Where:** Bordeaux, France.
- **Grapes:** Sauvignon Blanc, Sémillon, Merlot.

cards.title: Fronsac
cards.body:
Hilly Right Bank appellation west of Libourne: sturdy, value Merlot.

- **Where:** Bordeaux, France.
- **Grapes:** Merlot, Cabernet Franc.

cards.title: Castillon
cards.body:
Castillon Côtes de Bordeaux: limestone slopes east of Saint-Émilion, a source of value Merlot.

- **Where:** Bordeaux, France.
- **Grapes:** Merlot, Cabernet Franc.

cards.title: Côtes de Bourg
cards.body:
Right bank of the Gironde opposite Margaux: robust, good-value Merlot-based reds.

- **Where:** Bordeaux, France.
- **Grapes:** Merlot.

cards.title: Blaye
cards.body:
Blaye Côtes de Bordeaux: rolling hills north of Bourg, fruity reds and some whites.

- **Where:** Bordeaux, France.
- **Grapes:** Merlot, Sauvignon Blanc.

cards.q: Which grape is most associated with **Margaux**?
cards.explain: Margaux: Thin gravel soils give the most perfumed, silky wines of the Médoc. Château Margaux is its First Growth.

cards.q: Which grape is most associated with **Pessac-Léognan**?
cards.explain: Pessac-Léognan: The northern Graves, on Bordeaux's doorstep. Smoky, earthy reds and the best oaked dry whites. Home of First Growth Haut-Brion.

cards.q: Match each region to its signature grape
cards.explain: Each region is matched with a grape it is known for, as in the cards above.

cards.title: Côte Chalonnaise
cards.body:
Value Burgundy from villages such as Mercurey, Givry, Rully and Montagny; also Bouzeron (Aligoté).

- **Where:** Burgundy, France.
- **Grapes:** Pinot Noir, Chardonnay.

cards.title: Saint-Joseph
cards.body:
A long strip on the west bank: fresh, peppery Syrah and some white Marsanne-Roussanne.

- **Where:** Rhône Valley, France.
- **Grapes:** Syrah, Marsanne & Roussanne.

cards.title: Cornas
cards.body:
100% Syrah from a warm granite amphitheater: dark, tannic and wild.

- **Where:** Rhône Valley, France.
- **Grapes:** Syrah.

cards.title: Gigondas
cards.body:
Grenache-based reds beneath the jagged Dentelles de Montmirail: robust and spicy.

- **Where:** Rhône Valley, France.
- **Grapes:** Grenache, Syrah, Mourvèdre.

cards.title: Vacqueyras
cards.body:
Gigondas' neighbor: generous, value Grenache blends.

- **Where:** Rhône Valley, France.
- **Grapes:** Grenache, Syrah.

cards.title: Anjou
cards.body:
Dry and sweet Chenin Blanc (Coteaux du Layon, Quarts de Chaume, Bonnezeaux), reds and the famous off-dry Rosé d'Anjou.

- **Where:** Loire Valley, France.
- **Grapes:** Chenin Blanc, Cabernet Franc.

cards.title: Savennières
cards.body:
Intense, mineral, long-lived dry Chenin Blanc from steep schist slopes.

- **Where:** Loire Valley, France.
- **Grapes:** Chenin Blanc.

cards.title: Saumur
cards.body:
Tuffeau limestone country: Saumur-Champigny reds, dry Chenin and lots of traditional-method sparkling wine.

cards.title: Lebanon
cards.body:
One of the oldest wine cultures on earth, from Phoenician traders to the Temple of Bacchus at Baalbek. Today it is known for structured red blends from the high Bekaa Valley.

- **Grapes:** Cinsault, Cabernet Sauvignon, Syrah, Carignan, Obaideh.
- **Climate:** Mediterranean, but the vineyards sit high: the Bekaa Valley floor is around 1,000 m, giving hot days, cold nights and a long, dry growing season.
- **Quality system:** No formal appellation system yet; wines are labeled by producer, region and grape.
- Château Musar (founded 1930) made Lebanon famous, with long-lived reds released years after the vintage.
- Château Ksara, founded by Jesuits in 1857, keeps its wine in Roman-era limestone caves.

cards.title: Bekaa Valley
cards.body:
The heart of Lebanese wine, from Zahlé south to the West Bekaa (Kefraya, Ammiq): home to Ksara and many leading estates. Ripe, spicy red blends with fresh acidity from the altitude.

- **Where:** Lebanon.
- **Grapes:** Cabernet Sauvignon, Cinsault, Syrah.
- **Climate:** High plateau (about 1,000 m): sunny, dry summers with cool nights.

cards.title: Baalbek
cards.body:
The northern Bekaa, near the Roman Temple of Bacchus. Drier and higher, with old bush vines and a growing number of new estates.

- **Where:** Lebanon.
- **Grapes:** Cinsault, Carignan.

cards.title: Mount Lebanon
cards.body:

- **Where:** Lebanon.
- **Grapes:** Obaideh, Merwah, Cinsault.

units.title: Words to know
units.summary: The vocabulary and styles the exams use, in short lists.

cards.title: Words to know
cards.body:
- **Chaptalization:** Adding sugar to the must to increase final alcohol; allowed in some cool regions.
- **Acidification:** Adding acid to the must in hot regions where grapes lack it.
- **Fining:** Adding an agent (bentonite, egg white) to remove haze-causing particles.
- **Filtration:** Passing wine through a filter to remove particles and microbes.
- **Bâtonnage:** Stirring the lees in a barrel to add creamy texture.
- **Whole-bunch fermentation:** Fermenting grapes with stems attached, for fragrance and structure.
- **Grey rot:** The harmful form of Botrytis that ruins grapes in wet conditions.
- **Rootstock:** The root part of a grafted vine, often American, chosen for pest resistance or vigor.

cards.q: What does **Bâtonnage** mean?
options: Port from a declared exceptional year, bottled young to age for decades.
Drying grapes after harvest to concentrate them, as for Amarone.
Stirring the lees in a barrel to add creamy texture.
cards.explain: Bâtonnage: Stirring the lees in a barrel to add creamy texture.

cards.q: What does **Grey rot** mean?
options: Supplying water to vines artificially; banned or restricted in many European regions.
A fungal disease that thrives in warm, wet weather, attacking leaves and fruit.
The harmful form of Botrytis that ruins grapes in wet conditions.
Botrytized grapes used to make sweet Tokaji in Hungary.
cards.explain: Grey rot: The harmful form of Botrytis that ruins grapes in wet conditions.

cards.title: Words to know
cards.body:
- **Downy mildew:** A fungal disease that thrives in warm, wet weather, attacking leaves and fruit.
- **Powdery mildew:** A fungal disease that coats green parts of the vine in grey powder, even in dry weather.
- **Canopy:** The vine's shoots and leaves above ground.
- **Canopy management:** Positioning shoots and leaves to control sunlight on the grapes and airflow.
- **Guyot:** A cane-pruned training system with one or two canes tied along a wire.
- **Bush vine:** A free-standing, head-trained vine, common in hot, dry regions (gobelet).
- **VSP:** Vertical shoot positioning: shoots trained upwards between wires.
- **Yield:** The amount of grapes or wine produced per hectare.
